<a id="smtcore-08-f2"></a>
#### smtcore_08-F2: theory_seq reads arithmetic values and bounds from `theory_inf_arith`, which the C++ `get_th_arith` casts reject

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/smt_theory_seq_axioms.go:233-241` (`(*SMTTheorySeq).arith`), used by `getArithValue` (245), `lowerBound` (278), `upperBound` (298) and through them `getNumValue`, `getLengthValue`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_seq.cpp:3469-3487` (`get_th_arith<T>`, `get_arith_value`), 3506-3530 (`lower_bound`, `upper_bound`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
template <class T> static T* get_th_arith(context& ctx, theory_id afid, expr* e) {
    theory* th = ctx.get_theory(afid);
    if (th && ctx.e_internalized(e)) return dynamic_cast<T*>(th);
    else return nullptr;
}
static bool get_arith_value(...) {
    theory_mi_arith* tha = get_th_arith<theory_mi_arith>(ctx, afid, e);
    if (tha) return tha->get_value(ctx.get_enode(e), v);
    theory_i_arith* thi = get_th_arith<theory_i_arith>(ctx, afid, e);
    if (thi) return thi->get_value(ctx.get_enode(e), v);
    return false;
}
```
Only `theory_arith<mi_ext>` and `theory_arith<i_ext>` are accepted. With `theory_inf_arith` (`theory_arith<inf_ext>`, registered for `smt.arith.solver=5` at `smt_setup.cpp:745,803`, and by opt's farkas engine) both casts fail, so `get_num_value`, `get_length`, `lower_bound` and `upper_bound` all return false.

**Go behavior.** All three C++ instantiations are the one Go type `*SMTTheoryArith` (flags `integerExt`, `infExt`), and the helper only tests the Go type:
```go
a, ok := t.state.Theory(fid).(*SMTTheoryArith)
if !ok || !t.eInternalized(e) {
    return nil
}
return a
```
so an `infExt` theory (created by `NewSMTTheoryInfArith` in `smt_setup_basic_arithmetic.go:39`, `smt_setup_mixed_arithmetic.go:15`) is used as if it were `theory_mi_arith`.

**Impact.** String/sequence problems run with `smt.arith.solver=5` (or under the optimizer's `optsmt_engine=farkas`): g3's theory_seq sees lengths and bounds (fixed_length, branch_unit_variable, reduce_length_eq, ...) that the C++ cannot see. Different search, different models, and g3 terminates on inputs where the C++ does not.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed.
```
(set-option :smt.arith.solver 5)
(declare-const s String)
(declare-const t String)
(assert (= (str.len s) 2))
(assert (= (str.len t) 1))
(assert (not (= (str.at s 0) t)))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```
`build/z3`: `sat`, `s = "\x10\x00"`, `t = "\x00"` (`-st`: `seq-length-coherence 4`, no `seq-fixed-length`, final-checks 6).
`g3`: `sat`, `s = "\x00\x00"`, `t = "\x02"` (`-st`: `seq-fixed-length 1`, final-checks 3).
Without the `set-option` line both binaries print the g3 output and identical statistics (except `rlimit-count`).
Second input, same option on the command line: `(declare-const s String)(declare-const t String)(assert (= (str.++ s "a") (str.++ "a" t)))(assert (= (str.len s) 2))(check-sat)` — `g3 smt.arith.solver=5` prints `sat`; `build/z3 smt.arith.solver=5` does not terminate within 20 s.

**Fix.** In `arith`, return nil for the inf variant:
```go
a, ok := t.state.Theory(fid).(*SMTTheoryArith)
if !ok || a.infExt || !t.eInternalized(e) {
    return nil
}
```
(`!integerExt && !infExt` is `theory_mi_arith`, `integerExt` is `theory_i_arith`.) `getArithValue`, `lowerBound` and `upperBound` need no change; they all go through `arith`.

**Regression test.** SMT-LIB vector `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/seq_inf_arith_no_length_values.smt2` with the first input above; `scriptResults` entry `"sat\n(model \n  (define-fun s () String\n    \"\\x10\\x00\")\n  (define-fun t () String\n    \"\\x00\")\n)\n"`; check with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`. A unit test can go in `pkg/smtcore/theory_seq_empty_test.go` next to `TestSMTSequenceTheoryFixedLengthDecomposition`, which builds its solver with `smtModelGeneratorFixture(t)` and `NewSMTSolver(m, nil, "ALL", SMTSolverConfig{...})` and asserts `2 <= (str.len x) <= 2`: the same set-up with `smt.arith.solver=5` in the solver parameters must leave the sequence theory's `stats.fixedLength` at 0 after `CheckSat` (it becomes 1 today). I did not check which test helper sets that parameter, so the SMT-LIB vector is the simpler lock-in.

<a id="smtcore-08-f3"></a>
#### smtcore_08-F3: `PropagateCore` drops both cancellation / resource-limit checks of `context::propagate`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/smt_theory_propagation.go:365-446` (`(*SMTInternalizerState).PropagateCore`)
- C++: `src/smt/smt_context.cpp:1729-1770` (`context::propagate`), lines 1739-1742 and 1760-1763

**C++ behavior.** Every round of the propagation loop checks twice, and rolls `m_qhead` back when it stops:
```cpp
unsigned qhead = m_qhead;
if (!bcp()) return false;
if (!propagate_th_case_split(qhead)) return false;
if (get_cancel_flag()) { m_qhead = qhead; return true; }
...
m_qmanager->propagate();
if (inconsistent()) return false;
if (resource_limits_exceeded()) { m_qhead = qhead; return true; }
if (!can_propagate()) { ... return true; }
```
`get_cancel_flag()` is `!m_manager.limit().inc()` (`smt_context.cpp:132`), so each round also adds 2 to the rlimit counter; `resource_limits_exceeded()` additionally tests the search timeout and records `m_last_search_failure` (TIMEOUT / CANCELED / MEMOUT).

**Go behavior.** `PropagateCore` goes from `propagateTheoryCaseSplits` straight to relevancy, and from the quantifier manager straight to `canPropagate()`:
```go
s.relevancyBatch.end = len(s.assignedLiterals)
s.relevancyBatch.caseSplitsDone = true
}
if err = s.propagateRelevancyAssignments(); err != nil {
...
if s.inconsistent { return false, nil }
if !s.canPropagate() { return true, nil }
```
There is no `Canceled()` call, no `s.resourceLimitsExceeded()` call (the hook exists, `smt_internalizer_state.go:153`, and is only used by the quantifier manager) and no restore of `propagationHead`.

**Impact.** (a) A cancel, timeout or exhausted rlimit is not noticed until the whole propagation fixpoint (theory propagation, E-matching instantiation rounds) is done; the C++ leaves after the current round. (b) The `rlimit-count` statistic is lower than the C++ by 2 per propagation round, so a given `rlimit=N` trips at a different point. (c) `m_qhead` is not rolled back on the early exit. The same kind of check inside `context::bcp` (`smt_context.cpp:333`, one `limit().inc()` per propagated literal) is also missing from `Propagate()` in `smt_boolean_propagation.go:257`, outside this shard; the two together are consistent with the lower g3 `rlimit-count` on every input I ran.

**Reproduction.** Indirect only. `(declare-fun f (Int) Int)(declare-const x Int)(assert (= (f x) 3))(check-sat)` with `-st`: all statistics equal, `rlimit-count` 72 (g3) vs 75 (z3), which is what one BCP literal (+1) and one propagate round (+2) would give. On every other input in this audit g3's count is likewise lower (240 vs 252, 334 vs 344, 56902 vs 104693). A direct `rlimit=N` comparison is not possible today because g3 ignores `rlimit` (see "Needs verification").

**Fix.** In `PropagateCore`:
1. Remember the round's `qhead` in a value that is not advanced: add a field `qhead int` to `smtRelevancyAssignmentBatch`, set it to `caseSplitHead` where the batch is created (line 380), and at the top of each loop iteration copy it to a local `qhead := s.relevancyBatch.qhead` after the batch exists (`relevancyBatch.head` cannot be used, `propagateRelevancyAssignments` advances it, and the batch is reset at line 399).
2. Inside the `if !s.relevancyBatch.caseSplitsDone { ... }` block, after `caseSplitsDone = true`, add
```go
if canceled, err := s.manager.Canceled(); err != nil {
    return false, err
} else if canceled {
    s.propagationHead = qhead // m_qhead = qhead
    s.relevancyBatch = smtRelevancyAssignmentBatch{}
    return true, nil
}
```
3. After the quantifier-manager step and its `if s.inconsistent { return false, nil }`, before `canPropagate()`, add
```go
if s.resourceLimitsExceeded != nil {
    exceeded, err := s.resourceLimitsExceeded()
    if err != nil { return false, err }
    if exceeded { s.propagationHead = qhead; return true, nil }
}
```
When `resourceLimitsExceeded` is nil (stand-alone fixtures) fall back to `s.manager.Canceled()` so the increment still happens. The sibling per-literal check in `Propagate()` (bcp) belongs to `smt_boolean_propagation.go`.

**Regression test.** New file `pkg/smtcore/smt_theory_propagation_cancel_test.go`, `TestSMTPropagateCoreChecksCancelLikeContextPropagate`. Fixture as in `TestSMTInternalizerGateProofReservedConstants`: `m := astTestManager(t)`, `_, _, s := smtInternalizerFixture(t, m, nil)`, `a := smtRelevancyBool(t, m, "prop-cancel-a")`, `s.Internalize(a, true)`, `lit, _ := s.Literal(a)`, `s.AssignLiteral(lit, NewSMTBooleanAxiom())`. Register a recording theory first (`theory := &smtInternalizerTestTheory{SMTTheoryBase: base}; s.RegisterTheory(theory)`, as `smtClosestVariableFixture` does). Part 1: `head := s.propagationHead; m.Limit.Cancel(); ok, err := s.PropagateCore()`; expect `ok == true`, `err == nil`, `s.propagationHead == head`, and `theory.propagationCalled == false`. Part 2: `m.Limit.ResetCancel(); before := m.Limit.Count(); s.PropagateCore()`; expect `m.Limit.Count()-before` to be exactly 2 per propagation round (2 if the single Boolean constant needs one round; plus 1 per BCP literal once the bcp check is ported). Today the difference is 0. Once `rlimit` works from the command line, `-st` on the one-assertion input above must report `rlimit-count 75`.

<a id="smtcore-08-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_08-F4: `smtArithRatBitsize` counts the denominator of integers (`rational::bitsize` does not)

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/smt_theory_arith_nl.go:273-275` (`smtArithRatBitsize`), used at 290 and 295 (`mulBoundOf`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_arith_nl.h:346-347` (`theory_arith<Ext>::mul_bound_of`), `src/util/mpq.h:793`, `src/util/mpz.cpp:1863-1868`

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
get_manager().limit().inc((target.is_lower_open() || target.minus_infinity()) ? 1 : target.get_lower_value().bitsize());
// mpq.h
unsigned bitsize(mpq const & a) { return is_int(a) ? bitsize(a.m_num) : bitsize(a.m_num) + bitsize(a.m_den); }
// mpz.cpp
if (is_nonneg(a)) return log2(a) + 1; else return mlog2(a) + 1;   // log2(0) == 0
```
So an integer `n != 0` costs `BitLen(|n|)`, zero costs 1, and only non-integers add the denominator.

**Go behavior.**
```go
func smtArithRatBitsize(q *big.Rat) uint {
	return uint(q.Num().BitLen() + q.Denom().BitLen())
}
```
For a non-zero integer this is `BitLen(|n|) + 1` (the denominator 1 has bit length 1). Zero and non-integers happen to agree.

**Impact.** Non-linear arithmetic only: each closed integer endpoint of the running product in `mul_bound_of` adds one resource unit too many, so `rlimit-count` drifts and an rlimit trips earlier than in the C++. No effect on answers.

**Reproduction.** not attempted: `rlimit-count` already differs for the reasons in F3, so the off-by-one cannot be isolated with the binaries.

**Fix.**
```go
func smtArithRatBitsize(q *big.Rat) uint {
	n := uint(q.Num().BitLen())
	if n == 0 {
		n = 1 // mpz bitsize(0) = log2(0) + 1
	}
	if q.IsInt() {
		return n
	}
	return n + uint(q.Denom().BitLen())
}
```

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/smt_theory_arith_ratops_test.go` with `TestSMTArithRatBitsizeMatchesMpq`, a table test on `big.NewRat`: `0/1 -> 1`, `1/1 -> 1`, `5/1 -> 3`, `-5/1 -> 3`, `255/1 -> 8`, `256/1 -> 9`, `1/2 -> 3`, `-1/3 -> 3`, `7/4 -> 6`.

<a id="smtcore-09-f1"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F1: array InternalizeTerm never attaches a theory var to a non-array-op argument (ite array), so axioms are lost and the answer is wrong

- Severity: critical
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_array.go:213-230` (`SMTArrayTheory.InternalizeTerm`); consequence in `pkg/smtcore/theory_array_parents.go:454-461` (`Relevant`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_array.cpp:260-288` (`theory_array::internalize_term`), `src/smt/theory_array_full.cpp:262-289`

**C++ behavior.** After `internalize_term_core(n)`, it does `enode* arg0 = ctx.get_enode(n->get_arg(0)); if (!is_attached_to_var(arg0)) mk_var(arg0);` for select and store. The full theory does the same for every map argument and for the default argument.

**Go behavior.** Go attaches a var only to `node` (the select/store itself). When arg0 is an array-sorted `ite`, `internalizeTermITE` creates its enode with no array var. Later `Relevant` reads `node.arguments[0].TheoryVar(...) == -1` and returns `ast.ErrASTDomain`. The relevancy propagator aborts on that error. In the default solver path the error disappears (it surfaces nowhere), so parent-select registration and axiom 2 are never added.

**Impact.** Wrong `sat` on unsat inputs (soundness). `default` over an ite errors out ("array default axiom: g3: AST source precondition"), giving `unknown` or an error where z3 says `sat`.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed:
```
(declare-const a (Array Int Int))
(declare-const b (Array Int Int))
(declare-const c Bool)
(declare-const i Int)
(declare-const j Int)
(declare-const v Int)
(assert (not (= (select (ite c (store a i v) b) j) (select a j))))
(assert (not (= i j)))
(assert (not (= (select b j) (select (ite c (store a i v) b) j))))
(check-sat)
```
z3: `unsat`; g3: `sat`. Also `(assert (= (default (ite c a b)) 3)) (check-sat)`: z3 `sat`, g3 `unknown` (reason: array default axiom precondition).

**Fix.** In `InternalizeTerm`, right after attaching `node`, attach a var to each argument enode that is not attached yet, following C++: `arguments[:1]` for store/select/default, and all arguments for map. Note that `CreateVariable` gives a var to any enode.
```go
var attach []*SMTEnode
switch op {
case ast.ASTArrayOpStore, ast.ASTArrayOpSelect, ast.ASTArrayOpDefault:
    attach = node.arguments[:1]
case ast.ASTArrayOpMap:
    attach = node.arguments
}
for _, arg := range attach {
    if !t.IsAttachedToVariable(arg) {
        if _, err = t.CreateVariable(arg); err != nil { return false, err }
    }
}
```
(C++ attaches the args in full::internalize_term before mk_var(node) for map/default. With this placement the overlay build gave traces identical to z3 on all vectors I tested.) Separately, a theory `Relevant` error must not vanish. Find where `CheckSat` drops it (it is not reported to the user) and make the error reach the user.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/array_ite_select_axiom2.smt2` (the input above), `scriptResults` entry `"unsat\n"`. Add `array_default_over_ite.smt2` (`(declare-const a (Array Int Int)) (declare-const b (Array Int Int)) (declare-const c Bool) (assert (= (default (ite c a b)) 3)) (check-sat)`), expected `"sat\n"`. Check both with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

<a id="smtcore-09-f2"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F2: UTVPI parityConflict/enforceParity turn fractional or infeasible Int-vertex states into an internal error

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/smt_utvpi_graph.go:132-134` (`parityConflict`), `:212-214` (`enforceParity`); caller `pkg/smtcore/theory_utvpi.go:357-360`, `:451`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_utvpi_def.h:423-458` (`check_z_consistency`), `:713-769` (`enforce_parity`)

**C++ behavior.** `r1.is_int()`/`r2.is_int()` are only `SASSERT`s. Release builds just compare `is_even()` (false for non-integers) and continue. `enforce_parity` ends with `SASSERT(m_graph.is_feasible())`, again debug-only.

**Go behavior.** It returns `errSMTDiffGraphDomain` when an Int vertex has a fractional assignment, or when the graph is infeasible after parity repair. `FinalCheck` turns the parityConflict error into GIVEUP. `modelValues` passes the error up, so the run ends with "smt: invalid difference-logic graph operation".

**Impact.** `smt.arith.solver=4` with Int terms compared to fractional constants, or mixed Int/Real: g3 returns `unknown` or an error where z3 returns `unsat`/`sat`. 46 of 200 random mixed-sort scripts differed.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed:
```
(set-logic ALL)
(set-option :auto_config false)
(set-option :smt.arith.solver 4)
(declare-const x0 Int)
(assert (<= (to_real x0) (/ 2.0 3.0)))
(assert (>= (to_real x0) (/ 2.0 3.0)))
(check-sat)
```
z3: `unsat`; g3: `unknown` (reason: invalid difference-logic graph operation). Also work/smtcore_09/fuzz/mixed_133.smt2: z3 `sat`, g3 `unknown`. Some other mixed inputs make native z3 loop forever in `enforce_parity` (`r1.smt2`). Do not try to match those.

**Fix.** In `parityConflict`, drop the non-integer early return. `parityOK` already treats non-integers as odd, which matches `is_even`. Then the same-SCC check runs as in C++, so the conflict path produces `unsat`. In `enforceParity`, drop the final `IsFeasible` check (C++ only asserts it). For the F1-style "invalid rational value passed as an integer" case, Go matches C++ (`unknown`) and should keep doing so.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/utvpi_fractional_int_bounds.smt2` (above), expected `"unsat\n"`. Add the mixed_133 script as `utvpi_mixed_parity_sat.smt2`, expected `"sat\n"`. Run the C++ reference test.

<a id="smtcore-09-f3"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F3: instantiate_default_store_axiom builds default(base) before the epsilon equalities

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed (trace)
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_array_default_values.go:65-101` (`defaultConstructorValue`, store case)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_array_full.cpp:715-735`

**C++ behavior.** `has_large_domain` → `def2 = mk_default(arg0)`. Otherwise it builds the epsilons and the `eq`s, then `mk_and`, then `defA = mk_default(arg0)`, then `mk_ite`.

**Go behavior.** It creates `baseDefault` before the large-domain test and before the epsilons, so AST ids shift. Every later trace line and id-based order differs.

**Reproduction.** `(declare-const a (Array (_ BitVec 2) Int)) (declare-const i (_ BitVec 2)) (declare-const v Int) (push) (assert (= (default (store a i v)) 7)) (check-sat)` with `trace=true`. z3: `#32 epsilon!0, #33 =, #34 default`. g3: `#32 default, #33 epsilon!0`.

**Fix.** Call `MkFamilyApp(... OP_ARRAY_DEFAULT, base)` inside the `large` branch, and in the small branch after `MkAndArray` and `GetArg(count-1)`, right before `MkIte`.

**Regression test.** Add a trace-order test in the package that already tests the default-store axiom: build the store above and check that the epsilon's AST id is lower than the default term's id. Or add the vector to the C++ trace comparison if one exists.

<a id="smtcore-09-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F4: mk_interface_eqs pairs the class roots instead of get_enode(th_var)

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed (trace)
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_array_shared.go:111-123` (`makeInterfaceEqualities`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_array_base.cpp:428-470` (`collect_shared_vars`, `mk_interface_eqs`)

**C++ behavior.** It pushes `r->get_th_var(get_id())` and later uses `get_enode(v1)->get_owner()`, which is the enode that owns the var, not necessarily the root (for example, the root is an ite and the var belongs to `a`).

**Go behavior.** It uses `root.owner`, so it builds different equality atoms (`= #26 #30` instead of `= #24 #30`) and adds extra ones.

**Reproduction.** `(declare-fun f ((Array Int Int)) Int)`, `(push) (assert (= (f (ite c a b)) 1)) (assert (= (f d) 2)) (check-sat)`. Trace diff at the first interface equality (sh1.smt2).

**Fix.** `v := root.TheoryVar(t.FamilyID()); roots = append(roots, t.variables[v])`. Leave the sharing test as it is, on the root.

**Regression test.** Unit test in pkg/smtcore building that scenario and checking that the created equality atom's arguments are `a` and `d`. Or add the vector to the trace reference.

<a id="smtcore-09-f5"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F5: restoreArraySorts releases ext skolem decls back to front; C++ releases front to back

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed (trace)
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_array_sorts.go:52-58`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_array_base.cpp:526-537`, `src/util/ref_vector.h:39-55`

**C++ behavior.** `dealloc(funcs)` → `~ref_vector` → `dec_range_ref(begin, end)`. That recycles decl ids in ascending order, so the free-id stack pops them in reverse.

**Go behavior.** It DecRefs the last element first, so later AST ids come out in a different order. After popping a 2-dimensional array scope, the next terms get swapped ids (`#39 g #28` vs `#39 f #26`).

**Reproduction.** rs2.smt2: `(Array Int Int Int)` select in a push/pop, then UF terms in a new push. The trace diverges at `[mk-app] #39`.

**Fix.** Loop `for len(declarations) != 0 { DecRef(declarations[0]); declarations = declarations[1:] }`.

**Regression test.** Add to the C++ trace-reference vectors, or unit-test the AST ids that follow a pop.

<a id="smtcore-09-f6"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F6: assertDelayedStoreAxioms runs the map axioms per variable; C++ runs every axiom 2b first, then every map axiom

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed (trace)
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_array_parents.go:504-535`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_array.cpp:377-387`, `src/smt/theory_array_full.cpp:756-779`

**C++ behavior.** `theory_array::assert_delayed_axioms` runs over all vars (2b). Then the full theory runs a second loop over all vars, calling `instantiate_axiom_map_for(v)` with the sizes read once.

**Go behavior.** It interleaves the two per variable, so axioms, AST ids and search order differ. It also omits draining `m_eqsv`, but that queue is never filled in this C++, so the omission has no effect.

**Reproduction.** work/smtcore_09/mb1.smt2 (map/or/not over Bool arrays). The trace diverges at `[mk-app] #108`.

**Fix.** Use two passes as in C++: first the 2b loop over `0..len(arrayData)`, then, if `!t.simple`, the map loop with `numMaps`/`numSelects` read up front. (Validated: mb1 and 5 fuzz cases became trace-identical.)

**Regression test.** Add mb1.smt2 as `array_map_delayed_order.smt2` (expected `sat\n`) to the C++ reference set.

<a id="smtcore-09-f7"></a>
#### smtcore_09-F7: Boolean array terms get their bool_var after the axioms instead of inside internalize_term_core

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed (trace)
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_array.go:132-159` (`InternalizeAtom`) together with `InternalizeTerm:213-230`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_array.cpp:241-258` (`internalize_term_core`)

**C++ behavior.** It runs `mk_enode`, then `mk_var`, then `if (m.is_bool(n)) { mk_bool_var; set_var_theory; set_enode_flag }` before any select/store or map handling.

**Go behavior.** `InternalizeTerm` runs all of its axiom work first. Only afterwards does `InternalizeAtom` call `MkBoolVar`, so bool-var numbering and decision order differ (mb2.smt2: different first decision).

**Fix.** In `InternalizeTerm`, right after attaching the var: if the expression is Boolean and has no bool var, call `MkBoolVar`, `SetVariableTheory` and `setEnodeFlag(v, true)`. `InternalizeAtom`'s later lookup will then find it. (Validated on the overlay build.)

**Regression test.** Add mb2.smt2 to the trace-reference set (expected `sat\n`).

<a id="smtcore-10-f1"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F1: `internalizeSplice` creates every argument's variable and bits before adding any bit (concat order)

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_bv_operators.go:543-571` (`(*SMTBitVectorTheory).internalizeSplice`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_bv.cpp:823-839` (`theory_bv::internalize_concat`)

**C++ behavior.** Arguments are visited last to first, and each argument's bits are added before the next argument's variable is created:
```cpp
while (i > 0) {
    i--;
    theory_var arg = get_arg_var(e, i);          // may mk_var + mk_bits (new bit2bool atoms)
    literal_vector::const_iterator it  = m_bits[arg].begin();
    literal_vector::const_iterator end = m_bits[arg].end();
    for (; it != end; ++it)
        add_bit(v, *it);                         // may call mk_new_diseq_axiom (new eq atom, axiom)
}
find_wpos(v);
```

**Go behavior.** Two separate loops: first `nativeVariable` for all arguments, then `registerBitLiteral` (add_bit) for all collected literals:
```go
for k := len(arguments) - 1; k >= 0; k-- {
    v, err := t.nativeVariable(nodes[k])
    ...
    literals = append(literals, bits...)
}
...
for index, literal := range literals {
    if err := t.registerBitLiteral(expression, uint32(index), literal); err != nil {
```

**Impact.** When a non-last concat argument has no BV variable yet (ite terms, since `apply_sort_cnstr` is not invoked for them) and `add_bit` for a later argument finds a static disequality, the Boolean variables and ASTs are created in a different order than in C++. Variable numbering shifts, the search diverges, and the model can differ.

**Reproduction.** Input (C++ `:mk-bool-var 584 :conflicts 15`, Go `:mk-bool-var 647 :conflicts 13`):
```smt2
(declare-const v0 (_ BitVec 4))
(declare-const v1 (_ BitVec 4))
(declare-const v2 (_ BitVec 4))
(declare-const v3 (_ BitVec 4))
(declare-const p0 Bool)
(declare-const p1 Bool)
(declare-const p2 Bool)
(declare-const k Int)
(declare-fun f ((_ BitVec 4)) (_ BitVec 4))
(declare-fun g ((_ BitVec 8)) (_ BitVec 4))
(push)
(assert (bvule (bvmul (bvudiv v0 (bvnand v1 v3)) (f v0)) #xb))
(assert (= (concat ((_ extract 3 2) (ite p2 v3 v0)) ((_ extract 1 0) v1)) v0))
(assert (bvslt (ite p2 (bvsmod v2 v1) ((_ zero_extend 2) ((_ extract 1 0) (ite p0 v0 v1)))) ((_ zero_extend 2) ((_ extract 1 0) v1))))
(assert (= v2 v0))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```
z3 model: `v3=#xc v2=#xf v0=#xf p2=true p0=false v1=#x3`, `f = (ite (= x!0 #xf) #x0 #x0)`. g3 model: `v2=#x7 v0=#x7 p2=true v1=#x3 v3=#x6`, `f = (ite (= x!0 #x7) #x0 #x0)`.
Trace diff with `-tr:bv -tr:bv_diseq_axiom`: C++ emits the two `found new diseq axiom` records for `(extract[1:0] v1)` and then `internalizing atom: (bit2bool[0] (if p2 (extract[3:2] v3) (extract[3:2] v0)))`; Go emits them in the opposite order. The same first divergence was seen under `(set-logic QF_AUFBV)`.

**Fix.** In `internalizeSplice`, keep the pre-check loop (it must stay side-effect free), then merge the two later loops:
```go
t.bits[expression] = nil
t.literalBits[expression] = true
t.bitTrail = append(t.bitTrail, expression)
index := uint32(0)
for k := len(arguments) - 1; k >= 0; k-- {
    v, err := t.nativeVariable(nodes[k])       // get_arg_var
    if err != nil { return false, err }
    if int(v) >= len(t.bitLiterals) { return false, ast.ErrASTDomain }
    bits := t.bitLiterals[v]                    // slice header copy, as the C++ iterators
    if operation == 40 { /* bounds check */ bits = bits[low : high+1] }
    for _, literal := range bits {
        if err := t.registerBitLiteral(expression, index, literal); err != nil { return false, err }
        index++
    }
}
return true, t.findWatchedPosition(variable)
```
The expression fallback (`operationBits` case 37 through `argumentBits(expression, true)`) has the same all-variables-first shape; it is only reached when an argument's bits are not held as literals, but should be interleaved the same way.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/theory_bv_occurrences_test.go` with `TestSMTBVConcatInterleavesArgumentVariablesAndBits`, using `bvOccurrenceFixture(t)`: internalize `(bvnot v1)` as a term, then `(concat (ite p x y) ((_ extract 1 0) v1))` with 2-bit `x`, `y`; assert that the Boolean variable of the static-disequality equality atom between the concat and `(bvnot v1)` is smaller than the Boolean variable of `(bit2bool[0] (ite p x y))`. Script vector `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/bv_concat_ite_static_diseq_order.smt2` = the input above; `scriptResults` value = the z3 output (`sat` plus the z3 model listed above, verbatim from `build/z3`). `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` checks it against the C++.

<a id="smtcore-10-f2"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F2: dense `InternalizeAtom` uses the sparse `decompose` instead of the dense shape match, rejecting offset terms

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_dense_diff_logic.go:208-238` (`(*SMTDenseDiffTheory).InternalizeAtom`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_dense_diff_logic_def.h:153-181` (`theory_dense_diff_logic<Ext>::internalize_atom`)

**C++ behavior.** Four fixed shapes; `s` and `t` are then internalized as whole terms, so an already attached offset term `(+ k x)` is accepted:
```cpp
if (m_autil.is_add(lhs, arg1, arg2) && is_times_minus_one(arg2, s)) { t = to_app(arg1); }
else if (m_autil.is_add(lhs, arg1, arg2) && is_times_minus_one(arg1, s)) { t = to_app(arg2); }
else if (m_autil.is_mul(lhs, arg1, arg2) && m_autil.is_minus_one(arg1)) { s = to_app(arg2); t = mk_zero_for(s); }
else if (!m_autil.is_arith_expr(lhs)) { t = to_app(lhs); s = mk_zero_for(t); }
else { found_non_diff_logic_expr(n); return false; }
source = internalize_term_core(s);
target = internalize_term_core(t);
```

**Go behavior.** It calls `t.syntax.decompose(lhs)`, the port of the sparse theory's `decompose_linear`, which flattens nested sums:
```go
terms, signs, err := t.syntax.decompose(lhs)
...
if len(terms) == 2 && signs[0] != signs[1] { ... } else if len(terms) == 1 { ... } else {
    t.unsupported = true
    return false, nil
}
```
For `(+ (+ 1 x) (* -1 y))` it gets three terms and gives up. It also accepts shapes the C++ rejects (`(- x)`, `(* x -1)`, sums nested on the right).

**Impact.** `arith_eq_adapter::mk_axioms` builds exactly `(<= (+ t1 (* -1 t2)) 0)` atoms. Whenever an offset term takes part in an equality or disequality under the dense solver, Go marks the problem as non-difference-logic and answers `unknown`.

**Reproduction.**
```smt2
(set-logic ALL)
(set-option :auto_config false)
(set-option :smt.arith.solver 3)
(declare-const x Int)
(declare-const y Int)
(declare-fun f (Int) Int)
(assert (= (f (+ x 1)) 5))
(assert (= (f y) 6))
(assert (<= (- y x) 1))
(assert (>= (- y x) 1))
(check-sat)
```
z3: `unsat`. g3: `unknown`. Replacing the two `f` assertions by `(assert (<= (- (f (+ x 1)) (f y)) 0))` gives z3 `sat`, g3 `unknown`.

**Fix.** Replace the `decompose` block by the four C++ cases, in the same order: binary `+` whose second argument is `(* -1 s)` (binary `*`, first argument the numeral -1); binary `+` whose first argument is such a product; binary `*` whose first argument is -1 (then `t` is the zero of `s`'s sort); `lhs` not an arithmetic-family application (then `s` is the zero of its sort); otherwise `found_non_diff_logic_expr` and `return false`. Keep `s := t.term(source)` before `u := t.term(target)`. Add small helpers `denseTimesMinusOne(h) (arg, ok)` and `denseIsArithExpr(h)` next to `forcedDifferenceEquality`, which already contains the product test.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/theory_dense_diff_equality_test.go` with `TestSMTDenseDifferenceAtomAcceptsAttachedOffsetTerm`, using `newSMTDenseEqualityFixture(t, true, config)`: internalize the term `(+ 1 x)` and `y`, internalize `(<= (+ (+ 1 x) (* -1 y)) 0)` with `f.state.Internalize(atom, true)`, and assert `!f.theory.unsupported`, `len(f.theory.atoms) == 1`, and that the atom's `target` is the variable of `(+ 1 x)` and `source` the variable of `y`. Script vectors `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/dense_offset_equality_adapter.smt2` (input above, expected `unsat\n`) and `dense_offset_difference_sat.smt2` (the variant, expected `sat\n`); run `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

<a id="smtcore-10-f3"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F3: `propagateRecognizer` returns an error where C++ release continues with an empty recognizer table

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_datatype_recognizers.go:21-26` (`(*SMTDatatypeTheory).propagateRecognizer`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_datatype.cpp:750-751,776-788` (`theory_datatype::propagate_recognizer`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
CTRACE("datatype", d->m_recognizers.empty(), ctx.display(tout););
SASSERT(!d->m_recognizers.empty());
```
The `SASSERT` is debug-only. In the reference build the loop runs over zero recognizers, `num_unassigned == 0`, and `ctx.set_conflict(...)` is called with no literals and no equalities.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if len(data.recognizers) == 0 {
    if err = t.traceDatatypeEmptyRecognizers(); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return ast.ErrASTDomain
}
```

**Impact.** Reached with `smt.relevancy=1`: `assign_eh` is called for every assigned atom, but recognizers are only registered in `relevant_eh`. C++ answers `unsat`, which is wrong for these inputs; Go answers `unknown`. Neither is the correct `sat`, and the two differ. 6 of 30 random datatype scripts hit this.

**Reproduction.**
```smt2
(set-option :smt.relevancy 1)
(declare-datatypes () ((L nil (cons (hd Int) (tl L)))))
(declare-const l L)
(declare-const b Bool)
(assert (or (not b) (is-cons l)))
(check-sat)
```
z3: `unsat`. g3: `unknown`. Without the option both print `sat`.

**Fix.** This needs an owner decision.
- Mechanical: drop the `return ast.ErrASTDomain`, so the loop sees no recognizers and `setDatatypeConflict(literals, equalities)` runs with empty slices. This matches the reference and reproduces its unsound `unsat`.
- Preferred: repair both sides the same way. Later upstream Z3 registers the recognizer at this point, as far as I recall (verify against upstream before backporting): `if (d->m_recognizers.empty()) { theory_var w = recognizer->get_arg(0)->get_th_var(get_id()); add_recognizer(w, recognizer); }`. In Go: `if len(data.recognizers) == 0 { if err = t.addRecognizer(trigger.arguments[0].TheoryVar(t.FamilyID()), trigger); err != nil { return err }; root, data, err = t.rootData(variable) }`, keeping the trace call first.
Either way, record the choice in the manifest entry for `src/smt/theory_datatype.cpp`.

**Regression test.** Script vector `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/datatype_relevancy1_unregistered_recognizer.smt2` (input above). Expected `scriptResults` value is `unsat\n` for the mechanical option or `sat\n` once both sides are repaired; `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` checks agreement. Unit test `TestSMTDatatypeFalseRecognizerWithoutRegisteredSlots` in `pkg/smtcore/theory_datatype_conflicts_test.go` using `newSMTDatatypeConflictFixture(t, false)`: internalize `(is-cons l)` with relevancy enabled and not marked relevant, assign it false, call `dt.Assign(variable, false)`, and assert no Go error is returned.

<a id="smtcore-10-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F4: datatype occurs check returns early when the context is already inconsistent

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_datatype_occurs.go:122-124` (`(*smtDatatypeOccursCheck).run`), caller `pkg/smtcore/theory_datatype.go:585-611` (`FinalCheck`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_datatype.cpp:424-447` (`theory_datatype::final_check_eh`), `489-514` (`occurs_check_enter`)

**C++ behavior.** `final_check_eh` visits every root. A `mk_split` that produces a conflict does not stop the loop: later roots still get `occurs_check` and `mk_split`. `occurs_check_enter` never tests `ctx.inconsistent()`.

**Go behavior.**
```go
constructor, err := t.classConstructor(app)
if err != nil {
    return false, err
}
if state.Inconsistent() {
    return true, nil
}
```
`FinalCheck` then returns `SMTFinalCheckContinue` immediately.

**Impact.** After a split conflict, the splits and occurs checks for the remaining roots are skipped: fewer recognizer atoms and Boolean variables are created, and `datatype splits`, `datatype occurs check` and `mk bool var` differ. No wrong answer seen. 4 of 60 random datatype scripts hit it.

**Reproduction.**
```smt2
(declare-datatypes () ((L nil (cons (hd Int) (tl L)))))
(declare-const x L)
(declare-const y L)
(declare-const z L)
(declare-const a Int)
(assert (> a 5))
(assert (or (> a 0) (and (not (is-nil x)) (not (is-cons x)))))
(assert (> (hd y) 0))
(assert (> (hd z) 0))
(check-sat)
```
`-st`: z3 `:datatype-occurs-check 9 :datatype-splits 7 :mk-bool-var 21`; g3 `:datatype-occurs-check 8 :datatype-splits 5 :mk-bool-var 19`. With `-tr:datatype`, after the `x` split C++ prints `creating split: ((_ is (nil () L)) y)` and `... z)` and then `final check 'datatype ok: continue inconsistent 1`; Go stops after the first `occurs check loop` record for `y`.

**Fix.** Delete the three-line `if state.Inconsistent() { return true, nil }` block. Nothing else is needed: `setDatatypeConflict` already ignores a second conflict, and `split` is valid in an inconsistent state as in C++.

**Regression test.** `TestSMTDatatypeFinalCheckVisitsAllRootsAfterSplitConflict` in `pkg/smtcore/theory_datatype_occurs_test.go`, built like `TestSMTDatatypeOccursEvidenceOrderAndScopeRecovery`: a two-constructor recursive datatype, roots `x`, `y`, `z` with theory variables, both recognizers of `x` assigned false and not relevant; call `dt.FinalCheck()` and assert `SMTFinalCheckContinue`, `state.Inconsistent()`, `dt.statistics.splits == 3`, `dt.statistics.occursChecks == 3`. Script vector `datatype_final_check_split_conflict.smt2` (input above, expected `sat\n`) for the C++ reference runner.

<a id="smtcore-10-f5"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F5: dense equality axioms are not built the way `arith_eq_adapter::mk_axioms` builds them

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_dense_diff_equality.go:119-258` (`installDenseEqualityAxioms`, `denseEqualityBounds`, `denseRelationAxioms`)
- C++: `src/smt/arith_eq_adapter.cpp:83-227` (`arith_eq_adapter::mk_axioms`), `src/smt/theory_dense_diff_logic_def.h:222-245,280-293`

**C++ behavior.** `mk_axioms(n1, n2)` first orders the pair (`if (n1->get_owner_id() > n2->get_owner_id()) std::swap(n1, n2);`), returns if already processed, then builds `t1_eq_t2 = ctx.mk_eq_atom(t1, t2)`, `minus_one`, `zero`, `t3`, `s`, `le`, `ge` in that order, and only then internalizes.

**Go behavior.**
```go
equality, err := state.manager.MkEq(leftNode.Owner(), rightNode.Owner())   // raw, v1/v2 order
...
if err = state.Internalize(equality, true); err != nil {                   // before the processed check
...
return t.installDenseEqualityAxioms(equality, variable, leftNode.Owner(), rightNode.Owner(), true)
```
`installDenseEqualityAxioms` orders the pair only for the `processed` key; the bounds are built from `left`/`right` as passed. `denseEqualityBounds` creates the zero numeral after the product and the sum.

**Impact.** On `new_eq_eh`/`new_diseq_eh` Go internalizes a second, unordered equality atom, and builds `le`/`ge` over `t2 - t1` when `v1` has the larger owner id. Extra Boolean variables, different axioms, different propagation order.

**Reproduction.** Run with `-st smt.auto_config=false smt.arith.solver=3`:
```smt2
(declare-const x Int)
(declare-const y Int)
(declare-fun f (Int) Int)
(assert (= (f x) 5))
(assert (= (f y) 6))
(assert (<= (- y x) 0))
(assert (>= (- y x) 0))
(check-sat)
```
Both print `unsat`; z3 `:dd-assertions 8 :mk-bool-var 16`, g3 `:dd-assertions 7 :mk-bool-var 17`.

**Fix.** Use the existing source port, as the sparse theory does. In `NewSMTDenseDiffTheory` set `adapter.source = true`. `InternalizeEquality`: on the forced shape call `t.adapter.mkAxiomsSource(enode(lhs), enode(rhs))` and return; otherwise, if `t.config.EagerEqAxioms` and both enodes have a variable, call it too (the body of `SMTIntegerDiffTheory.InternalizeEquality`). `NewEquality`/`NewDisequality`: `t.adapter.NewEquality(left, right)` / `t.adapter.NewDisequality(left, right)`. `Restart`: `t.adapter.Restart()`. Then delete `installDenseEqualityAxioms`, `denseEqualityBounds`, `denseRelationAxioms` and `denseEqualityOperandsAttached`. Fix F2 first, otherwise the adapter's atoms over offset terms are still rejected.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/theory_dense_diff_equality_test.go` with `TestSMTDenseDifferenceRelationEventOrdersPairByOwnerID`, using `newSMTDenseEqualityFixture`: give `x` and `y` variables through one atom, count `len(f.state.boolExpr)`, call `f.theory.NewEquality(vy, vx)`, and assert the equality atom is `(= x y)` (not `(= y x)`), the lower bound is `(<= (+ x (* -1 y)) 0)`, exactly three Boolean variables were added, and a second `NewDisequality(vx, vy)` adds none. Script vector `dense_equality_axiom_order.smt2` with the two `set-option` lines of F2 and the input above, expected `unsat\n`.

<a id="smtcore-10-f6"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F6: dense `FinalCheck` does not implement `theory::assume_eqs`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_dense_diff_logic.go:413-448` (`(*SMTDenseDiffTheory).FinalCheck`)
- C++: `src/smt/smt_theory.h:361-385` (`theory::assume_eqs`), `src/smt/theory_dense_diff_logic_def.h:388-398`, `src/smt/theory_dense_diff_logic.h:125-141` (`var_value_hash`, `var_value_eq`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
for (theory_var v = 0; v < num; v++) {
    enode * n = get_enode(v);
    if (n != nullptr && is_relevant_and_shared(n)) {
        other = table.insert_if_not_there(v);
        if (other != v) {
            enode * n2 = get_enode(other);
            if (assume_eq(n, n2)) result = true;
        }
    }
}
return result;
```
All variables are visited, the first variable with a value stays the representative, and the table compares assignment values only.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if other := values[key]; other != nil && other.root != node.root {
    progress, err := t.state.assumeEquality(other, node)
    ...
    if progress {
        return SMTFinalCheckContinue, nil
    }
} else {
    values[key] = node
}
```
It returns on the first new equality, replaces the representative when the roots are already equal, and adds the sort to the key.

**Impact.** One interface equality per final check instead of all of them: more final checks, different atoms and clause order.

**Reproduction.** Run with `-st smt.auto_config=false smt.arith.solver=3`:
```smt2
(declare-const a Int)
(declare-const b Int)
(declare-const c Int)
(declare-const d Int)
(declare-fun f (Int) Int)
(assert (<= (- (f a) (f b)) 100))
(assert (<= (- (f c) (f d)) 100))
(assert (<= (- a b) 5))
(assert (<= (- c d) 5))
(check-sat)
```
Both `sat`; z3 `:final-checks 2 :mk-bool-var 28 :mk-clause 3`, g3 `:final-checks 4 :mk-bool-var 30 :mk-clause 7`. Part of the Boolean variable gap is F5.

**Fix.**
```go
values := make(map[[2]string]SMTTheoryVar)       // rational, infinitesimal
result := false
for v, node := range t.variables {
    if !t.state.isRelevant(node.owner) { continue }
    shared, err := smtSharedArithmeticNode(t.SMTTheoryBase, node, false)
    if err != nil { return SMTFinalCheckGiveUp, err }
    if !shared { continue }
    key := [2]string{t.values[v].rational.RatString(), t.values[v].infinitesimal.RatString()}
    other, found := values[key]
    if !found { values[key] = SMTTheoryVar(v); continue }      // insert_if_not_there
    progress, err := t.state.assumeEquality(node, t.variables[other])   // assume_eq(n, n2)
    if err != nil { return SMTFinalCheckGiveUp, err }
    result = result || progress
}
if result { return SMTFinalCheckContinue, nil }
```
If the sort component is kept on purpose (the C++ would pair an Int with a Real variable of equal value), say so in a comment and in the manifest.

**Regression test.** `TestSMTDenseDifferenceAssumeEqsVisitsAllSharedVariables` in `pkg/smtcore/theory_dense_diff_logic_test.go` (setup as in `TestSMTDenseTheoryPropagationConflictAndScope` plus an uninterpreted `f` over four constants so they are shared): after one `theory.FinalCheck()` assert `SMTFinalCheckContinue` and `state.statistics.NumInterfaceEqs == 3`. Script vector `dense_assume_eqs_all.smt2` (two `set-option` lines plus the input above and `(get-model)`), expected `sat` and the model `b=0 a=0 d=0 c=0`, `f = (ite (= x!0 0) 0 0)` as printed by `build/z3`.

<a id="smtcore-10-f8"></a>
#### smtcore_10-F8: sparse difference logic ignores `smt.arith.dump_lemmas`

- Severity: medium

#### smtcore_10-F15: (outside this shard) `update-field` over a constructor is rewritten by Go and left unchanged by the reference C++

```cpp
if (c_decl != m_util.get_accessor_constructor(f)) {

...

```
`f` is the update-field declaration, not the accessor. `get_accessor_constructor(f)` reads a second parameter that does not exist and returns no constructor, so the result is the unchanged constructor term.

**Go behavior.** It resolves the accessor with `DatatypeUpdateAccessor(decl)` and replaces the field.

**Impact.** Different simplifier output and different sat/unsat answers. The Go answer is the semantically right one. This also caused the AST-id shifts in the random datatype scripts that used `update-field`.

```smt2
(declare-datatypes () ((C red green blue)))
(declare-datatypes () ((P (mkp (fst Int) (snd C)))))
(declare-const p0 P)
(declare-const i Int)
(declare-const j Int)
(assert (= ((_ update-field fst) (mkp i red) j) p0))
(assert (not (= (fst p0) j)))
(check-sat)
(simplify ((_ update-field fst) (mkp i red) j))
```
z3: `sat`, `(mkp i red)`. g3: `unsat`, `(mkp j red)`.

**Fix.** Owner decision. Preferred: patch the C++ fork (`func_decl * acc = m_util.get_update_accessor(f);`, then use `acc` in both places, as later upstream does), rebuild the reference, and record it in the manifest entry for `src/ast/rewriter/datatype_rewriter.cpp`. The mechanical alternative is to make `rewriteUpdate` return its first argument whenever it is a constructor application.

<a id="smtcore-11-f1"></a>
#### smtcore_11-F1: `SMTLRATheory.InternalizeEquality` ignores theory variables inherited through merges, so equality-adapter axioms are skipped

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_lra.go:632-652` (`InternalizeEquality`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_lra.cpp:773-784` (`theory_lra::imp::internalize_eq_eh`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
enode * n1 = get_enode(lhs);
enode * n2 = get_enode(rhs);
if (n1->get_th_var(get_id()) != null_theory_var &&
    n2->get_th_var(get_id()) != null_theory_var && n1 != n2) {
    m_arith_eq_adapter.mk_axioms(n1, n2);
}
```
`get_th_var` also returns a variable that the enode inherited as a class root (`merge_theory_vars`). `mk_axioms` receives the equality's own enodes `n1` and `n2`.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if n1 != nil && n2 != nil && n1 != n2 && t.IsAttachedToVariable(n1) && t.IsAttachedToVariable(n2) {
    return t.equalityAdapter.MkAxioms(n1.TheoryVar(t.FamilyID()), n2.TheoryVar(t.FamilyID()))
}
```
`IsAttachedToVariable` requires `t.variables[var] == node`, which means the enode created the variable. An enode that only carries an inherited root variable is rejected. Even when the call happens, `MkAxioms` turns the variable numbers back into enodes through `t.Enode(var)`. That yields the variable's owner, for example `(g y)`, rather than the equality's operand `x`. So the axioms are built over a different pair of terms.

**Impact.** In QF_UFLRA or QF_LRA with a UF constant that gained an arithmetic variable by merging, the `(<= (+ x (* -1 c)) 0)` / `>=` triangle is never created. The search, the model and the statistics then differ from z3.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with both binaries.
```
(set-logic QF_UFLRA)
(declare-fun g (Real) Real)
(declare-fun h (Real) Bool)
(declare-const x Real)
(declare-const y Real)
(declare-const c Real)
(push)
(assert (<= (g y) 3.0))
(assert (>= c 1.0))
(assert (h x))
(check-sat)
(assert (= (g y) x))
(check-sat)
(assert (= x c))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```
- **z3:** `c = x = 25019/25000`, `y = 1.0`. Its statistics show `:arith-eq-adapter 2`, `:arith-fixed-eqs 1`, `:mk-bool-var 11`.
- **g3:** `c = x = 1.0`, `y = 2.0`. Its statistics show `:arith-eq-adapter 1`, no fixed-eqs, `:mk-bool-var 9`.
- **Traces:** z3's trace has `internalize_eq_eh (= x c)` followed by `mk_axioms #30 #27 x c`. g3 never emits it.

**Fix.**
1. In `InternalizeEquality`, test `n1.TheoryVar(t.FamilyID()) != SMTNullTheoryVar && n2.TheoryVar(t.FamilyID()) != SMTNullTheoryVar && n1 != n2`.
2. Change the adapter entry point to take enodes, for example `MkAxiomsNodes(n1, n2 *SMTEnode)`, with the current body starting after the `t.Enode` lookups.
3. Have `NewEquality` and `NewDisequality` call it with `t.Enode(v1)` and `t.Enode(v2)`, which matches `get_enode(v)` in C++.
4. `Restart` already has the enodes, so pass them directly instead of round-tripping through `TheoryVar`.

**Regression test.**
- **Unit test:** add `TestSMTLRAInternalizeEqualityInheritedRootVariable` to `pkg/smtcore/theory_lra_axioms_test.go`, using `newLRAFrontendFixture`, `f.variable` and `f.assert`.
  1. Internalize `(g y)` through `internalizeDef`.
  2. Create a UF constant `x` without an LRA variable.
  3. Merge `x` with `(g y)` via `f.s` so that `x` becomes root.
  4. Internalize `(= x c)`.
  5. Expect `equalityAdapter.NumAxioms()` to grow by 1 and the processed pair to be `{x, c}`, not `{(g y), c}`.
- **CLI vector:** add the script above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/lra_inherited_eq_adapter.smt2`. Its `scriptResults` entry is the z3 output above. `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` checks it against the C++.

<a id="smtcore-11-f2"></a>
#### smtcore_11-F2: `SMTFloatingPointTheory.ModelValue` treats an `fp` triple of numerals as a final value, so models print `(fp ...)` and model evaluation stops working

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_fpa.go:673-677` (`ModelValue`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_fpa.cpp:741-744` (`theory_fpa::mk_value`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
if (m_fpa_util.is_rm_numeral(owner) ||
    m_fpa_util.is_numeral(owner)) {
    return alloc(expr_wrapper_proc, owner);
}
```
`is_numeral` accepts only `OP_FPA_NUM`, `±inf`, `NaN` and `±zero` (`fpa_decl_plugin.cpp:98-134`). An `(fp b e s)` owner goes on to the `is_fp` branch. That branch builds an `fpa_value_proc` with three dependencies and canonicalizes the value through `mpf`, giving for example `(_ +zero 8 24)`.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if value, valueErr := state.manager.IsValue(owner); valueErr != nil {
    return nil, valueErr
} else if value {
    return NewSMTExpressionValueProcedure(owner)
}
```
`IsValue` (`floatingPointValue`) is true for `OP_FPA_FP` when all three arguments are values. So the raw `(fp #b0 #x00 #b0...)` becomes the model value.

**Impact.** The class root is the converted `(fp ...)` term when relevancy is 0, for example with `set-logic QF_FP`. In that case:
- Models print `(fp #b0 #x00 #b000...)` instead of `(_ +zero 8 24)`.
- `eval` and `get-value` of FP operations on such constants are left unevaluated: `(fp.isZero (fp ...))` is printed instead of `false`. The resulting model is wrong as an evaluator.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with both binaries.
```
(set-logic QF_FP)
(declare-const rm RoundingMode)
(declare-const z (_ FloatingPoint 8 24))
(push)
(assert (= z ((_ to_fp 8 24) rm 0.5)))
(check-sat)
(get-value (z))
(eval (fp.isZero z))
(eval (fp.add RNE z z))
```
- **z3:**
  ```
  sat
  ((z (fp #b0 #x7e #b00000000000000000000000)))
  false
  (fp #b0 #x7f #b00000000000000000000000)
  ```
- **g3:** the same first two lines, then `(fp.isZero (fp #b0 #x7e ...))` and an unevaluated `(fp.add roundNearestTiesToEven ...)`.
- **Value 0.0:** with the same script and `0.0` instead of `0.5`, z3 prints `(_ +zero 8 24)` and g3 prints `(fp #b0 #x00 #b000...)`.

**Fix.**
1. Replace the `IsValue` test with exact `is_rm_numeral || is_numeral`: the owner is in the FPA family and its kind is one of the five rounding-mode constants, `FPAOpNumeral`, `FPAOpPositiveInf`, `FPAOpNegativeInf`, `FPAOpNaN`, `FPAOpPositiveZero` or `FPAOpNegativeZero`.
2. Use the existing `t.operation(owner)` for the check; add a helper `smtFPAIsSourceNumeral(own, op)` next to `smtFPARoundingNumeral` in `theory_fpa_hooks.go`.
3. `Relevant` (`theory_fpa_hooks.go:880`) uses `IsValue` in place of `is_numeral(n, val)` too. It is currently safe only because `FPAOpFP` returns earlier, but switch it to the same helper.

**Regression test.**
- **Unit test:** add `TestSMTFloatingPointModelCanonicalizesFPTripleRoot` to `pkg/smtcore/theory_fpa_test.go`, using `smtFloatingPointSolver`.
  1. Set relevancy level 0 and `SetProduceModels(true)`.
  2. Assert `x = (fp #b0 #b00 #b0)` built with `MkFamilyApp(family, ast.FPAOpFP, ...)` on BV numerals.
  3. Expect `ConstantInterpretation(x)` to have kind `ast.FPAOpPositiveZero`.
- **CLI vector:** add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/fpa_fp_triple_model_value.smt2` with the script above. The expected `scriptResults` output is the z3 output shown above. Check it with `TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference`.

  - `pkg/smtcore/theory_dl.go:241-249` (`InternalizeAtom`) and `:363-371` (`assertConstraint`)

  - `src/smt/smt_context.h:1184-1186`

```cpp
literal lit(ctx.get_literal(e));
ctx.mark_as_relevant(lit);       // -> mark_as_relevant(bool_var2expr(lit.var()))

```

```go
if literal.Var() != SMTTrueBoolVar {
    atom, atomErr := state.BoolExpression(literal.Var())
    ...
```

**Impact.** At the default `smt.relevancy=2`, FPA problems take a different decision sequence and give different models.

```

(declare-const x1 (_ FloatingPoint 2 2))
(declare-const x2 (_ FloatingPoint 2 2))
(push)
(assert (fp.lt (fp.mul RNE x2 x0) (fp.add RTP x0 x0)))
(assert (fp.leq x1 (fp.mul RNE x1 x2)))
(assert (fp.lt (fp.add RTP x2 x2) (fp.neg x0)))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```
- **z3:** `x1 = (fp #b1 #b00 #b1)`.
- **g3:** `x1 = (fp #b1 #b10 #b1)`.
- Both give `x2 = (_ -oo 2 2)` and `x0 = (fp #b0 #b00 #b1)`.
- Statistics differ: conflicts 66 for z3 vs 73 for g3, decisions 1207 vs 1485.

**Fix.** In all three Go sites, mark the true literal too: use `state.boolExpr[SMTTrueBoolVar]` (the `true` expression) or `MkTrue()`, as `smtLRAAxiomCall.base` does, and call `state.markRelevant` on it. `theory_bv_conversion.go:334-337` (`markLiteralRelevant`) has the same guard; it is outside this shard, but check that its C++ caller also marks `true`. Then rerun the FPA vectors.

**Regression test.**
- **CLI vector:** add the script as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/fpa_relevancy_true_literal.smt2`. Its `scriptResults` entry is the z3 output above:
  ```
  sat
  (model
    (define-fun x2 () (_ FloatingPoint 2 2)
      (_ -oo 2 2))
    (define-fun x1 () (_ FloatingPoint 2 2)
      (fp #b1 #b00 #b1))
    (define-fun x0 () (_ FloatingPoint 2 2)
      (fp #b0 #b00 #b1))
  )
  ```
  Check it with `TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference`.
- **Unit test:** add `TestSMTFloatingPointAssertTrueMarksTrueRelevant` to `pkg/smtcore/theory_fpa_test.go`. Call `t.assertConstraint` on an expression that internalizes to `true_literal`, for example the side condition `(bvule (bv_wrap rm) #b111)`, and assert `s.relevancy.IsRelevant(trueExpr)`.

<a id="smtcore-11-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_11-F4: `SMTLRATheory.PushScope` copies the whole `unassigned` vector on every scope (O(vars) per decision), so memory and time grow quadratically

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed (measured)
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_lra.go:826` (`PushScope`) and `:864-865` (`PopScopes`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_lra.cpp:594-598` (`updt_unassigned_bounds`, `vector_value_trail`) and `811-824` (`push_scope_eh`)

**C++ behavior.** Each change to `m_unassigned_bounds[v]` pushes a `vector_value_trail` entry. `push_scope_eh` records only sizes.

**Go behavior.**
```go
t.scopes = append(t.scopes, smtLRAFrontendScope{..., unassigned: append([]uint32(nil), t.unassigned...)})
```
Every search decision allocates a full copy of the vector.

**Impact.** With N real variables and a search depth near N, memory grows as N² × 4 bytes. The script `(or (<= xi 1.0) (>= xi 2.0))` for i < 16000 under QF_LRA takes 2.99 s and 1.29 GB in g3, against 0.55 s and 64 MB in z3. With 4000 variables it takes 143 MB, against 26 MB in z3. Comparable UF-only and flat-LRA scripts need only 190–280 MB in g3, so the excess comes from this snapshot. Larger instances can run out of memory where z3 is fine.

**Reproduction.** `python3 $S/work/smtcore_11/gen_lra_deep.py 16000 > d.smt2`, then run each binary under `/usr/bin/time -f "%es %MKB"`. The numbers are as above; both answer `sat`.

**Fix.** Replace the snapshot with an undo trail:
1. In `updateUnassignedBounds`, append `{v, old}` to `t.unassignedTrail`.
2. Store `len(t.unassignedTrail)` in `smtLRAFrontendScope`.
3. In `PopScopes`, restore entries in reverse down to that length.
4. Keep the existing `clear` of entries for variables created after the scope.

**Regression test.** Add `TestSMTLRAUnassignedBoundsTrailRestore` to `pkg/smtcore/theory_lra_propagation_test.go`, using `newLRAFrontendFixture`.
1. Push two scopes.
2. Change `unassigned[v]` through propagation in each scope.
3. Pop 1 and then 1 more, checking the exact values after each pop.
4. Also assert that `len(t.scopes[i].unassigned)` is no longer kept, or that an allocation benchmark stays flat as the scope count grows.

<a id="smtcore-11-f5"></a>
#### smtcore_11-F5: LRA `Relevant` builds the rem / to_int axiom terms in a different order from `mk_rem_axiom` / `mk_to_int_axiom`

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_lra_operator_axioms.go:162-193` (to_int) and `246-271` (rem)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_lra.cpp:880-888` and `900-913`

**C++ behavior.**
- **`mk_rem_axiom`:** creates `zero`, `rem`, `mod` and `mmod = -mod` before `dgez = mk_literal(mk_ge(divisor, zero))`. It then emits `mk_axiom(~dgez, mk_eq(rem, mod))` completely before building `mk_eq(rem, mmod)`.
- **`mk_to_int_axiom`:** with GCC's right-to-left argument order the creation sequence is `to_r`, `0`, `sub(to_r, x)`, `le`, `1`, `sub(x, to_r)`, `ge`. Only after both atoms exist does it internalize `lo` and then `hi`.

**Go behavior.**
- **rem:** creates `mod`, then the `ge` literal, which is already internalized, and only then `-mod`. It internalizes both equalities before emitting either clause.
- **to_int:** creates `0` and `1` before the first `sub`, and internalizes `lo` before `hi` is built.

The same defect in `theory_arith` is recorded as smtcore_07-F4 and FUZZ-F2. This is the LRA copy.

**Impact.** AST ids, bool-var numbering and clause/internalization order differ, and with them hash-table order and traces. It is reachable only with Int `rem` or `to_int` under the LRA backend, which is rare because setup chooses theory_arith for integer problems.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: the CLI setups that select LRA reject Int terms.

**Fix.**
- **rem:** build `mod`, then `-mod` (C++ `rem` is the existing term), then `ge` plus its literal. Then build `eq(term, mod)` and emit its clause, then build `eq(term, -mod)` and emit its clause.
- **to_int:** build `toReal`, `zero`, `sub1`, the `le` app, `one`, `sub2` and the `ge` app first. Then internalize `lo`, emit its unit, internalize `hi`, and emit its unit.

**Regression test.** Extend `TestSMTLRAOperatorFloorAndIsIntAxioms` and `TestSMTLRAOperatorIntegerDivisionRemainderClauseShapes` in `pkg/smtcore/theory_lra_operator_axioms_test.go`. Assert the order of the new `f.s.boolExpr` entries and of the AST ids: for rem, expect the `-mod` id below the `>=` id and the clause list `[¬ge∨eq1]` added before `eq2` is internalized.

<a id="smtcore-11-f6"></a>
#### smtcore_11-F6: `SMTTheoryOptimizationUtil.IsLinear` accepts n-ary multiplication; C++ `is_mul(t, t1, t2)` matches only binary

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_opt.go:112-136` (`IsLinear`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_opt.cpp:51-61` and `src/ast/arith_decl_plugin.h:295` (`MATCH_BINARY(is_mul)`)

**C++ behavior.** For `(* 2 x y)`, `is_mul(t, t1, t2)` fails because there are 3 arguments, so the term falls to `else return false`.

**Go behavior.** `case smtArithOpMul` reads only arguments 0 and 1. If argument 0 is a numeral, it pushes argument 1 and accepts. Argument 2 (`y`) is never examined, so `(* 2 x y)` is reported as linear.

**Impact.** `SMTTheoryArith` and difference-logic `add_objective` (`smt_theory_arith_opt.go:33`, `theory_diff_logic_objective.go:85`) would accept a non-linear objective that C++ rejects. In the one test tried, `(maximize (* 2 x y))` with the box priority, both binaries gave the same objective values, so the visible effect is unconfirmed.

**Fix.** In the `smtArithOpMul` case, read `GetNumArgs`. If it is not 2, `return false, nil`, as the default branch does.

**Regression test.** Extend `TestSMTTheoryOptimizationLinearAndNumeralRecognition` in `pkg/smtcore/theory_opt_test.go`. Build `(* 2 x y)` with `MkFamilyApp(arith, smtArithOpMul, nil, []{two, x, y})` and expect `IsLinear` to return `false`. The existing binary `(* 2 x)` case should stay `true`.

<a id="smtcore-12-f1"></a>
#### smtcore_12-F1: findStringAutomatonInitialBounds errors when the language has no nonzero-length word; the C++ release build continues

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_automaton_bounds.go:128` (`findStringAutomatonInitialBounds`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:6962-6990` (`theory_str::find_automaton_initial_bounds`)

**C++ behavior.**
```
bool zero_sol_exists = refine_automaton_lower_bound(aut, rational::zero(), nonzero_lower_bound);
if (zero_sol_exists) {
    regex_last_lower_bound.insert(str, rational::zero());
    if (!nonzero_lower_bound.is_minus_one()) { ... rhs.push_back(m.mk_or(rhs1, rhs2)); }
    else { UNREACHABLE(); }
} else {
    if (!nonzero_lower_bound.is_minus_one()) { ... } else { UNREACHABLE(); }
}
```
In the release reference build `UNREACHABLE()` is `__builtin_unreachable()` (`src/util/debug.h:72`), so no error is raised. The trace of `build/z3` shows that it still asserts the length lemma and goes on solving. For `ri2` below it asserts `(or (not (str.in.re x ...)) (>= (str.len x) N))`; for `ri1` it asserts `(or (not ...) (or (= (str.len x) 0) (>= (str.len x) N)))`.

**Go behavior.**
```
if nonzero == -1 {
    return ast.ErrASTDomain // Native UNREACHABLE: no nonzero solution.
}
```
The error abandons final check, and the solver answers `unknown`.

**Impact.** Any z3str3 membership whose regex language is empty, or contains only the empty string (for example `re.inter` of disjoint languages, or of `a*` and `b*`), gives `unknown` where the C++ answers `sat` or `unsat`.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with both binaries:
```
(set-option :smt.string_solver z3str3)
(declare-const x String)
(assert (str.in.re x (re.inter (str.to.re "a") (str.to.re "b"))))
(check-sat)
```
z3: `unsat`, g3: `unknown`. With `(re.inter (re.* (str.to.re "a")) (re.* (str.to.re "b")))`: z3 `sat`, g3 `unknown`. With `(str.in.re (str.++ x "a") (re.inter (re.+ (str.to.re "a")) (re.+ (str.to.re "b"))))`: z3 `unsat`, g3 `unknown`.

**Fix.** Do not return an error in either `nonzero == -1` arm. Reproduce what the GCC release build does: build the same right-hand side, using the sentinel `nonzero` value as the bound numeral. The `>=` term is still built; only the `UNREACHABLE` arm differs. In the `!zeroAccepted` arm, also set `regexLastLower[word]` to that value. Confirm the numeral by printing the asserted lemma from `build/z3` with `trace=true` (the `[mk-app]` for the bound). Do not add a fallback that the C++ lacks.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/str_regex_inter_empty.smt2` with the three asserts above as separate `push`/`pop` blocks. Expected `scriptResults` entry: `"unsat\nsat\nunsat\n"`. Check it against the C++ with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

#### smtcore_12-F2: z3str3 gives a wrong `unsat` for `(= i (str.to.int x)) (= i 12)`

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed (the divergence); root cause not localized
- Go: z3str3 search path; the divergence is seen in `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_conversion*.go` and the regex-automaton stage (`theory_str_automaton_*.go`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:1707-1751, 9486-9570, 9926-10650`

**C++ behavior.** With the default parameters, `build/z3` answers `sat` in 0.07 s.

**Go behavior.** g3 answers `unsat` after about 0.8 s and about 34k Boolean variables; z3 creates 13k.
- The canonical AST traces agree up to the regex path constraints. g3 then builds roughly three times as many terms: path-constraint conjunctions `ch10..ch70`, and 77 instead of 13 `(not (and (str.in.re x ..) (= (str.len x) N)))` lemmas.
- For other targets: `i = 15, 16, 17, 19, 35, 40, 80` time out (over 15 s) in g3, while z3 answers `sat`.
- The C++ itself answers `unsat` on the same script with `smt.relevancy=0`. So the unsound lemma exists in the original z3str3, and g3 reaches it on the default path while the C++ does not.

**Impact.** A wrong answer on a short and plausible input (an `unsat` that should be `sat`), and hangs on neighboring values.

**Reproduction.**
```
(set-option :smt.string_solver z3str3)
(declare-const x String)(declare-const i Int)
(assert (= i (str.to.int x)))
(assert (= i 12))
(check-sat)
```
z3: `sat`; g3: `unsat`. The result is unchanged with `smt.str.strong_arrangements=false`, `fast_length_tester_cache=true` or `arith.solver=2`. With `smt.phase_selection=1` or `smt.random_seed=3`, both answer `sat`.

**Fix.** Not localized. Next step: diff the canonical `trace=true` streams; the scripts are in `$S/work/smtcore_12/canon.py` and `sdiff.sh`. The first divergences are:
- a reordered `re.range` / `re.*` construction in `instantiateStringToInt` (Go builds `firstDigit` before `digits`; GCC evaluates the right `mk_concat` argument, the star, first);
- swapped `and` argument orders in the path constraints;
- an extra `(or (not (and ..)) (= (str.++ ch0 ch1) "..."))` implication that g3 asserts and z3 does not.

Fix these in order, from earliest to latest, until the answers match. The first item is concrete: in `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_conversion.go:93-105`, build `digit` and `digits` (the star) before `firstDigit`, to follow GCC's right-to-left argument evaluation of `u.re.mk_concat(range(1,9), star(range(0,9)))`.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/str_to_int_value.smt2` (the script above, plus pushes for `i = 15` and `i = 35`), with expected output `"sat\nsat\nsat\n"`, checked with `TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference`.

<a id="smtcore-12-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_12-F4: PB simplex picks pivots and counts rows differently (deterministic tie-break instead of `m_random()%n`)

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/math/simplex/simplex.go:458-495` (`Solver.selectPivot`) and `:240-307` (`AddRationalRow`), reached from `pkg/smtcore/theory_pb_simplex.go`
- C++: `src/math/simplex/simplex_def.h:538-575` (`select_pivot_core`), `sparse_matrix_def.h` (`add_row`)

**C++ behavior.** On a tie in `(num, col_sz)`, it does `n++; if (m_random()%n == 0) { result = x_j; ... }`.

**Go behavior.** Ties are broken by the smallest variable index; there is no random draw. The manifest records this as intentional ("random tie choice ... not reached by retained consumers"). However, `theory_pb` with `smt.pb.enable_simplex=true` is a retained consumer that reaches it. In addition, Go's row-elimination loop in `AddRationalRow` reports a different `simplex add rows` count.

**Impact.**
- `:simplex-num-pivots` and `:simplex-add-rows` differ, and so do the pivot sequence, infeasible rows and conflict clauses.
- In a fuzz run, all 40+ PB simplex scripts with any difference differed in these statistics; the answers were never wrong.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed:
```
(set-option :auto_config false)
(set-option :smt.pb.enable_simplex true)
(set-option :smt.pb.enable_compilation false)
(set-logic ALL)
(declare-const a Bool)(declare-const b Bool)(declare-const c Bool)
(assert ((_ at-least 2) (not a) b c))
(check-sat)
```
`-st`: z3 `:simplex-num-pivots 2`, g3 `1`. The script in `$S/work/smtcore_12/s1.smt2` also shows z3 `:simplex-add-rows 6 / pivots 7` against g3 `5 / 6`.

**Fix.** In `selectPivot` (non-Bland branch), port the C++ tie handling: keep `n`. On a strict improvement set `n = 1`; on an equal `(dep, col)` pair do `n++` and take the candidate when `random()%n == 0`. Use a `z3rand.Generator` owned by the `Solver` and seeded like `simplex`'s `m_random` (default seed 0). Before changing it, check whether arithmetic consumers rely on the deterministic order (`arithmeticPolicy`), and keep that order if they do. Port the `add rows` counter to count exactly where `sparse_matrix::add` / `mk_row` increment `m_stats.m_add_rows`. Update the manifest deviation.

**Regression test.** Add the script above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/pb_simplex_pivot_stats.smt2` with `-st`, and compare with `TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference`. As a unit test in `pkg/math/simplex/simplex_test.go`, `TestSelectPivotRandomTie` builds a row with two equal-cost candidates and checks the choice produced by seed 0.
