<a id="smtcore-13-f2"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F2: instantiateSubstring creates its atoms in a different order than the C++

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_extract.go:137-345` (`instantiateSubstring`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:1583-1652` (`instantiate_axiom_Substr`)

**C++ behavior.**
- `argumentsValid_terms` pushes `mk_ge(pos, zero)` before it builds `mk_strlen(base)`.
- `lenOutOfBounds` builds a fresh `mk_strlen`/`mk_mul` before `mk_and(argumentsValid_terms)`.
- `case2_conclusion` is `m.mk_and(eq(base, t0.t1), eq(len t0, pos), eq(expr, t1))`. Under GCC the third argument is evaluated first, so the order is `eq(expr,t1)`, then `len(t0)`, then `eq(len t0,pos)`, then `mk_concat(t0,t1)`, then `eq(base,…)`.
- Locals are `expr_ref`s released in reverse declaration order, and `th_rewriter rw` is destroyed at the end of its inner block.

**Go behavior.** Go builds `length`, `negativeLength`, `outside` and `inside` before `positionValid`, and builds `valid` before `endOutside`. Case 2 is built in left-to-right order (`concat`, then `eq(word,…)`, then `eq(len,pos)`, then `eq(expr,t1)`). All temporaries are held in one premises vector that is released forward.

**Impact.** Every `str.substr` term gets different Boolean variable numbers, enode creation and basic-axiom queue order. The trace diverges right after the substr axiom (for example `(= (str.len t0!tmp1) 0)` against `(= "" t0!tmp1)`), and the search afterwards diverges with it.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed by trace diff (`-tr:mk_bool_var`) on:
```
(declare-const x String)
(assert (= (str.substr x 1 2) "ab"))
(check-sat)
```
The divergence starts at bool var 231. It also shows on `(= (str.substr x i 2) "ab") (= (str.len x) 5)`. After the rewrite below, all three probes produce identical traces.

**Fix.** Rewrite `instantiateSubstring` to follow the C++ statement order:
- `zero` and `minusOne` first.
- `ge(pos,0)`, then `len`/`mul`/`add`/`ge`/`not` for "inside", then `ge(len,0)`.
- A second `len`/`mul` and `add(pos,len,mul)` for `lenOutOfBounds`.
- Then `mk_and(valid)`, `not(valid)`, `""`, `eq(expr,"")`, `implies`.
- Then `t0`, `t1` and the case-2 conjuncts in the order `eq(expr,t1)`, `len(t0)`, `eq(len,pos)`, `concat`, `eq(base,concat)`.
- Case 3 stays left to right, because it uses `push_back`.

Release locals in reverse declaration order (one group per `expr_ref` or `expr_ref_vector`), and close the fresh rewriter before them. A working version is in `$S/work/smtcore_13/pkgcopy/smtcore/theory_str_extract.go`.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_extract_test.go` (or add a vector) with a check of the Boolean-variable creation order. Better, add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/str_substr_order.smt2`, with the input above plus `(set-option :smt.string_solver z3str3)` and `(get-model)`. Add it to the `TestTraceGolden` vector list using the `mk_bool_var` tag (`go test -tags g3trace ./cmd/g3 -run TestTraceGolden`).

<a id="smtcore-13-f3"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F3: unknown regex operators make z3str3 answer `unknown` where the C++ answers `sat`

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_regex.go:99-101` (`regexTextKey`); `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_regex_lengths.go:52-53` (`checkRegexLengthLinearity`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:1836-1839` (`get_std_regex_str`); `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:6759-6762` (`check_regex_length_linearity_helper`)

**C++ behavior.** Both functions end in `UNREACHABLE()` followed by a return (`return zstring("")` and `return false`). In the release reference build (`-DNDEBUG`), `UNREACHABLE()` only marks the path as unreachable, so the code continues: `re.complement`, `re.inter` and `re.loop` are registered and solved by the automata stage.

**Go behavior.**
- `regexTextKey` returns `fmt.Errorf("string theory regex operation %d is not supported")`.
- `checkRegexLengthLinearity` returns `ast.ErrASTDomain`.

Either error aborts the check with `unknown`.

**Impact.** Any z3str3 problem containing `re.complement`, `re.inter` or `re.loop` under `str.in.re` gets `unknown` where the C++ gives `sat`.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with `smt.string_solver=z3str3`:
```
(declare-const x String)
(assert (str.in.re x (re.inter (re.* (str.to.re "ab")) (re.* (str.to.re "abab")))))
(assert (= (str.len x) 4))
(check-sat)
```
- g3: `unknown`
- z3: `sat`, `x="abab"`

Results with `re.complement` (`(str.in.re x (re.complement (str.to.re "ab")))`, length 2) and `((_ re.loop 1 3) (str.to.re "ab"))`:

| Input | g3 | z3 |
|---|---|---|
| `re.complement` | `unknown` | `sat`, `x="pA"` |
| `re.loop` | `unknown` | `sat`, `x="abab"` |

With the fix, six such probes (including negated, nested and `re.++`-wrapped ones) give identical output and identical `-st` statistics.

**Fix.**
- In `regexTextKey`, change the `default` case to `return "", nil` (the release fallthrough to `return zstring("")`).
- In `checkRegexLengthLinearity`, change the `default` case to `return false, nil`.

Do not change `instantiateLegacyRegexAxiom`: there the C++ really is `NOT_IMPLEMENTED_YET`, which exits.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/str_regex_inter_loop.smt2`:
```
(set-option :smt.string_solver z3str3)
(declare-const x String)
(assert (str.in.re x (re.inter (re.* (str.to.re "ab")) (re.* (str.to.re "abab")))))
(assert (= (str.len x) 4))
(check-sat)
(get-value (x))
```
- Expected entry in `scriptResults`: `"sat\n((x \"abab\"))\n"`.
- Add a unit test in `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_regex_lengths_test.go` asserting that `checkRegexLengthLinearity` on an `re.inter` term returns `(false, nil)`.

<a id="smtcore-13-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F4: concat arrangements create equality atoms too early or in the wrong order (types 2, 3 and 6)

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_suffix_arrangements.go:96`; `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_prefix_arrangements.go:70` and `:294-301`; `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_literal_boundaries.go:293-300`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:3526-3866` (type 2), `:3889-4229` (type 3), `:4451-4666` (type 6)

**C++ behavior.**
- The parent atom `ctx.mk_eq_atom(concatAst1, concatAst2)` is created only where it is used: inside each split branch, and in the split -1 branch after `implyR = mk_or(arrangement_disjunction)`.
- Type 6 builds `implyR` before the premise.
- In type 3, split -1, `ctx.mk_eq_atom(mk_strlen(x), mk_strlen(cropStr))` creates `len(cropStr)` before `len(x)` (GCC right-to-left).

**Go behavior.**
- Types 2 and 3: `parentEq, err := pin(t.state.MkEqAtom(left, right))` runs at the top of each function, before any option.
- Type 6: `premise` is built before `conclusion`.
- Type 3: `length` is created before `cropLength`.

**Impact.** The Boolean variable for the parent equality, and the `str.len` enodes, get different numbers. The trace and the case-split order diverge on every type 2/3/6 arrangement.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed by trace diff. Each of the following diverges from the C++ and matches after the fix:
- `(= z (str.++ x y)) (= z (str.++ m "cab")) (= (str.len z) 5)`: bool var 37 is created 3 records early in g3.
- The same input with `(str.++ "abc" n)`.
- `(= z (str.++ "abc" y)) (= z (str.++ m "cab")) (= (str.len z) 5)` (type 6).
- `(= (str.++ x y) (str.++ "abc" n))` (type 3, length order).

**Fix.**
- Types 2 and 3: make `parentEq` lazy (a closure that creates it on first use). Call it immediately before `guards.add(parentEq)` in splits 0 and 2, first thing in split 1, and after `MkOrArray(options)` in split -1.
- Type 6: move `MkOrArray(options)` before `MkEqAtom(left, right)`.
- Type 3, split -1: create `MkSequenceLength(prefix)` before `MkSequenceLength(x)`.

Patched versions are in the work dir.

**Regression test.** Add the three probes above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/str_arrangement_order_{2,3,6}.smt2`, with `(set-option :smt.string_solver z3str3)` and `(get-model)`, and add them to the `TestTraceGolden` vector set with the `mk_bool_var` tag. Expected outputs come from `<repo>/build/z3`. For example, the type-2 probe gives `sat`.

<a id="smtcore-13-f5"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F5: UTVPI InternalizeTerm creates an enode before its arguments are internalized

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_utvpi.go:251-257` (`InternalizeTerm`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_utvpi_def.h:539-542` (`theory_utvpi::mk_term`)

**C++ behavior.** Before making the enode, `mk_term` internalizes every argument:
```
for (unsigned i = 0; i < n->get_num_args(); ++i) { mk_term(to_app(n->get_arg(i))); }
th_var target = mk_var(ctx.mk_enode(n, false, false, true));
```

**Go behavior.** Go calls `t.state.MkEnode(expression, ...)` directly. For a term such as `(- x)` or `(+ x 1)`, the argument numerals and terms may have no enode yet. `MkEnode` then fails with `AST source precondition` and the whole check returns `unknown`.

**Impact.** With `smt.arith.solver=4`, any UTVPI term used under an uninterpreted function returns `unknown`.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with `(set-option :auto_config false)(set-option :smt.arith.solver 4)`:
```
(declare-const x Int)
(declare-fun g (Int) Bool)
(assert (g (- x)))
(assert (<= x 2))
(check-sat)
```
- g3: `unknown`, with `:reason-unknown "smt kernel internalize assertions: internalize formula child 0: g3: AST source precondition"`.
- z3: `sat`.

`(g (- x))` with `(not (g 2))` and `x = -2` behaves the same way: g3 says `unknown`, z3 says `sat` with `x = -2`.

**Fix.** Before `MkEnode` in `InternalizeTerm`, call `t.state.Internalize(arg, false)` for each argument of `expression`. That is the context-level equivalent of `mk_term` on each argument, since the arithmetic theory is the owner.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/utvpi_term_under_uf.smt2` with the header above and `(get-value (x))`.
- Expected entry in `scriptResults`: `"sat\n((x 0))\n"` (z3 gives `x 0`).
- Run the C++ reference check with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE`.

<a id="smtcore-13-f6"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F6: UTVPI ApplySortConstraint creates graph variables for every arithmetic enode, and model values bypass the arithmetic factory

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_utvpi.go:125-137` (`ApplySortConstraint`); `:462-475` (`ModelValue`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_utvpi.h` (no `apply_sort_cnstr` override); `src/smt/theory_utvpi_def.h:898-905` (`mk_value`)

**C++ behavior.**
- `theory_utvpi` does not override `theory::apply_sort_cnstr`, which does nothing. An Int constant that occurs only under an uninterpreted function gets no theory variable, so the model completes it from the arithmetic factory.
- `mk_value` returns `m_factory->mk_num_value(num, is_int)`, which registers the value so that later fresh values avoid it.

**Go behavior.**
- `ApplySortConstraint` attaches a graph variable to every arithmetic enode, which gets value 0. For interpreted terms it also sets `t.unsupported = true`.
- `ModelValue` builds the numeral directly with `ArithmeticNumeralRat`, without registering it in the factory.

**Impact.**
- Models differ: unconstrained Int constants get 0 instead of distinct fresh values.
- An `unknown` can come from the spurious `unsupported` flag. With F7 below fixed, `(h (+ p q)) (< p 0.5)` answers `sat` instead of g3's earlier `unknown`.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with the UTVPI header from F5:
```
(declare-const x Int)
(declare-const k Int)
(declare-fun g (Int) Bool)
(assert (g k))
(assert (not (g x)))
(assert (<= x 0))
(assert (>= x 0))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```
- g3: `k = 0`, `x = 0`, and the model's `g` table reads `(ite (= x!0 0) true (ite (= x!0 0) false ...))`. That table contradicts itself: g must be true at 0 for k and false at 0 for x.
- z3: `k = 1`, `x = 0`.

The probes with three constants and with an uninterpreted sort also differ (g3 `j=0`, z3 `j=2`). After the fix, together with F7, 15 UTVPI probes and all 7 existing `utvpi_*.smt2` vectors are byte-identical to z3.

**Fix.**
- Make `ApplySortConstraint` return `nil`, as `SMTIntegerDiffTheory.ApplySortConstraint` already does.
- Store the `ArithmeticFactory` created in `InitializeModel`.
- In `ModelValue`, return `factory.MkNumValue(&t.values[v], t.graph.integer[v])`.

**Regression test.** Add the input above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/utvpi_uf_fresh_values.smt2` (with `(get-value (k x))`).
- Expected entry in `scriptResults`: `"sat\n((k 1) (x 0))\n"`.
- Also re-run the existing `utvpi_*` vectors with `TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference`.

<a id="smtcore-13-f7"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F7: UTVPI InternalizeTerm returns on a two-term sum before creating its variables

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_utvpi.go:236-239`
- C++: `src/smt/theory_utvpi_def.h:526-538` (`mk_term`)

**C++ behavior.** `mk_coeffs` calls `mk_var` on every linearized term, which internalizes it and attaches a theory variable. Only after that does `coeffs.size() == 2` return `null_theory_var`.

**Go behavior.** Go returns `false` when `len(t.linearizer.terms) == 2`, before calling `t.variable(...)` on the terms.

**Impact.** For `(h (+ p q))`, the reals `p` and `q` never get UTVPI variables. Their model values then come from elsewhere: g3 gives `q = 1.0`, z3 gives `0.0`.

**Reproduction.** With F6 fixed and the UTVPI header:
```
(declare-const p Real)
(declare-const q Real)
(declare-fun h (Real) Bool)
(assert (h (+ p q)))
(assert (< p 0.5))
(check-sat)
(get-model)
```
- g3 (patched for F6): `p = 0.0`, `q = 1.0`.
- z3: `p = 0.0`, `q = 0.0`.

After moving the check, the output is identical. The unpatched g3 answers `unknown` here.

**Fix.** Move the `len(terms) == 2` return so it comes after the loop that calls `t.variable(term.expression)`.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/utvpi_two_term_uf_arg.smt2` with the input above.
- Expected entry in `scriptResults`: `"sat\n((p 0.0) (q 0.0))\n"`, using `(get-value (p q))`.

<a id="smtcore-13-f8"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F8: the weighted MaxSAT theory sorts costs ascending; the C++ sorts descending

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_wmaxsat.go:154-156` (`setCostConflict`), `:199-201` (`MakeBlock`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_wmaxsat.h:130-136` (`compare_cost`), `theory_wmaxsat.cpp:236-246`, `:276-285`

**C++ behavior.** `compare_cost` is `m_mpz.gt(w[v], w[w])`, so `block()` and `mk_block()` take the heaviest variables first, until the weight reaches `min_cost`.

**Go behavior.** Go uses `weight.Cmp(...) < 0`, so the lightest variables come first. The conflict clause and the blocking clause therefore contain a different (usually larger) set of literals.

**Impact.** With `opt.maxsat_engine=wmax`, different conflict clauses and blocking lemmas change the search. In the probe the final objective was the same, but the conflict traces differ, and models can differ.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed by trace diff (`-tr:conflict`) with `opt.maxsat_engine=wmax`. The input has 5 soft constraints with weights 4, 3, 2.5, 6, 1 over Int guards (`x2.smt2` in the work dir).
- g3's first theory conflict is `w!5 w!3`.
- z3's is `w!3` alone.

After flipping the comparison, the conflict trace matches up to AST id numbering.

**Fix.** Change both comparators to `> 0`. `std::sort` is not stable; for equal weights, check whether the C++ tie order matters (normally the input order).

Related gaps:
- Go `FinalCheck` raises a cost conflict, while the C++ `final_check_eh` only normalizes and returns `FC_DONE`. Go `Assign` recomputes the cost from all assignments instead of the trail-based `m_zcost`.
- The statistics `wmaxsat num blocks` and `wmaxsat num props` are missing. z3 `-st` prints `:wmaxsat-num-blocks`.

**Regression test.** Add a unit test in `pkg/smtcore/theory_wmaxsat_test.go`, built like the existing wmax tests. Use weights 1, 5, 2 with `minimumCost = 5`, all three true. The expected `MakeBlock()` result is the single literal `(not w_b)` (weight 5), not three literals.

<a id="smtcore-13-f9"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F9: refineBound builds the guard conjunction before the right-hand side

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_str_regex_stage.go:328-372` (`refineBound`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_str.cpp:10238-10277` (`final_check_eh`, upper and lower bound refinement)

**C++ behavior.** The `lhs` items are pushed into a vector, and the `rhs` atoms are then built. `mk_and(lhs)` is created only at `assert_implication`, after `rhs`.

**Go behavior.** `guard := MkAndArray([member, bound])` is created before `rhs`.

**Impact.** The `and` node is created at a different point, which can change enode and Boolean-variable order when the guard is internalized. I patched this, but the one probe that hits it (`re.+` of a union with a length above 12) still diverges for an unrelated reason. So I could not isolate the effect.

**Reproduction.** Not isolated (see above).

**Fix.** Create `guard` after `rhs`, just before `f.imply`.

**Regression test.** Include a golden-trace vector with `(str.in.re x (re.+ (re.union (str.to.re "abc") (str.to.re "abcdefghijk"))))` and `(> (str.len x) 12)` once the other divergences are fixed.

<a id="smtcore-13-f10"></a>
#### smtcore_13-F10: theory_wmaxsat FinalCheck raises a conflict that the C++ final_check_eh does not

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/theory_wmaxsat.go:299-313` (`FinalCheck`)
- C++: `src/smt/theory_wmaxsat.cpp:181-185` (`final_check_eh`)

**C++ behavior.** `if (m_normalize) normalize(); return FC_DONE;`. All blocking happens in `assign_eh`, through `m_zcost` and `m_assigned`, with trail entries.

**Go behavior.** `FinalCheck` recomputes the cost from all true slack literals. If `cost >= minimumCost` it calls `setCostConflict` and still returns `Done`. `Assign` also recomputes the cost from scratch and blocks even when the variable was already counted or disabled. The C++ returns early with `if (m_assigned[tv] || !m_enabled[tv]) return;`.

**Impact.** There is an extra conflict at final check, and the conflict points differ when a disabled or re-assigned variable is involved. The search order diverges under `opt.maxsat_engine=wmax`.

**Reproduction.** Not separately isolated: F8 dominates the observed trace diff.

**Fix.** Port the C++ cost bookkeeping:
- Keep a trail-restored cost (push the old value on assign, restore on pop), plus `assigned` and `costs` vectors that are popped with the scope.
- In `Assign`, skip variables that are already assigned or disabled. Otherwise add the weight and call `block` once `cost >= min`.
- `FinalCheck` only returns `Done`.

**Regression test.** In `pkg/smtcore/theory_wmaxsat_test.go`, use one variable whose weight equals the minimum cost. Disable it, assign it true, run `FinalCheck`, and expect no conflict (`state.inconsistent == false`).

<a id="smtcore-14-f1"></a>
#### smtcore_14-F1: `Context.CheckSat` (plain `check-sat`) never applies `timeout` or `rlimit`; `Push`/`Pop` never push the resource limit

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/cmd_context/context.go:1428` (`(*Context).CheckSat`, solver branch at line 1456), `pkg/cmd_context/context.go:1283` (`Push`), `:1304` (`Pop`). **Outside this shard.** The producer, `pkg/smtcore/util_context_params.go:181-193` (`(*ContextParams).update`, fields `state.Timeout`, `state.RLimit`), is in the shard and is correct.
- C++: `src/cmd_context/cmd_context.cpp:1459-1460,1497-1500` (`cmd_context::check_sat`), `:1331` (`cmd_context::push`), `:1447-1449` (`cmd_context::pop`), `:1536-1544` (`cmd_context::get_consequences`)

**C++ behavior.** Every solver check runs under a cancel handler, a timer and
a scoped resource limit taken from `context_params`:
```cpp
unsigned timeout = m_params.m_timeout;
unsigned rlimit  = m_params.rlimit();
...
else if (m_solver) {
    m_check_sat_result = m_solver.get();
    m_solver->set_progress_callback(this);
    cancel_eh<reslimit> eh(m().limit());
    scoped_ctrl_c ctrlc(eh);
    scoped_timer timer(timeout, &eh);
    scoped_rlimit _rlimit(m().limit(), rlimit);
    try { r = m_solver->check_sat(num_assumptions, assumptions); }
```
`push()` does `m().limit().push(m_params.rlimit());` and `pop(n)` ends with
`while (n--) m().limit().pop();`. `get_consequences` has the same four
scoped objects as `check_sat`.

**Go behavior.** The solver branch calls the solver with nothing around it:
```go
c.progressError = nil
if err = c.solver.SetProgressCallback(c); err != nil {
    return lbool.Undef, err
}
status, err = c.solver.CheckSat(assumptions)
```
No `control.NewScopedTimer`, no `ResourceLimit().Push`. The only places in
`pkg/cmd_context` that push a limit or start a timer are `check-sat-using`
(`tactic_commands.go:452-475`), `apply`, `simplify`, `eval`, fixedpoint and
the optimization branch (`optimization_execution_scope.go`). `Push`/`Pop`
never touch `c.manager.ResourceLimit()`.

**Impact.** Any script or command line that relies on `timeout=`, `-t:`,
`rlimit=`, `(set-option :timeout N)` or `(set-option :rlimit N)` with plain
`(check-sat)` / `(check-sat-assuming ...)`: C++ answers `unknown` when the
budget runs out, `g3` ignores the budget, so it either returns a different
answer (`sat` where C++ says `unknown`) or runs without bound.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed.
`check_sat_rlimit.smt2`:
```
(set-option :rlimit 1)
(declare-const x Int)
(declare-const y Int)
(assert (> x 0))
(assert (< y x))
(check-sat)
(get-info :reason-unknown)
```
`z3`: `unknown` / `(:reason-unknown "max. resource limit exceeded")`.
`g3`: `sat` / `(:reason-unknown "")`.

Timeout: an 11-hole pigeonhole instance in QF_UF (12 pigeons, the usual
`(or p_i_0 .. p_i_10)` and pairwise `(or (not p_a_h) (not p_b_h))` clauses,
then `(check-sat)`), run with `timeout=1000`: `z3` prints `unknown` after
1.0 s; `g3` printed nothing in 20 s (killed). Same with `rlimit=100000`
(`z3` 0.05 s `unknown`; `g3` killed at 20 s). Replacing `(check-sat)` by
`(check-sat-using smt)` makes `g3` honor the timeout (1.02 s, `unknown`,
`"canceled"`), which isolates the gap to the plain check-sat path.

Push/pop sibling:
```
(set-option :rlimit 1)
(declare-const x Int)
(push)
(assert (> x 0))
(check-sat)
(get-info :reason-unknown)
(pop)
(set-option :rlimit 0)
(assert (< x 5))
(check-sat)
```
`z3`: `unknown`, `(:reason-unknown "canceled")`, `sat`.
`g3`: `sat`, `(:reason-unknown "unknown")`, `sat`.

**Fix.**
1. In `(*Context).CheckSat`, solver branch, read the context parameters and
   wrap the solver call in the same four scopes, in the C++ construction
   order (handler, timer, limit) and release them in reverse:
   ```go
   state, err := c.parameters.State()
   if err != nil { return lbool.Undef, err }
   limit := c.manager.ResourceLimit()
   handler := &contextTimeoutHandler{limit: limit, active: true} // cancel_eh<reslimit>
   timer, err := control.NewScopedTimer(state.Timeout, handler)  // scoped_timer
   if err != nil { handler.close(); return lbool.Undef, err }
   limitScope, err := control.NewLimitScope(limit, state.RLimit) // scoped_rlimit
   if err != nil { _ = timer.Close(); handler.close(); return lbool.Undef, err }
   status, err = c.solver.CheckSat(assumptions)
   limitScope.Close()
   err = errors.Join(err, timer.Close())
   handler.close()
   ```
   `contextTimeoutHandler` (`results.go:34`) and the pattern in
   `beginOptimizationExecution` (`optimization_execution_scope.go:16`) already
   exist. Use `state.Timeout`/`state.RLimit` directly, as the C++ uses
   `m_params.m_timeout` / `m_params.rlimit()`.
2. `(*Context).Push`: for each scope, after recording the scope and before
   `c.solver.Push()`, call `c.manager.ResourceLimit().Push(state.RLimit)`.
3. `(*Context).Pop`: after the trails are restored, call
   `c.manager.ResourceLimit().Pop()` once per popped scope.
4. Give `(*Context).Consequences` (`pkg/cmd_context/result_access.go:61`,
   which calls `c.solver.GetConsequences` bare at line 72) the same scopes
   as step 1 (`cmd_context.cpp:1536-1544`).

**Regression test.** SMT-LIB vectors (the runner feeds the file through
`run(bytes.NewReader(script), &out)`, so `set-option` in the file is enough):
- `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/check_sat_rlimit.smt2` = the first script above;
  `scriptResults["check_sat_rlimit.smt2"] = "unknown\n(:reason-unknown \"max. resource limit exceeded\")\n"`.
- `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/check_sat_rlimit_push_pop.smt2` = the push/pop
  script above; expected `"unknown\n(:reason-unknown \"canceled\")\nsat\n"`.
- Both are checked against the C++ by
  `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.
- Unit test in `pkg/cmd_context/context_test.go`,
  `TestCommandContextCheckSatHonorsResourceLimit`: `c := contextFixture(t)`,
  `contextMust(t, c.SetUIntOption("rlimit", 1))`, declare two Int constants
  and assert `x > 0`, `y < x` the way the neighboring tests build assertions,
  then `status, err := c.CheckSat(nil)`; expect `err == nil`,
  `status == lbool.Undef`, and that `c.manager.ResourceLimit()` has no pushed
  limit left afterwards. (Existing vectors `tactic_resource_limit_recovery.smt2`
  and `mbqi_boolean_skolem_budget.smt2` only cover `check-sat-using`.)

<a id="smtcore-14-f2"></a>
#### smtcore_14-F2: `SMTWatchList.InsertLiteral` / `RemoveLiteral` are O(n) per call where the C++ is O(1); quadratic on wide binary-clause fan-out

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/watch_list.go:85` (`(*SMTWatchList).InsertLiteral`), `pkg/smtcore/watch_list.go:106` (`(*SMTWatchList).RemoveLiteral`)
- C++: `src/smt/watch_list.h:165` (`watch_list::insert_literal`), `src/smt/watch_list.cpp:98` (`watch_list::remove_literal`), `src/smt/watch_list.cpp:37` (`watch_list::expand`)

**C++ behavior.** Literals grow downward from the end of the buffer, so a
new literal is written in front of the others without moving them, and the
buffer grows geometrically:
```cpp
void insert_literal(literal const & l) {
    if (m_data == nullptr || begin_lits_core() <= end_cls_core() + sizeof(literal))
        expand();
    begin_lits_core() -= sizeof(literal);
    *(reinterpret_cast<literal *>(m_data + begin_lits_core())) = l;
}
```
`remove_literal` shifts only the literals *in front of* the removed one and
then advances `begin_lits`; removing the newest literal moves nothing. (The
C++ context never calls `remove_literal` at all: binary clauses stay in the
watch lists until the context dies.)

**Go behavior.** Index 0 is the newest literal, so every insert shifts the
whole slice, and every removal shifts everything *behind* the removed
element:
```go
w.literals = append(w.literals, 0)
copy(w.literals[1:], w.literals[:len(w.literals)-1])
w.literals[0] = literal
...
copy(w.literals[i:], w.literals[i+1:])
w.literals = w.literals[:len(w.literals)-1]
```
The Go context does call `RemoveLiteral`, newest clause first, from
`closeClause` (`smt_boolean_propagation.go:206`) inside `popTo`
(`smt_internalizer_state.go:1218`), so each removal is the worst case.
The iteration order `Literals()` exposes is correct; only the cost differs.

**Impact.** A literal that occurs in N binary clauses costs N^2/2 literal
moves to build and again to tear down. Any input with one guard literal in
front of many clauses (`(=> p (and a1 ... aN))`, selector-guarded
assertions, at-most-one encodings) slows down quadratically; large N looks
like a hang.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. Generated script: `(set-option :smt.auto_config false)`,
`(declare-const p Bool)`, `(declare-const a_i Bool)` and
`(assert (or (not p) a_i))` for i < N, `(assert (or p a0))`, `(check-sat)`.

| N | z3 | g3 |
|---|---|---|
| 20000 | 0.14 s | 1.3 s |
| 80000 | 0.70 s | 6.2 s |
| 320000 | 3.5 s | 39.5 s |

`perf record` on `g3` at N = 320000: 42.4% of all samples are
`runtime.memmove`, 19.5% under `(*SMTInternalizerState).addClause` (the
inlined `InsertLiteral`) and 20.6% under `(*SMTInternalizerState).popTo`
(the inlined `RemoveLiteral`).

**Fix.** Keep the source layout: free space in front of the literals.
```go
type SMTWatchList struct {
	clauses []*SMTClause
	lits    []SMTLiteral // lits[begin:] are live, newest first
	begin   int
}

func (w *SMTWatchList) Literals() []SMTLiteral { // nil receiver as today
	return w.lits[w.begin:]
}
func (w *SMTWatchList) InsertLiteral(l SMTLiteral) error {
	if w == nil { return ast.ErrASTHandle }
	if w.begin == 0 { // expand(): grow by half, keep literals at the end
		live := len(w.lits)
		capacity := live + live/2 + 4
		grown := make([]SMTLiteral, capacity)
		copy(grown[capacity-live:], w.lits)
		w.lits, w.begin = grown, capacity-live
	}
	w.begin--
	w.lits[w.begin] = l
	return nil
}
func (w *SMTWatchList) RemoveLiteral(l SMTLiteral) bool {
	i := w.FindLiteral(l) // index within Literals()
	if i < 0 { return false }
	live := w.lits[w.begin:]
	copy(live[1:i+1], live[:i]) // shift the prefix, as remove_literal does
	w.begin++
	return true
}
```
Adjust `Size` (`len(w.clauses) + len(w.lits) - w.begin`), `Reset`
(`w.begin = len(w.lits)`), `ResetAndReleaseMemory` (`w.lits, w.begin = nil, 0`)
and `FindLiteral` (range over `w.lits[w.begin:]`). No caller changes: the
order returned by `Literals()` is unchanged, so traces stay identical.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/watch_list_test.go`
(`TestSMTWatchListTypedRegionsAndRemoval` shows the helpers:
`var watches SMTWatchList`, `NewSMTLiteral(v, sign)`). Add
`TestSMTWatchListLiteralInsertAndNewestFirstRemovalAreAmortizedConstant`:
insert `NewSMTLiteral(i, false)` for i in 0..299999, check
`Literals()[0] == NewSMTLiteral(299999,false)` and
`Literals()[299999] == NewSMTLiteral(0,false)`, then remove them newest
first (i from 299999 down to 0), checking `RemoveLiteral` returns true and
`Size()` ends at 0; fail if the whole test takes longer than 2 s (today the
two loops move about 360 GB of memory, tens of seconds; the fixed version
takes milliseconds). Add a middle-removal case after growth (insert 10 literals,
remove the 4th newest, expect the remaining nine in unchanged relative
order) to lock in the prefix shift. For an end-to-end guard, add the N =
80000 fan-out script as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/binary_watch_fanout.smt2`
with `scriptResults` value `"sat\n"`.

<a id="smtcore-14-f3"></a>
#### smtcore_14-F3: `ProtoModel.Eval` returns the evaluator's exception instead of catching it and returning false

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/proto_model/proto_model.go:269` (`(*ProtoModel).Eval`)
- C++: `src/smt/proto_model/proto_model.cpp:86` (`proto_model::eval`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
bool proto_model::eval(expr * e, expr_ref & result, bool model_completion) {
    m_eval.set_model_completion(model_completion);
    m_eval.set_expand_array_equalities(false);
    try {
        m_eval(e, result);
        return true;
    }
    catch (model_evaluator_exception & ex) {
        (void)ex;
        TRACE("model_evaluator", tout << ex.msg() << "\n";);
        return false;
    }
}
```
`model_evaluator_exception` is `rewriter_exception`
(`src/model/model_evaluator.h:29`): thrown for "max. steps exceeded",
"max. memory exceeded" (`model_evaluator.cpp:282-287`) and for cancellation
(`rewriter_def.h:654-656,689-691`). The caller sees `false` and carries on.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if err := p.evaluator.Evaluate(term, out); err != nil {
    return false, err
}
return true, nil
```
`Evaluate` (`pkg/model/model_evaluator.go:259`) returns the Go
`rewriterException` unchanged, so `Eval` never returns `(false, nil)`.
All five callers propagate the error (`smt_model_checker.go:443,693`,
`smt_recursive_functions.go:96`, `smt_model_finder_auf_prepare.go:39`,
`smt_candidate_validation.go:67`), and the whole quantifier model check
aborts with it.

**Impact.** MBQI and model validation when an evaluation hits
`model_evaluator.max_steps` / `model_evaluator.max_memory`, or when a
timeout or resource limit fires inside a proto-model evaluation. C++
treats the term as "could not evaluate" (the model finder drops it from the
instantiation set, `assert_neg_q_m` returns early, and so on); Go ends the
check with the exception text as the reason. The answer stays `unknown`,
but the reason text and the path taken differ.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed.
```
(set-option :model_evaluator.max_steps 9)
(set-option :smt.auto_config false)
(set-option :smt.mbqi true)
(declare-sort U 0)
(declare-fun f (U) U)
(declare-fun p (U) Bool)
(declare-const a U)
(assert (forall ((x U)) (p x)))
(assert (p (f (f (f (f (f (f (f (f a))))))))))
(check-sat)
(get-info :reason-unknown)
```
`z3`: `unknown` / `(:reason-unknown "Sort mismatch at argument #1 for function (declare-fun not (Bool) Bool) supplied sort is U")`.
`g3`: `unknown` / `(:reason-unknown "smt search quantifier model check: max. steps exceeded")`.

The first evaluation that needs more than 9 steps here is the model
finder's `eval` of the instantiation-set term `(f (f ... a))` through the
proto model, which is why I attribute the `g3` message to `ProtoModel.Eval`;
I did not single-step it. The sibling `model::eval`
(`src/model/model.cpp:79-90`) has the same catch and its Go port
`(*Model).Evaluate` (`pkg/model/model_eval.go:13`, outside this shard) also
returns the error, so that one needs the same change.

Caveat for whoever fixes this: the C++ path after a swallowed failure is
itself fragile. With `max_steps` at 7 or less on this input, `z3`
segfaults in `model_finder::restrict_sks_to_inst_set` (called from
`model_checker::check`), because `assert_neg_q_m` returned early and left
`sks` empty. A mechanical port of the catch must keep a bounds check there
instead of indexing out of range.

**Fix.**
1. In `(*ProtoModel).Eval` (the `rewriter` package is already imported):
   ```go
   if err := p.evaluator.Evaluate(term, out); err != nil {
       if rewriter.IsRewriterException(err) {
           // catch (model_evaluator_exception &): TRACE("model_evaluator", msg); return false
           return false, nil
       }
       return false, err
   }
   ```
   Emit the `model_evaluator` trace line with the exception message before
   returning, as the C++ does.
2. Make each caller (all outside this shard) follow its C++ counterpart on
   `ok == false`:
   - `smt_model_finder_auf_prepare.go:39` (`auf_solver::eval`,
     `smt_model_finder.cpp:575`) already maps `!ok` to a null value. No
     change.
   - `smt_candidate_validation.go:67` (`smt_context_inv.cpp:442,449`,
     `if (!m_proto_model->eval(n, res, false)) return true;`) already
     handles `!success`. No change.
   - `smt_model_checker.go:443`, in `auxiliaryCounterexamples`
     (`model_checker::assert_neg_q_m`, `smt_model_checker.cpp:107`): C++ is
     `if (!m_curr_model->eval(q->get_expr(), tmp, true)) return;`. Go
     discards `ok`; return early instead, and guard the later
     `restrict_sks_to_inst_set` equivalent against an empty skolem vector
     with an explicit error (C++ is undefined there).
   - `smt_recursive_functions.go:96`, in `checkRecursiveFunction`
     (`model_checker::check_rec_fun`, `smt_model_checker.cpp:337`): C++
     ignores the return value and tests the possibly null result with
     `m.is_true` / `m.is_false`; read a null result the same way.
   - `smt_model_checker.go:693`, in `checkQuantifier` (the universe
     enumeration): it also discards `ok`. I found no `proto_model::eval`
     call for it in `smt_model_checker.cpp`, so what `false` should mean
     there is for that file's reviewer to decide.

**Regression test.** New test in
`pkg/smtcore/proto_model/proto_model_test.go`,
`TestProtoModelEvalReturnsFalseOnEvaluatorException`. Build the services
the way `protoFixtureWithConfig` does, but before `NewProtoModel` set
`max_steps` to 0 in the `params` value passed as
`ModelEvaluatorConfig.Params`, with
`name := "max_steps"; protoMust(t, context.SetUIntName(&params, &name, 0))`
(the evaluator reads module `model_evaluator` through that local value). Then, as in
`TestProtoModelCleanupOwnsRewrittenFallbackUntilInstalled`, make a Bool
function `d` with `m.MkFuncDecl`, register a `model.NewFunctionInterpretation`
for it with `SetElse(true)`, build `m.MkApp(d, []ast.ASTHandle{yes})`, and
call `ok, err := p.Eval(app, protoPin(t, m, ast.ASTHandle{}), true)`.
Expected: `err == nil` and `ok == false` (today: `ok == false`,
`err` = "max. steps exceeded"). Add a second call with `max_steps` left at
its default and expect `ok == true`. The script above can go in as
`pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/proto_eval_max_steps.smt2`, but note the C++
reason text there comes from the fragile path described above, so pin only
the first line (`unknown`) unless the callers are ported exactly.

<a id="smtcore-14-f4"></a>
#### smtcore_14-F4: `ProtoModel.Cleanup` does not remove unused auxiliary declarations from the model's declaration list

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/smtcore/proto_model/cleanup.go:165` (`(*ProtoModel).Cleanup`)
- C++: `src/smt/proto_model/proto_model.cpp:219-221` (`proto_model::cleanup`), `:190` (`proto_model::remove_aux_decls_not_in_set`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
if (found_aux_fs.size() != m_aux_decls.size()) {
    remove_aux_decls_not_in_set(m_decls, found_aux_fs);
    remove_aux_decls_not_in_set(m_func_decls, found_aux_fs);
    for (func_decl* faux : m_aux_decls) {
        if (!found_aux_fs.contains(faux)) {
            unregister_decl(faux);
        }
    }
    m_aux_decls.swap(found_aux_fs);
}
```
`model_core::unregister_decl` (`src/model/model_core.cpp:86`) erases from
`m_const_decls` / `m_func_decls` but not from `m_decls`; the first
`remove_aux_decls_not_in_set` call is what keeps `m_decls` consistent.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if found.Len() != p.aux.Len() {
    for _, entry := range p.aux.Entries() {
        ...
        if err = p.core.Core().UnregisterDeclaration(entry.Key); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    p.aux = found
}
```
`ModelCore.UnregisterDeclaration` / `UnregisterConstant`
(`pkg/model/model_functions.go:161`, `pkg/model/model_core.go:223`) shrink
`functionDeclarations` / `ConstantDeclarations` only, like the C++. Nothing
prunes `ModelCore.declarations` (the `m_decls` vector), so after `Cleanup`
it still lists every dropped auxiliary declaration, whose model reference
has been released.

**Impact.** `ModelCore.NumDeclarations()` and `Declaration(i)` on a proto
model after `Cleanup` over-count and can hand out a handle to a released
declaration. Latent today: the only reader of those two accessors is
`pkg/tactic/tactic_extension_model_trace.go:122`, on final models, and
`FinalModelRetained` rebuilds the final model from the tables.

**Reproduction.** not attempted: no command-line path reads `m_decls` of a
proto model after cleanup.

**Fix.** Add a `ModelCore` method that filters `md.declarations` in place
(keep `d` unless it is auxiliary and not in the found set, preserving
order), and call it from `Cleanup` inside the
`found.Len() != p.aux.Len()` block, before the unregister loop:
```go
if err = p.core.Core().RetainDeclarations(func(d ast.ASTHandle) (bool, error) {
    aux, err := p.aux.Contains(d)
    if err != nil || !aux { return true, err }
    return found.Contains(d)
}); err != nil {
    return err
}
```
The second C++ call (on `m_func_decls`) needs no Go counterpart; the
unregister loop already removes those entries in the same relative order.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/smtcore/proto_model/cleanup_test.go` with
`TestProtoModelCleanupDropsUnusedAuxiliaryDeclarations`, using
`protoFixture`, `protoSymbol`, `protoPin` as the existing test does: make
two unary Bool functions `g` and `aux` (`m.MkFuncDecl`), give each a
`model.NewFunctionInterpretation(m, 1)` with `SetElse(true)`, register `g`
with `p.Core().RegisterFunction(g, fiG)` and `aux` with
`p.RegisterAuxFunction(aux, fiAux)`, call `p.Cleanup()`. Expected:
`p.Core().NumDeclarations()` is 1, `p.Core().Declaration(0)` is `g`, and
`p.Core().FunctionInterpretation(aux)` is nil (today `NumDeclarations()`
is 2 and `Declaration(1)` is `aux`).

### Area: SAT solver (`pkg/sat`, from `src/sat`)

*sat_01.* 96 Go files (9301 lines) of `pkg/sat`: DIMACS parsing, clause storage/sets, cleaner, asymmetric branching, elim_eqs, integrity checker, config, extension glue, plus three families with **no C++ counterpart in `src/`** (`sat_big*`, `sat_aig_*`, `sat_cut*`/`sat_lut*`). The files that port real 4.7.1 C++ (asymm_branch, cleaner, elim_eqs, clause storage/set, config, justification, integrity checker, par) are faithful: with the foreign transitive reduction switched off, g3 and `build/z3` produced identical statistics on 10 random SAT instances, apart from the renamed key in F2. The serious problem is `sat_big*`: a binary-implication-graph transitive reduction that does not exist in this C++ tree runs by default inside every SCC pass, deletes binary clauses and draws from the solver's random generator, so search, statistics and models diverge from the reference (confirmed). Findings: 0 critical, 1 high, 3 medium, 3 low. All 96 files were read in full.

*sat_02.* 53 Go files (9428 lines) of `pkg/sat`: SCC, the whole SAT simplifier (subsumption, blocked clauses, variable elimination, cleanup, reports, traces), solver construction/teardown, clause creation/attach/detach, push/pop, and conflict resolution (first-UIP, unsat core, init). All 53 files were read in full against `src/sat/sat_scc.cpp`, `sat_simplifier.cpp/.h`, `sat_clause_use_list.h/.cpp`, `sat_solver.cpp/.h`. Fidelity is very good with one exception: the Go SCC pass contains a transitive-reduction step (plus RNG draws, a parameter, a report field and statistics keys) that does not exist in this repository's C++. It is on by default and changes models, statistics and search on ordinary inputs. With `sat.scc=false` on both binaries, about 200 differential runs (random 3-SAT, Tseitin circuits with blocked-clause/variable elimination, assumption/unsat-core scripts) were identical in models, cores and `-st` statistics (memory/time lines excluded); with `(using-params sat :scc.tr false)` in g3 only, 16 further runs matched default C++ except for the statistics key of F2. Counts after de-duplication: 1 medium, 2 low. This reviewer also found the transitive-reduction defect and the renamed statistics key independently; they are recorded once, as sat_01-F1 and sat_01-F2 (numbering here therefore starts at F3).

*sat_03.* 56 files of `pkg/sat`: consequence generation (`get_consequences`, bounded and literal forms, core chunking), solver copy, decisions, display/DIMACS, dynamic subsumption, lemma minimization, GC and restart, model construction and the SAT model converter, MUS, mutex extraction, the parallel portfolio, and probing. The algorithms are, branch for branch, faithful to `sat_solver.cpp`, `sat_mus.cpp`, `sat_probing.cpp` and `sat_model_converter.cpp`; differential runs agree with `build/z3` (see Coverage notes at the end of "Needs verification"). Three divergences survive, all reproduced with the binaries: 1 high, 1 medium, 1 low. All three sit in container/orchestration code rather than in the search algorithms.

*sat_04.* This shard holds the core of `sat::solver` (propagation, search loop, simplify_problem, user push/pop, gc_var, statistics/status display, watch lists, var_queue heap, uint_set, the simplifier kernel's subsumption and resolution helpers), the Go-only `sat_xor_finder*` files, and the `inc_sat_solver` port in `pkg/sat/sat_solver/`. The solver core is a close statement-by-statement port: `propagate_core`, `check`, `bounded_search`, `propagate_and_backjump_step`, `simplify_problem`, `user_pop`/`gc_var`, the heap and the subsumption kernel all matched the C++ on re-reading. Differential runs agree with `build/z3` on 60 random incremental QF_BV scripts (sat/unsat, models, unsat cores, all SAT statistics) and on QF_FD scripts (cores, consequences, interpreted-atom reasons). Two confirmed divergences: the `sat.dimacs.display` comment lines come out in a different order (in this shard), and `check-sat-assuming` accepts non-literal assumptions (parser, outside this shard; it is what reaches the inc_sat_solver non-literal path). Counts: 0 critical, 0 high, 2 medium, 1 low. (sat_04-F1 covers the same sorted DIMACS atom lines as sat_05-F1; fix both sort sites together.)

*sat_05.* This shard is pkg/sat/tactic: goal2sat (`GoalTranslator`), sat2goal (`recoverSATGoal`), atom2bool_var, the SAT model converter and the `sat` / `sat-preprocess` tactics. Every file was compared with src/sat/tactic/{goal2sat,atom2bool_var,sat_tactic}.cpp/.h and src/ast/expr2var.cpp. The port is very faithful. The visit/convert logic, the clause order for or/and/ite/iff, `ite_extra`, unsupported-operator messages, dependency/assumption handling, unit/binary/clause recovery, and the model converter all match the C++. I also ran differential checks, about 2,700 generated scripts across 7 modes: plain Boolean, interpreted atoms with `apply sat`/`sat-preprocess`/`:print_model_converter`, xor/=>/distinct, named cores, cores with interpreted atoms, preprocess+smt models, with and without `-st`. They found no answer, model, core or goal difference. The only statistics differences are the known sat_01-F2 SCC key, plus an rlimit gap that comes from named assertions outside this shard (see Needs verification). Findings: 0 critical, 0 high, 1 medium, 1 low.

<a id="sat-01-f1"></a>
#### sat_01-F1: `satBIG.reduceTransitive` runs by default in every SCC pass; the C++ has no transitive reduction, no `scc.tr` parameter and no `sat_big`

- Severity: high
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/sat/sat_big_reduce.go:62` (`satBIG.reduceTransitive`), `pkg/sat/sat_big_edges.go:40-52` and `pkg/sat/sat_big_dfs.go:24-27` (shuffles that draw from the solver RNG), `pkg/sat/sat_big_solver.go:12` (`initLifecycle`). Trigger, outside this shard: `pkg/sat/sat_scc.go:95-99,356-360`, `pkg/sat/sat_scc_transitive.go:5-50`, `pkg/sat/sat_scc_report.go:25-32`.
- C++: `src/sat/sat_scc.cpp:61-224` (`scc::operator()`), `src/sat/sat_scc_params.pyg`. There is no `src/sat/sat_big.h` or `sat_big.cpp` (the `// Source:` headers of all six `sat_big*.go` files name files that do not exist; `git log --all -- src/sat/sat_big.cpp` is empty; the code arrived in commit 8331bcfc8 "sat: port big transitive reduction").

**C++ behavior.** `scc::operator()` ends immediately after equivalence elimination, and the only parameter is `scc`:
```cpp
        m_num_elim += to_elim.size();
        elim_eqs eliminator(m_solver);
        eliminator(roots, to_elim);
        TRACE("scc_detail", m_solver.display(tout););
        CASSERT("scc_bug", m_solver.check_invariant());
        return to_elim.size();
```
```
params=(('scc', BOOL, True, 'eliminate Boolean variables by computing strongly connected components'),))
```
No binary clause is removed and `m_rand` is not touched.

**Go behavior.** `satSCC.Update` reads a parameter the C++ does not have, defaulting to true, and `run` then calls the reduction:
```go
	key = "scc.tr"
	transitive, e := cfg.context.GetBoolFallbackName(local, &key, &g, true)
	...
	if c.transitive {
		if e = c.reduceTransitive(); e != nil {
```
`initBIG` builds the graph with the solver's own generator (`newSATBIG(&c.solver.decision.rng)`), and `doneAddingEdges`/`initDFSNumbers` call `b.random.Next()` for every edge list with two or more entries and for the root list (length minus one draws each). `reduceTransitive` then detaches every binary clause that is implied by a path (`l.detachBinClause(u.Negated(), v, edge.learned)`) and may assign units. Up to 11 rounds for non-learned and 11 for learned binaries run per SCC pass.

**Impact.** Every SAT run that reaches `simplify_problem` (after the 100-conflict burst, or at once with `sat.burst_search=0`) diverges from the C++:
1. Binary clauses are deleted that the C++ keeps, which changes resolution, subsumption, propagation order, models and all later statistics.
2. Even when nothing is deleted, the shuffles advance `decision.rng`, so every later `m_rand()` draw in `next_var` (random_freq 0.01) differs.
3. New user-visible surface: tactic parameter `scc.tr` is accepted (the C++ rejects it) and listed in `(help-tactic)`; the verbose SCC report gains ` :elim-bin N`; statistics gain `sat-scc-elim-binary`.
4. `hasBinaryEdge` (`sat_big_reduce.go:53`) scans the whole edge snapshot for every deleted edge (O(edges x deletions)); `inDeleted` is a linear list scan. The upstream code this imitates scans one watch list.
The reduction itself looks equivalence-preserving (each deleted clause is implied by a path of non-deleted clauses, the direct edge and its contrapositive are excluded), so no wrong sat/unsat answer was found; the defect is fidelity.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. Input (`$S/work/sat_01/small/s6_4.smt2`):
```
(set-option :sat.burst_search 0)
(declare-const a Bool)
(declare-const b Bool)
(declare-const c Bool)
(declare-const d Bool)
(declare-const e Bool)
(declare-const f Bool)
(assert (or b (not c)))
(assert (or c a))
(assert (or b a))
(assert (or a (not f)))
(assert (or f e))
(assert (or a e))
(assert (or b e))
(assert (or (not e) c))
(assert (or b c))
(assert (or (not c) (not b) (not a)))
(assert (or b (not f) (not c)))
(assert (or (not c) (not a) f))
(assert (or (not d) (not c) (not a)))
(assert (or (not c) (not a) (not f)))
(assert (or e b d))
(assert (or (not b) c e))
(assert (or (not f) c (not d)))
(assert (or (not a) d b))
(check-sat-using sat)
(get-model)
```
`build/z3` prints `sat` and a model with f=false, b=true, c=true, a=false, e=true. `g3` prints the same five plus an extra `(define-fun d () Bool false)`. Replacing the check with `(check-sat-using (using-params sat :scc.tr false))` makes g3's output byte-identical to z3's; z3 itself rejects that variant with `(error "line 26 column 43: invalid using-params combinator, unknown parameter scc.tr")`.
Further evidence, default parameters: random 3-SAT, 250 variables, ratio 4.2, no binary clauses at all (so nothing is eliminated): z3 1702 conflicts, g3 12319; with `scc.tr false` g3 has 1702 and identical statistics. With `sat.random_freq=0` g3 equals z3 on those instances, which isolates the RNG draws. `-v:10 sat.burst_search=0` on a three-clause chain `(or (not a) b) (or (not b) c) (or (not a) c)` plus three ternary clauses shows z3 ` (sat-scc :elim-vars 0 :clauses 3 ...` versus g3 ` (sat-scc :elim-vars 0 :elim-bin 1 :clauses 3 ...`, `:mk-binary-clause 6` versus `5`, and g3's extra `:sat-scc-elim-binary 1`.

Independent confirmation from the DIMACS fuzzer: on five random 3-SAT files (60 to 150 variables) whose `-st` statistics differed from `build/z3` (for example 325 conflicts in g3 against 363 in z3 on an 80-variable instance, and `(sat-subsumer ... :threshold 99999678)` against `99999673` in the first simplifier round at `-v:10`), a scratch build with the `scc.tr` default changed to `false` gave statistics identical to z3 on all five. About one random instance in ten of this size is affected.

A second reviewer (shard sat_02) found the same defect independently with a smaller script, in which no binary clause is removed and the whole difference comes from the random draws:

```
(declare-const x1 Bool)
(declare-const x3 Bool)
(declare-const x4 Bool)
(declare-const x5 Bool)
(declare-const x7 Bool)
(assert (or x3 x5 (not x1)))
(assert (or x5 x4 x7))
(assert (or x4 x3))
(assert (or x4 x7))
(check-sat-using (using-params sat :burst_search 0))
(get-model)
```

`build/z3` prints `sat` and the model `x3=false x1=false x5=false x4=true x7=false`; `g3` prints `sat` and `x3=false x1=false x4=true` (x5 and x7 are missing). `(help-tactic)` prints the `scc.tr` line 11 times in g3 and never in z3.

**Fix.** Remove the feature; it is not part of the code being ported.
1. `pkg/sat/sat_scc.go`: delete the `if c.transitive { ... }` block (356-360); delete fields `big`, `numElimBinary`, `reportNumElimBinary`, `transitive` (29-36); in `Update` drop lines 95-99 and return after setting `c.enabled`; `resetStatistics` resets only `numElim`; `collectStatistics` takes one key again (see F2); drop line 210; `collectSCCParamDescrs` (445-450) inserts only `scc`.
2. `pkg/sat/sat_scc_report.go:25-32`: delete the `:elim-bin` block.
3. Delete `pkg/sat/sat_scc_transitive.go`, `sat_big.go`, `sat_big_dfs.go`, `sat_big_edges.go`, `sat_big_reach.go`, `sat_big_reduce.go`, `sat_big_solver.go` and their tests (`sat_big_test.go`, `sat_big_solver_test.go`, `sat_scc_transitive_test.go`). `satAIGFinder` (`sat_aig_finder*.go`, F7) is the only other user of `satBIG` and is test-only; delete it with them.
4. Tests that currently lock in the non-source behavior must change: `sat_scc_transitive_test.go` (`TestSATSCCTransitiveParameterUpdate` asserts "source scc.tr default"), `sat_solver_statistics_test.go:27-28,57,71,81,86-90,182`, `sat_solver_report_params_test.go:15` (`satSolverChildDescriptorNames` ends in `scc scc.tr`).

<a id="sat-01-f3"></a>
#### sat_01-F3: malformed DIMACS input: different diagnostic text and exit status

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/sat/dimacs.go:62-64` (`dimacsStreamBuffer.parseInt`), surfaced through `pkg/shell/dimacs_frontend.go:126` and `pkg/cmd/g3/main.go:263-270`
- C++: `src/sat/dimacs.cpp:78-82` (`parse_int`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
    if (*in < '0' || *in > '9') {
        std::cerr << "(error, \"unexpected char: " << *in << "\")\n";
        exit(3);
```
**Go behavior.**
```go
		return 0, fmt.Errorf("%w: %d", ErrDIMACSUnexpectedChar, b.value)
```
The error reaches the generic branch of `main`, which prints `ERROR: <err>` and exits with `ErrorInternalFatal`. The comment above `ParseDIMACS` documents returning an error instead of exiting, but the observable text and status still differ.

**Impact.** Scripts that key on the diagnostic or on exit status 3 see something else.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. File `bad1.cnf`:
```
p cnf 3 2
1 -2 0
2 x 0
```
z3: stderr `(error, "unexpected char: 120")`, exit 3. g3: stderr `ERROR: sat: DIMACS unexpected character: 120`, exit 110. An unterminated last clause (`2 3` at end of file) gives `(error, "unexpected char: -1")` / exit 3 versus `ERROR: sat: DIMACS unexpected character: -1` / exit 110.

**Fix.** In `pkg/sat/dimacs.go` return a typed error, e.g. `type DIMACSUnexpectedCharError struct{ Char int }` with `Error()` and `Unwrap() error { return ErrDIMACSUnexpectedChar }`. In `pkg/cmd/g3/main.go`, before the generic branch, add:
```go
		var dimacsError *sat.DIMACSUnexpectedCharError
		if errors.As(err, &dimacsError) {
			fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "(error, \"unexpected char: %d\")\n", dimacsError.Char)
			os.Exit(3)
		}
```

**Regression test.** `pkg/sat/dimacs_test.go`, extend `TestParseDIMACSMalformedInputPreservesReachedPrefix` to require `errors.As(err, &typed)` and `typed.Char` equal to 120, -1 and 0 for its three rows. `pkg/cmd/g3/dimacs_frontend_error_statistics_test.go`, extend `TestDIMACSFrontendMalformedPrefixAndStatistics` (it already feeds `"p cnf 2 2\n1 0\nx\n"` through `runArguments`) to check a small exported-for-test helper that maps the error to `(error, "unexpected char: 120")\n` and status 3.

<a id="sat-01-f4"></a>
#### sat_01-F4: `parseInt` accumulates in 64-bit `int`; a literal beyond 32 bits makes g3 allocate billions of variables where the C++ answers

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/sat/dimacs.go:65-74` (`dimacsStreamBuffer.parseInt`), `pkg/sat/dimacs.go:88-102` (`readClause`)
- C++: `src/sat/dimacs.cpp:66,84-89` (`parse_int`), `src/sat/dimacs.cpp:103-107` (`read_clause`)

**C++ behavior.** `int val = 0; ... val = val*10 + (*in - '0');` with a 32-bit `int`; the reference build wraps. `var = abs(parsed_lit)` and `while (static_cast<unsigned>(var) >= solver.num_vars()) solver.mk_var();` use 32-bit values.

**Go behavior.** `value := 0` is a 64-bit `int`, so no wrap; `for uint64(variable) >= uint64(n)` then calls `MkVar` until the count reaches the 64-bit value, and `BoolVar(variable)` truncates afterwards.

**Impact.** A corrupt or hostile CNF with one oversized literal exhausts memory in g3. Signed overflow is formally undefined in C++, so this is a divergence from the reference binary rather than from the language standard.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. File `big1.cnf` containing the single line `1 4294967298 0`: z3 prints `sat` and `1 -2` (4294967298 wraps to 2). g3 under `ulimit -v 4000000` dies with `fatal error: out of memory` inside `satSolverVariableState.mkVar` called from `dimacsStreamBuffer.readClause` (`dimacs.go:97`).

**Fix.** Make `parseInt` return `int32` and accumulate with wraparound, and keep the 32-bit comparisons:
```go
	var value int32
	for b.value >= '0' && b.value <= '9' {
		value = value*10 + int32(b.value-'0')
		b.advance()
	}
```
In `readClause`: `variable := parsed; if variable < 0 { variable = -variable }`, loop `for uint32(variable) >= n`, literal `MakeLiteral(BoolVar(uint32(variable)), parsed < 0)`.

**Regression test.** `pkg/sat/dimacs_test.go`, `TestParseDIMACSLiteralWrapsAt32Bits`: `solver, _, _ := satSolverCheckFixture(t)`; `ParseDIMACS(strings.NewReader("1 4294967298 0\n"), solver)` returns nil; `solver.sourceNumVars()` is 3; `solver.appendBinaryClauses(nil, false)` holds one pair, literals `MakeLiteral(1,false)` and `MakeLiteral(2,false)`.

<a id="sat-01-f6"></a>
#### sat_01-F6: `ReadDIMACSCNF` is a line/field tokenizer, not the C++ character scanner

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/sat/dimacs_parse.go:14-67` (`ReadDIMACSCNF`), consumed by `pkg/api/api_simple_solver_load_dimacs.go:19`
- C++: `src/sat/dimacs.cpp:64-127` (`parse_int`, `read_clause`, `parse_dimacs_core`), called from `src/api/api_solver.cpp:169-172`

**C++ behavior.** One character of lookahead; a number ends at the first non-digit, so `1-2 0` and `1+2 0` are the clause {1,-2} / {1,2}; values wrap at 32 bits.

**Go behavior.** `strings.Fields(line)` then `strconv.ParseInt(field, 10, 32)`: `1-2` is one field and is rejected with `ErrDIMACSParse`; values outside int32 are rejected; `strings.Fields` also splits on Unicode spaces (U+0085, U+00A0) that the C++ treats as an unexpected character.

**Impact.** Only the API path that loads a `.dimacs` file. Inputs the shell front end (which uses the faithful `ParseDIMACS`, `dimacs.go:112`) accepts are rejected here.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted from the command line (API only). The shell path was checked: `1-2 0` / `2 +3 0` / `-0` gives `unsat` in both binaries.

**Fix.** Implement `ReadDIMACSCNF` on top of `dimacsStreamBuffer`: loop `skipWhitespace`; on -1 stop; on `c`/`p` `skipLine`; otherwise read literals with `parseInt` until 0 and append the clause, tracking the largest magnitude. Delete the `strings.Fields` loop. Apply F4's 32-bit `parseInt` first.

**Regression test.** `pkg/sat/dimacs_parse_test.go`, next to `TestParseDIMACSRetainsClauseOrderAndSigns`: `ReadDIMACSCNF(strings.NewReader("p cnf 3 2\n1-2 0\n2 +3 0 c tail\n"))` must return clauses `[[1,-2],[2,3]]` and `VariableCount == 3`.

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/sat/sat_aig_*.go` (22 files), `pkg/sat/sat_cut*.go` (15 files), `pkg/sat/sat_lut_*.go` (8 files); internal defect at `pkg/sat/sat_lut_run.go:34-48` (`satLUTFinder.Run`)

**C++ behavior.** Not present in this tree.

**Go behavior.** `newSATCutSimplifierLive` (`sat_cut_simplifier_live.go:11`) is the only entry point and is called only from `_test.go` files, so none of this code runs in `g3`. Reading it for internal correctness found one defect: in `Run`, a clause `d` that passes the 32-bit variable filter but whose variables are not a subset of the base clause (e.g. base over variables 1,2,3 and `d` over 33,34,35) makes `l.extract` return false, and the fall-through still consumes it:

				if l.extract(d.Literals, pos) { ... found = true; break }

**Fix.** Delete the three families and their tests together with `sat_big*` (F1). If they are kept, guard the fall-through with `satLUTSubset(d.Literals, pos)`.

- C++: `src/sat/sat_solver.h:481` (`typedef hashtable<unsigned, u_hash, u_eq> index_set`), `src/sat/sat_solver.cpp:3293-3296` (`solver::fixup_consequence_core`), `:3618-3621` (`solver::extract_fixed_consequences1`), `src/util/hashtable.h:323-351,377-396,601-627`

**C++ behavior.** `index_set` is an open-addressing `core_hashtable` with identity hash, initial capacity 8, linear probing, and growth when `(size+deleted)*4 > capacity*3`. Its iterator walks the slots `0..capacity-1`, so the order of the elements is by `literal_index & (capacity-1)` (collisions resolved by insertion order), not by insertion order. That order is what the solver emits:
```cpp
// extract_fixed_consequences1
cons.push_back(lit);
index_set::iterator it = s.begin(), end = s.end();
for (; it != end; ++it) cons.push_back(to_literal(*it));
// fixup_consequence_core
for (; it != end; ++it) m_core.push_back(to_literal(*it));
```
`s |= m_antecedents.find(v)` inserts the stored set's elements in the stored set's slot order.

**Go behavior.** The set is an insertion-ordered dictionary, and `capture()` returns keys in insertion order:
```go
type satSolverIndexSet struct {
	keys   insdict.Dict[uint32, struct{}]
	...
for k := range s.keys.All() { s.view.keys = append(s.view.keys, k) }
```
The manifest records this as intentional ("SAT antecedents now use map[uint32]*satSolverIndexSet and concrete insdict.Dict[uint32,struct{}] sets. ... Native insertion order replaces physical bucket order. Removed source hashtable capacity, probing, tombstones ..."), and the header of `sat_solver_index_set.go` says "Concrete insertion-ordered indices for the retained SAT consequence algorithm." The deviation is observable.

**Impact.** Every consequence whose explanation has two or more assumptions can list them in a different order, which `inc_sat_solver` turns into a differently ordered `(and ...)` premise on stdout; the same holds for the unsat core rebuilt by `fixup_consequence_core` on the bounded path (`sat.restart.max` set) and for the `sat` TRACE lines at `sat_solver.cpp:3289` and `:3585`. The answers are logically equivalent, but the printed result differs from C++ on a seven-line input.

**Reproduction.** `$S/work/sat_03/c1.smt2`:
```
(set-logic QF_FD)
(declare-const a Bool)
(declare-const b Bool)
(declare-const c Bool)
(declare-const d Bool)
(declare-const e Bool)
(declare-const x Bool)
(declare-const y Bool)
(declare-const z Bool)
(assert (=> (and e d c b a) x))
(assert (=> (and c a) y))
(assert (=> (and x y d) z))
(get-consequences (a b c d e) (x y z))
```
`build/z3`:
```
sat

(=> (and b c d a e) x)
(=> (and c a) y)
(=> (and b c d a e) z)
```
`bin/g3` and `bin/g3fix5`:
```
sat

(=> (and d a b c e) x)
(=> (and a c) y)
(=> (and d a b c e) z)
```
`build_trace/z3 -tr:sat` shows the C++ set for `x` as `5: 0 4 1 2 3` (literal indices 0,8,2,4,6: slots 0,1,2,4,6); the Go order `0 2 3 4 1` is the order in which the clause `(5 -0 -2 -3 -4 -1)` was scanned. A three-assumption input (`(assert (=> (and c b a) x))`, `(get-consequences (a b c) (x))`) already differs: `(and a b c)` vs `(and b a c)`. A 120-instance random comparison (`$S/work/sat_03/fz_gen.py`) found no difference other than this ordering.

**Fix.** Port the table instead of substituting it, the way `pkg/ast/ast_obj_map.go`, `pkg/ast/rewriter/seq_rewriter_in_re.go` (`seqUMap`) and `pkg/muz/rel/compiler_variable_order.go` (`uMapOrder`) already do:
1. In `sat_solver_index_sets.go` replace `keys insdict.Dict[uint32, struct{}]` with a slot array (`[]struct{key uint32; used bool}`, length = capacity, initially 8) and a `size` counter.
2. `insert(k)`: if `size<<2 > cap*3`, allocate `2*cap` and re-place the used slots in slot order (`move_table`); then probe from `k & (cap-1)` to the end and wrap to the start; return if the key is found, otherwise take the first free slot.
3. `capture()`: collect used slots from index 0 upward.
4. `union(other)` (`operator|=`): insert `other`'s elements in `other`'s slot order. `assign(other)` (`operator=`): `reset()` then insert in `other`'s slot order. `reset()`: mark all slots free, and halve the capacity when `cap > 16` and more than 3/4 of the slots were already free (`hashtable.h:286-308`).
5. `satSolverIndexMap.insert(k, value)` is `m_table.insert(key_data(k, v))`: a copy construction (`copy_table` at the same capacity, source slot order) followed by a copy assignment into the map entry (`reset()` plus inserts in the temporary's slot order; `core_hashtable` has no move assignment). For exact layouts, keep the map itself as a ported `u_map` (slot array of entries, each holding its `satSolverIndexSet`), because `m_antecedents.reset()` only marks entries free and a reused entry keeps the capacity of its stale set; with a Go `map` plus fresh sets the order is right except for collision tie-breaks after a set has once grown past capacity 16.
6. The two trace helpers in `sat_solver_consequences_trace.go:69,132` iterate `row.keys.All()` directly; switch them to the slot-order iteration.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/sat/sat_solver_index_set_test.go` (it has `satNativeIndexValues(t, &set)` and uses `satSolverCheckFixture(t)`): add `TestSATSolverIndexSetSourceSlotOrder` that (a) inserts 6,4,2,8,16 and expects `[8 16 2 4 6]`; (b) inserts 0,2,4,6,8,10,12 and expects `[0 8 2 10 4 12 6]`, then inserts 14 and expects `[0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14]` (growth to 16); (c) builds `A={6}`, `B` by inserting 4 then 2, calls `A.union(&B)` and expects `[2 4 6]`; (d) stores `B` with `s.antecedents.insert(7, &B)` and expects `[2 4]` from `s.antecedents.find(7)`. The existing `TestSATSolverConsequenceNativeIndexOrderAndDeepMapCopy` keeps passing only because its keys 17,1,9 all collide in slot 1; the "4096-operation union/assignment oracle" test named in the manifest must compare against a slot-order model instead of insertion order. Add the input above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/get_consequences_fd_premise_order.smt2` with the `scriptResults` entry `"sat\n\n(=> (and b c d a e) x)\n(=> (and c a) y)\n(=> (and b c d a e) z)\n"`; `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` checks it against the C++.

<a id="sat-03-f2"></a>
#### sat_03-F2: `satParallelPortfolio` transfers the winning worker's model and core after all lanes ran; C++ transfers at first finish, so the owner's own `check` result overwrites it

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/sat/sat_solver_parallel_portfolio.go:27-40,42-75` (`checkParallelSpan`, `satParallelPortfolio.run`), `pkg/sat/sat_solver_parallel_result.go:7-27` (`adopt`)
- C++: `src/sat/sat_solver.cpp:830-880` (`solver::check_par`)

**C++ behavior.** Inside the lane loop, the first lane to finish records its result and, if it is a worker, copies its model or core into the owner immediately; only the other workers are cancelled, so the owner's own `check(num_lits, lits)` always runs to completion and its `init_search`/`mk_model` rewrite `m_core`/`m_model`. Only the statistics copy is after the loop.
```cpp
if (first) {
    if (r == l_true && i < num_extra_solvers)
        set_model(solvers[i]->get_model());
    else if (r == l_false && i < num_extra_solvers) {
        m_core.reset(); m_core.append(solvers[i]->get_core());
    }
    for (int j = 0; j < num_extra_solvers; ++j)
        if (i != j) rlims[j].cancel();
}
...
set_par(nullptr);
if (finished_id != -1 && finished_id < num_extra_solvers)
    m_stats = solvers[finished_id]->m_stats;
```

**Go behavior.** `run` executes the lanes in index order (workers first, owner last), which is exactly the C++ loop with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`, but it only records `p.finished, p.result` and defers the model/core copy to `adopt()`, called after the owner lane has finished:
```go
if err = p.run(count, span); err != nil { ... }
if err = p.adopt(); err != nil { ... }   // setModel(&winner.model) / core copy / stats
```
So the worker's model replaces the model the owner computed afterwards.

**Impact.** With `sat.parallel_threads > 1` the model (and, for unsat with assumptions, the core) reported by the Go port is worker 0's, while C++ reports the owner's. The C++ loop is racy for statistics, but not for the model: it is the owner's in every run, with or without real threads.

**Reproduction.** `$S/work/sat_03/par4.smt2`:
```
(set-option :sat.parallel_threads 2)
(set-option :sat.random_freq 1.0)
(declare-const p0 Bool)
(declare-const p1 Bool)
(declare-const p2 Bool)
(declare-const p3 Bool)
(declare-const p4 Bool)
(declare-const p5 Bool)
(assert (or p0 p1 p2))
(assert (or p3 p4 p5))
(assert (or (not p0) (not p3) p1))
(check-sat-using sat)
(get-value (p0 p1 p2 p3 p4 p5))
```
`build/z3` (five runs, and also with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`): `sat`, `p0 false, p1 false, p2 true, p3 true, p4 false, p5 false`. `bin/g3` and `bin/g3fix5`: `sat`, `... p3 false, p4 false, p5 true`. Replacing the first option by `(set-option :sat.random_seed 2531011)` (the owner's generator state after its one draw for the worker seed) gives the C++ parallel model in both binaries; `(set-option :sat.random_seed 38)` (the worker's seed) gives the Go parallel model in both binaries. With `-st` and `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` C++ reports `:decisions 4` (worker 0's statistics) together with the owner's model, which is what the fix below produces; with real threads the statistics vary between 4 and 3 from run to run.

**Fix.** In `satParallelPortfolio.run`, where `p.finished` is first set (`sat_solver_parallel_portfolio.go:61`), do the transfer before continuing with later lanes, and leave only the statistics copy in `adopt`:
```go
p.finished, p.result = i, r
if i < len(p.workers) {
	if err := p.transfer(p.workers[i], r); err != nil { // setModel / core copy
		return err
	}
}
for j, limit := range p.limits { ... }
```
`transfer` is the `switch p.result` part of today's `adopt` (`sat_solver_parallel_result.go:12-24`); `adopt` keeps `p.owner.copyParallelMainStatistics(winner)` (C++ line 878-880). The owner lane then overwrites model/core through its own `checkSpan`, as in C++. No other call site is affected.

**Regression test.** Add `TestSATParallelPortfolioOwnerLaneResultSurvivesChildWinner` to `pkg/sat/sat_parallel_portfolio_sat_test.go`, next to `TestSATParallelPortfolioChildWinnerPublishesModel`, using `satParallelPortfolioFixture(t, 2)` and `satSolverCheckFixture(t)`: build three solvers with `random_freq = 1.0`, six variables (`s.MkVar(false, true)`) and the three clauses above (`s.MkClause`): (1) the parallel fixture; (2) a single-lane fixture with `random_seed = 2531011`; (3) a single-lane fixture with `random_seed = 38`. After `Check(nil)` on each, require `AppendModel` of (1) to equal that of (2) and to differ from that of (3) (guards that the instance discriminates), and `s.decision.decisions` of (1) to equal that of (3) (statistics still come from the winning worker; at SMT level the two are 4 and 4, the owner alone has 3). The two existing child-winner tests cancel the owner, so they pass before and after. Add the input above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/sat_parallel_owner_model.smt2` with `scriptResults` entry `"sat\n((p0 false)\n (p1 false)\n (p2 true)\n (p3 true)\n (p4 false)\n (p5 false))\n"`; run the C++ comparison as `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` so the reference side is deterministic.

<a id="sat-03-f3"></a>
#### sat_03-F3: `exchangeParallelBound` never prints the `(sat-sync out: N in: M)` verbose line

- Severity: low
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/sat/sat_solver_parallel_exchange.go:5-52` (`satSolverConflictResolution.exchangeParallelBound`)
- C++: `src/sat/sat_solver.cpp:898-924` (`solver::exchange_par`)

**C++ behavior.** The function counts exported and imported units and reports them:
```cpp
if (lit.var() < m_par_num_vars) { ++num_out; out.push_back(lit); }
...
if (lvl(lit.var()) != 0 || value(lit) != l_true) { ++num_in; assign(lit, justification()); }
...
if (num_in > 0 || num_out > 0) {
    IF_VERBOSE(1, verbose_stream() << "(sat-sync out: " << num_out << " in: " << num_in << ")\n";);
}
```

**Go behavior.** The export and import loops are ported, without the counters and without the message; `grep -n "sat-sync" pkg/sat/*.go` finds nothing.

**Impact.** Verbose output at level 1 or higher lacks these lines whenever `sat.parallel_threads > 1` and a lane has level-0 units at a restart. No effect on search.

**Reproduction.** `$S/work/sat_03/par3.smt2` (a unit clause `(assert u)` in front of a random 140-variable, 590-clause 3-SAT instance, `(check-sat-using sat)`), run as `-v:1 sat.parallel_threads=2`: `build/z3` prints `(sat-sync out: 1 in: 0)` twice on stderr; `bin/g3` and `bin/g3fix5` print none, although they restart (eight `(sat-restart ...)` lines).

**Fix.** In `exchangeParallelBound` count `numOut` in the export loop and `numIn` in the import branch that calls `p.assign`, and after the import loop:
```go
if numIn > 0 || numOut > 0 {
	if enabled, err := diagnostic.ProcessVerboseEnabled(1); err != nil { return err } else if enabled {
		out, err := diagnostic.BorrowProcessVerboseStream() // then AppendCString/AppendUint32 as in
		...                                                  // sat_solver_consequence_verbose.go
	}
}
```
The text is `"(sat-sync out: "`, `numOut`, `" in: "`, `numIn`, `")\n"`. The message must be emitted also when the import loop stops early on `inconsistent`.

**Regression test.** Add `TestSATParallelExchangeSourceSyncVerbose` to `pkg/sat/sat_parallel_exchange_test.go`, capturing the verbose stream the way `TestSATSolverBoundedConsequencesSourceAbortVerbose` (`sat_solver_bounded_consequence_verbose_test.go`) does (`satInspectionStream`, `diagnostic.SetProcessVerboseStream`, `diagnostic.SetProcessVerbosityLevel(1)`): create a solver with `satSolverCheckFixture(t)`, one variable and the unit clause `MkClause([]Literal{MakeLiteral(0,false)})`, bind `SetParallelExchange(NewParallelUnitExchange())`, call `s.conflict.exchangeParallel()` at scope level 0 and expect the stream to contain exactly `"(sat-sync out: 1 in: 0)\n"`; call it again and expect no second line.

#### sat_04-F1: `Solver.finishDIMACS` sorts the atom map by variable; C++ prints `c <var> <atom>` lines in `obj_map` table order

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/sat/sat_solver/solver_trace.go:229` (`Solver.finishDIMACS`); same defect outside this shard at `pkg/sat/tactic/sat_tactic_trace.go:88` (`SATTactic.writeDIMACSAtoms`)
- C++: `src/sat/sat_solver/inc_sat_solver.cpp:165-169` (`inc_sat_solver::check_sat`); `src/sat/tactic/sat_tactic.cpp:71-75` (`sat_tactic::imp::operator()`)

**C++ behavior.** It iterates the `atom2bool_var` `obj_map` directly, in hash-table order:
```cpp
if (r == l_undef && m_solver.get_config().m_dimacs_display) {

    }
}
```

```go
entries, err := s.encoder.atoms.Entries()
...
sort.Slice(entries, func(left, right int) bool { return entries[left].Variable < entries[right].Variable })
for _, entry := range entries {
    if _, err = fmt.Fprintf(s.output, "c %d ", entry.Variable); err != nil {
```

**Impact.** Anyone using `sat.dimacs.display=true` on QF_BV (inc_sat_solver) or on the `sat` tactic gets the same DIMACS clauses but the variable/atom comment lines in a different order from z3. Output text differs; answers do not.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. `t2.smt2`:

(declare-const y (_ BitVec 3))

(push)

`build/z3 sat.dimacs.display=true t2.smt2`: the first comment block is `c 1 k!0`, `c 3 p`, `c 4 q`, `c 6 k!5`, `c 9 k!4`, `c 2 k!3`, `c 7 k!2`, `c 10 k!1`, `c 5 r`. `bin/g3` (and `g3fix5`) print `c 1 k!0`, `c 2 k!3`, `c 3 p`, `c 4 q`, `c 5 r`, `c 6 k!5`, `c 7 k!2`, `c 9 k!4`, `c 10 k!1`. The second block (after the second `p cnf`) differs the same way. I built a scratch binary with an overlay that deletes only the two `sort.Slice` lines (`$S/work/sat_04/ov/`, binary `$S/work/sat_04/g3nosort`). Make the same change in `pkg/sat/tactic/sat_tactic_trace.go` `writeDIMACSAtoms` (line 88 and the import). Keep `Expr2Var.Entries` returning `ObjMap` table order. That is what the C++ `obj_map` iteration produces, and the overlay build confirms it.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/sat_dimacs_display_atom_order.smt2` containing the script above. The CLI must run it with `sat.dimacs.display=true`. Check it against the C++ with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.
