- Assert that the `mk_empty` / `add_fact` / `operator()` lines appear in the order z3 shows.
- Store the vector as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/check_table_verbose.smt2`. Expected stdout is `sat`, which goes in the `scriptResults` table.
- Stdout is identical in both binaries, so the C++ reference runner (`G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`) will not catch the stderr part. The new test has to compare stderr itself.

<a id="muz-rel-02-f2"></a>
#### muz_rel_02-F2: external-relation rule evaluation is a Go-only evaluator, not the rel_context/dl_compiler pipeline

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_rules.go:72-698` (`classifyExternalFactRule`, `ExecuteExternalFactRulesWithOptions`), `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_head_assembly.go:29` (`assembleExternalRuleHead`), `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_schedule.go:28` (`planExternalRuleComponents`), `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_interpreted.go:132` (`filterExternalRuleInterpreted`); caller `pkg/muz/fp/datalog_external_rules.go:98`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/rel_context.cpp` (`saturate` → `transform_rules` → `compiler::compile`), `src/muz/rel/dl_compiler.cpp:449-740` (`compile_rule_evaluation_run`), `src/muz/rel/dl_external_relation.cpp`

**C++ behavior.**
- With the external plugin, C++ rules still go through the normal relation engine. `rel_context::transform_rules` applies coi filter, interp-tail simplifier, inliner, `mk_simple_joins` (at most two positive tails per rule) and the unbound compressor. The compiler then emits generic instructions.
- For a single tail, constants are removed with `make_select_equal_and_project`. Two tails use `make_join_project`, which drops columns not needed later (`get_local_indexes_for_projection`).
- Interpreted tails become one `mk_filter_interpreted` or `make_filter_interpreted_and_project`, using `binding[m_free_vars.size()-v]`.
- Each of these instructions becomes an `OP_RA_*` reduce/reduce_assign callback to the user (`OP_RA_PROJECT`, `OP_RA_JOIN`, `OP_RA_SELECT`, `OP_RA_FILTER`, `OP_RA_UNION`/`OP_RA_WIDEN`, and so on).
```cpp
SASSERT(pt_len<=2); //we require rules to be processed by the mk_simple_joins rule transformer plugin
...
make_select_equal_and_project(single_res, c, single_res_expr.size(), single_res, dealloc, acc);
...
make_filter_interpreted_and_project(filtered_res, app_renamed, remove_columns, filtered_res, dealloc, acc);
```

**Go behavior.**
- `ExecuteExternalFactRulesWithOptions` classifies each rule directly and does not run any of the rel_context transformers. Only the similarity compressor is applied, in `muz/fp`.
- Constant tail arguments are handled by clone + `FilterEqual` (`prepareExternalRuleTail`), not select-and-project.
- All positive tails are joined left to right with no intermediate projection (`JoinExternalRelations(value, secondValue, ...)`, lines 521-542). Unbound columns are added with `NewTotal` joins.
- Projection happens only in `assembleExternalRuleHead`. The recursion schedule (`planExternalRuleComponents`, initial delta = `Clone()` of the full head relation) is Go-designed.
- The file header calls this "specialized for ... external_relation operations".

**Impact.** API users who install external-relation callbacks (`SetExternalRelationCallbacks`) receive a different number, order and shape of `reduce`/`reduce_assign` calls than z3 sends:
- different `OP_RA_*` declarations and parameters;
- no `OP_RA_PROJECT` before joins;
- no auxiliary-predicate relations from `mk_simple_joins`;
- different fresh `T!n` constants.

Callbacks that keep state or use widening (`compile_with_widening`) can therefore produce different relations. Not reachable from SMT-LIB, because the external plugin is registered only through the API.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: there is no command-line path to the external plugin. Smallest scenario: a program with the rule `q(x) :- p(x, y), r(y, 1)` and recording callbacks. z3 issues a `select_equal_and_project`/`project` on `r` and a `join_project`. Go issues `clone`, `filter(= (:var 1) 1)`, `join`, then `project`/`rename` at head assembly.

**Fix.** Remove the Go-only evaluator. Route external predicates through the same `rel_context` pipeline that the table backends use: `transform_rules`, then the dl_compiler port in `pkg/muz/rel/compiler*.go`, then instruction execution. The compiler's generic project, join, filter, union and rename ops must dispatch to the `ExternalRelation` methods, which already implement the per-op `OP_RA_*` reductions faithfully.
- Delete `classifyExternalFactRule`, `planExternalRuleComponents` and `assembleExternalRuleHead` once their callers move to the compiler.
- Keep `ExternalRuleExecutionOptions` only as plumbing for `compile_with_widening` / `all_or_nothing_deltas` into the compiler.

**Regression test.**
- Add `TestExternalRelationCallbackSequenceMatchesCompiler` to `pkg/muz/fp`, next to the existing external-relation tests (`grep -l SetExternalRelationCallbacks pkg/muz/fp/*_test.go`).
- Build the engine and predicates with the same helpers those tests use. Install `rel.ExternalRelationCallbacks` that append the kind and parameters of every declaration to a slice, then return `ast.ASTHandle{}`/nil to use the fallback.
- Rules: `p(1,2). r(2,1). q(X) :- p(X,Y), r(Y,1).` Query `q`.
- Assert the recorded `OP_RA_*` sequence equals the sequence z3 produces. Capture it once from a small C program against `build/z3`'s `libz3` using `Z3_fixedpoint_init`, `Z3_fixedpoint_set_reduce_app` and `Z3_fixedpoint_set_reduce_assign_callback`, and store it in `pkg/muz/fp/test_vectors/external_callback_sequence.txt`.

<a id="muz-rel-02-f3"></a>
#### muz_rel_02-F3: external/interval product union with delta (and unaligned union) skips C++ `mk_empty`/`clone` callbacks

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/external_interval_product_union.go:144-204` (`ExternalIntervalProduct.Union`, `canonicalizeUnalignedUnion`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_product_relation.cpp:651-719` (`aligned_union_fn::operator()`), `:751-772` (`unaligned_union_fn::operator()`)

**C++ behavior.** The aligned union allocates a fresh delta for every component twice: once in the side-union loop, even when no side union is possible, and again in the basic-union loop.
```cpp
for (unsigned i = 0; i < num; ++i) {
    relation_base* idelta = delta ? &(*delta)[i] : nullptr;
    scoped_rel<relation_base> fresh_delta = idelta ? idelta->get_plugin().mk_empty(*idelta) : nullptr;  // 1st
    ...
}
for (unsigned i = 0; i < num; ++i) {
    ...
    scoped_rel<relation_base> fresh_delta = idelta ? idelta->get_plugin().mk_empty(*idelta) : nullptr;  // 2nd
    do_inner_union(i, i, itgt, src[i], fresh_delta.get());
```
For the external component, each `mk_empty` creates a fresh `T` constant and calls the user's `reduce_assign` with `OP_RA_EMPTY` (`dl_external_relation.cpp:136-145`). Order with delta and external first:
- loop 1: ext `mk_empty`, then interval `mk_empty`;
- loop 2: ext `mk_empty`, ext `OP_RA_UNION`, ext delta `OP_RA_UNION`, then the interval steps.

When the source spec differs from the target, `unaligned_union_fn` also clones the source product: `src_scoped = src0.clone()`. That calls `OP_RA_CLONE` on the external component with another fresh `T`.

**Go behavior.**
```go
owner.fresh, err = p.plugin.NewEmpty(p.sorts)          // one OP_RA_EMPTY only
... p.external.Union(source.external, owner.fresh, widen)
... delta.external.Union(owner.fresh, nil, false)
```
`canonicalizeUnalignedUnion` only relabels `kinds`. It never clones the source, so no `OP_RA_CLONE` is issued.

**Impact.** API users with the `external_relation` + `interval_relation` product representation see one fewer `OP_RA_EMPTY` per delta union and no `OP_RA_CLONE` on unaligned unions. All later fresh `T!n` names shift. Relation contents are unchanged.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: the product needs the API external plugin. Scenario: a recursive rule over a predicate whose representation is `(external_relation interval_relation)`. Count the `OP_RA_EMPTY` callbacks per semi-naive iteration: z3 issues two per head per iteration, Go one.

**Fix.** In `ExternalIntervalProduct.Union`, when `delta != nil`, mirror the two allocation loops in C++ component order (`p.kinds`):
1. For each component in order, create and immediately drop a fresh empty. For the external component, call `p.plugin.NewEmpty(p.sorts)` and close it at once. For the interval component, no callback is needed.
2. Then, for each component in order, create the second fresh empty, perform the basic union with it, and union it into the caller's delta.

In the unaligned case (`!externalIntervalProductKindsEqual(p.kinds, source.kinds)`), first call `source.Clone()`, which issues `OP_RA_CLONE` with a fresh `T`. Use the clone as the union source, and close it after the union.

**Regression test.**
- Add `TestExternalIntervalProductDeltaUnionCallbacks` to the existing `pkg/muz/rel/external_interval_product*_test.go` file. Reuse the product helpers already there (`NewSelectedExternalIntervalProduct` with `[]string{"external_relation","interval_relation"}`) and record callbacks in an `ExternalRelationCallbacks.ReduceAssign`.
- Call `target.Union(source, delta, false)`. Expect the recorded kinds `[EMPTY, EMPTY, UNION, UNION]`.
- Add a second case with source kinds in the opposite order. Expect `CLONE` before them.

<a id="muz-rel-02-f4"></a>
#### muz_rel_02-F4: external relation accessors build temporary applications to obtain declarations (extra ASTs, different ids)

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation.go:166-199` (`ExternalRelation.accessor`), `:95-121` (`NewEmpty`), `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_filter.go:11-44`, `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_transform.go:15-41,155-186`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_external_relation.cpp:40-58,60-70,136-146,170-175,195,231,265,298`

**C++ behavior.** Declarations are created directly, with no application:
`fn = m.mk_func_decl(fid, k, 0, nullptr, args.size(), args.c_ptr());`
The same holds for `OP_RA_EMPTY`, `OP_RA_FILTER`, `OP_RA_JOIN`, `OP_RA_PROJECT`, `OP_RA_RENAME` and the union declarations, which are created when the functor is built.

**Go behavior.** Go builds an application first (`MkDatalogStore`, `MkDatalogSelect`, `MkDatalogIsEmpty`, `MkDatalogEmpty`, `MkDatalogFilter`, `MkDatalogProject`, `MkDatalogUnion`, ...) and then takes `GetDecl`. Every operation therefore allocates one extra app node with an AST id that z3 never creates.

Use them in `accessor`, `NewEmpty`, `FilterInterpreted`, `Project`, `Rename`, `JoinExternalRelations`, `Union` and `FilterNegation`. In `NewEmpty`, keep the C++ order: relation sort, fresh `T`, then the `OP_RA_EMPTY` declaration.

**Regression test.** In `pkg/muz/rel/external_relation_test.go` (or a new `external_relation_ast_id_test.go`), record the next AST id before and after `rel.AddFact(...)` with a nil-callback plugin. Expect exactly the ids of the store declaration (first use only), and no app node.

<a id="muz-rel-03-f1"></a>
#### muz_rel_03-F1: `instr_io` load keeps an empty relation in the register instead of `make_empty`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_io.go:96-105` (`relationIOInstruction.Perform`, load branch)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_instruction.cpp:210-218` (`instr_io::perform`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
relation_base& rel = ctx.get_rel_context().get_relation(m_pred);
if (!rel.fast_empty()) {
    ctx.set_reg(m_reg, rel.clone());
}
else {
    ctx.make_empty(m_reg);
}
```

**Go behavior.**
```go
if !i.store {
    table, x := relations.GetFiniteRelation(i.predicate)
    ...
    clone, x := table.CloneFinite()
    ...
    return true, context.SetFiniteRegister(i.register, clone)
}
```
The finite load always installs a clone, even when the clone is empty. The explanation-register load in `instruction_explanation_io.go:6-17` does check `count == 0` and calls `MakeEmpty`. Only the ordinary finite path is wrong.

**Impact.** Every later instruction that guards on `ctx.reg(r)` being null now takes its "non-null" branch. Answers stay the same, but statistics change. Examples: `filter_by_negation` (`++m_filter_by_negation` only when both registers are non-null), `union` (no `++m_union` and no target/delta creation when the source is null), `join_project`, `project_rename`, `select_equal_and_project` and `filter_interpreted_and_project`. Registers that C++ leaves null are also allocated, which changes which relation kind an empty union target gets (`mk_empty(r_src)`). This happens in any stratified program whose lower stratum derives an empty IDB relation that a higher stratum reads.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. Input (`work/muz_rel_03/t4.smt2`):
```
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(define-sort s () (_ BitVec 3))
(declare-rel e (s s))
(declare-rel q (s))
(declare-rel r (s))
(declare-var x s)
(declare-var y s)
(rule (e #b000 #b001))
(rule (e #b001 #b010))
(rule (e #b010 #b011))
(rule (=> (and (e x y) (= y #b111)) (q x)))
(rule (=> (and (e x y) (not (q x))) (r x)))
(query r :print-answer true)
```
`g3 t4.smt2 fixedpoint.print_statistics=true` prints `:dl.filter_by_negation 1`. `build/z3` with the same parameter prints no `dl.filter_by_negation` entry, because the counter is 0. In z3's `-v:2` trace, `load q into 2` is followed by `filter_by_negation on 10(0) with 2(0)`, and register 2 is null there. The other `dl.*` counters agree.

**Fix.** In `relationIOInstruction.Perform`, load branch, test emptiness before cloning:
```go
table, x := relations.GetFiniteRelation(i.predicate)
if x != nil { return false, x }
count, x := table.Len()
if x != nil { return false, x }
if count == 0 {
    return true, context.MakeEmpty(i.register)
}
clone, x := table.CloneFinite()
...
```
`check_relation::fast_empty` forwards to the wrapped relation, so checked owners (`FormulaCheckedTable`, `FormulaCheckedFinitePair`, `FiniteCheckedPair`) should be emptied the same way. Only their `Len()` is needed. The existing test `TestMixedUnionPreservesLoadedEmptyHashRepresentation` (`instruction_sparse_runtime_test.go:153`) asserts the current deviation: the loaded empty Hash owner survives into the union. It must be changed to the C++ expectation. With a null target, `instr_union` creates `r_src.get_plugin().mk_empty(r_src)`, which is a Sparse target when the source is Sparse.

**Regression test.** In `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_io_test.go`, add `TestLoadOfEmptyRelationLeavesRegisterNull`. Use `cmd_context.NewStandaloneContext`, `rel.NewRelationManager`, a Bool-domain predicate and `relations.GetRelation`, as in `TestRelationInstructionsLoadCloneAndStoreOwnership`, but add no fact. Run `rel.NewLoadInstruction(relations, predicate, 0)` in a block, then assert `context.FiniteRegister(0)` returns `nil, nil`. Then run `rel.NewFilterByNegationInstruction(1, 0, []int{0}, []int{0})` with register 1 holding a one-row table, and assert `context.Statistics()` has `FilterByNegation == 0`.
For SMT-LIB coverage, the `.smt2` above can go in `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/rel_load_empty_stats.smt2`. Statistics output contains memory and time lines, so the `scriptResults` entry should compare only the `dl.` lines, or the test should be in Go. Running `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` cross-checks the `sat` answer.

<a id="muz-rel-03-f2"></a>
#### muz_rel_03-F2: `filter_interpreted` and `setNonemptyFiniteRegister` leave empty Sparse, lazy-sparse and checked results in the register

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_interpreted.go:186-236` (`interpretedFilterInstruction.Perform`); `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_finite_table.go:17-39` (`setNonemptyFiniteRegister`); `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_interpreted_project.go:129-133`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_instruction.cpp:551-555`, `606-612`, `400-408` (`instr_filter_interpreted::perform`, `instr_filter_interpreted_and_project::perform`, `instr_join::perform`)

**C++ behavior.** Every mutating or producing instruction ends unconditionally with
```cpp
(*fn)(r);
if (r.fast_empty()) {
    ctx.make_empty(m_reg);
}
```
For `table_relation`, `fast_empty()` is `m_table->empty()`. That is exact for sparse, hashtable and lazy tables, and `check_relation::fast_empty` forwards to the wrapped relation.

**Go behavior.**
```go
case *LazySparseTable:
    ... filterInterpretedCompiled(...)
    return true, nil                    // no emptiness test
case *FiniteCheckedPair:
    ... FilterInterpreted(...)
    return true, nil                    // no emptiness test
...
if len(kept) == 0 {
    switch table.(type) {
    case *SparseTable, *FiniteCheckedPair:
        return true, nil                // empty Sparse kept in register
    }
    return true, context.MakeEmpty(i.register)
}
```
and in `setNonemptyFiniteRegister`:
```go
case *FiniteCheckedPair, *FormulaCheckedTable, *FormulaCheckedFinitePair:
    // Preserve concrete empty owners selected by the relation manager.
```
The lazy branch of `filter_interpreted_and_project` also installs its result without the test.

**Impact.** Sparse is the default `datalog.default_table`. A rule whose interpreted tail rejects every row at runtime leaves an empty Sparse table in the register. The next `union` then counts `dl.union` and allocates a target where C++ returns early. Under `check_relation` / `default_table_checked`, empty join and join-project results also stay allocated. As in F1, answers stay the same, but statistics and register state diverge.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. Input (`work/muz_rel_03/t5.smt2`):
```
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(define-sort s () (_ BitVec 3))
(declare-rel e (s s))
(declare-rel q (s s))
(declare-rel r (s))
(declare-var x s)
(declare-var y s)
(rule (e #b000 #b001))
(rule (e #b001 #b010))
(rule (e #b010 #b011))
(rule (=> (and (e x y) (bvugt x y)) (q x y)))
(rule (=> (and (e x y) (not (q y x))) (r x)))
(query r :print-answer true)
```
With `fixedpoint.print_statistics=true`, g3 prints `:dl.union 5` and z3 prints `:dl.union 4`. The extra union is the one after `filter_interpreted 10 using (not (bvule (:var 0) (:var 1)))` empties register 10. z3 nulls register 10, so `union 10 into 1` is skipped. With `fixedpoint.datalog.default_table=hashtable` the union counts agree (4 = 4), which isolates the Sparse exemption. The remaining `dl.filter_by_negation` difference there is F1.

**Fix.**
1. In `interpretedFilterInstruction.Perform`, after each concrete branch (lazy, checked pair, generic), compute `count, err := table.Len()` and call `context.MakeEmpty(i.register)` when it is 0. Remove the `*SparseTable, *FiniteCheckedPair` exemption.
2. In `setNonemptyFiniteRegister`, remove the exemption for checked owners. Close the table and `MakeEmpty` for every kind, as `check_relation::fast_empty` forwards.
3. In `interpretedFilterProjectInstruction.Perform`, route the lazy result through `setNonemptyFiniteRegister` as well. `lazy_table::empty()` is evaluated in C++.
4. Check that no checked-mode caller depends on the preserved empty owner. The comment suggests one exists. With both F1 and F2 fixed, an empty register is recreated with `emptyFiniteLike(source)` exactly where C++ calls `mk_empty(r_src)`.

**Regression test.** In `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_sparse_runtime_test.go`, add `TestFilterInterpretedEmptiesSparseRegister` using `newTableRelationFixture(t)`. Install a one-row Sparse table (`NewSparseTable(signature, 0)`) in register 0. Run a `NewFilterInterpretedInstruction` whose condition is `false` (column/sort maps empty), then `NewUnionInstruction(0, 1, VoidRegister)`. Expect `context.FiniteRegister(0)` to be `nil` and `Statistics().Union == 0`. The SMT-LIB vector above can go in `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/rel_filter_empty_sparse_stats.smt2`; compare only the `dl.` statistics lines.

<a id="muz-rel-03-f3"></a>
#### muz_rel_03-F3: relation-explanation `filter_equal` / `filter_identical` / `join` skip their counters when the source register is empty

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_relation_explanation.go:337-361` (`performRelationExplanationTable`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_instruction.cpp:376-380`, `440-443`, `489-492`

**C++ behavior.** `++ctx.m_stats.m_join`, `++m_filter_eq` and `++m_filter_id` run before the `if (!ctx.reg(...))` early return.

**Go behavior.**
```go
if source == nil {
    switch i.kind {
    case "join", "project", "rename":
        return true, context.MakeEmpty(i.result)
    }
    return true, nil
}
switch i.kind {
case "filter_equal":
    context.stats.FilterEqual++
```
The ordinary path (`instruction_table.go`) and the finite explanation path (`instruction_explanation_table.go:59,78,94`) increment first, as C++ does. Only the relation-level explanation path drops the counts.

**Impact.** When `generate_explanations` runs over numeric or relation-product programs, `dl.joins`, `dl.filter_eq` and `dl.filter_id` are undercounted. Statistics only.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted. It needs a relation-level explanation program where these instructions see an empty register.

**Fix.** Move `context.stats.FilterEqual++`, `FilterIdentical++` and `Join++` above the `source == nil` check, for the matching `i.kind`. Keep `project`/`rename`/`union` as they are, because C++ counts those only after the null check.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_explanation_table_test.go` with `TestRelationExplanationCountsBeforeEmptyCheck`. Perform a `NewJoinInstruction` on an empty relation-explanation register and assert `Statistics().Join == 1`.

<a id="muz-rel-03-f4"></a>
#### muz_rel_03-F4: instruction diagnostics: no `-v:2` instruction log or `looping ...` line, and `DisplayHead`/annotation text differs

- Severity: low
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/instruction*.go` (all `Perform` and `DisplayHead` methods; `instruction_table.go:379-384` `columnsText`; `instruction_construct.go:369-377`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_instruction.cpp:184-186` (`log_verbose`), `335`, `print_container` (`src/util/container_util.h:71-80`)

**C++ behavior.** Every `perform` calls `log_verbose(ctx)`, which is `IF_VERBOSE(2, display(...))`, and the while loop prints `looping ... n` at verbosity 10. Column lists print through `print_container` as `(0,1)`. `join_project` prints `:cols-rows` for non-null registers. `filter_interpreted` prints `using <cond>`. Annotations are `"mk unary singleton"`, `"mk_total"`, `"assert signature"`, `"filter_interpreted <cond>"`, `"filter_equal <col> val: <nice value>"`, and `load`/`store` uses `bare_str()` names.

**Go behavior.** The `muz/rel` package emits no verbose output. `columnsText` prints `[0,1]`, the while head prints `while[...]`, and `filter_interpreted` omits the condition. `MakeAnnotations` for construct instructions stores the Go kind string (`"mk_unary_singleton"`, `"assert_signature"`). The filter_equal annotation prints the raw encoded element.

**Impact.** `-v:2` and higher show nothing for rel execution. z3 prints the full instruction trace, for example `load e into 0`, `join 3() and 4() into 5` and `filter_interpreted 10 using (not (bvule (:var 0) (:var 1)))`. `report_big_relations` annotations differ too.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed: `build/z3 -v:2 t5.smt2` prints the instruction trace to stderr; `g3 -v:2 t5.smt2` prints none.

**Fix.** Give `Instruction.Perform` access to the verbosity level. Before each operation, at the same point as C++ (for example after the null check in `filter_interpreted`, `union` and `project`, before it elsewhere), write `DisplayHead` plus `"\n"` to the verbose stream when verbosity is at least 2. Change `columnsText` to `(` `)` delimiters and add `:%d-%d` for non-null `join_project` registers. Print the condition in `filter_interpreted`. Use the C++ annotation strings.

**Regression test.** Unit test in `pkg/muz/rel/instruction_table_test.go`: `TestInstructionDisplayHeadMatchesPrintContainer`. Assert `NewJoinInstruction(3,4,[]int{0},[]int{1},5).DisplayHead` produces `join 3(0) and 4(1) into 5`.

<a id="muz-rel-04-f1"></a>
#### muz_rel_04-F1: `DisplayOutputTables` prints output relations in declaration order, not decl_set hash order

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/relation_manager_display_output.go:95-163` (`RelationManager.DisplayOutputTables`), fed by `pkg/muz/base/rule_set.go:295-300` (`RuleSet.OutputPredicates`, `outputOrder`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_relation_manager.cpp:517-530` (`relation_manager::display_output_tables`)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
const decl_set & output_preds = rules.get_output_predicates();
decl_set::iterator it=output_preds.begin();
for(; it!=end; ++it) { func_decl * pred = *it;
    relation_base * rel = try_get_relation(pred);
    if (!rel) { out << "Tuples in " << pred->get_name() << ": \n"; continue; }
    rel->display_tuples(*pred, out); }
```
`decl_set` is `obj_hashtable<func_decl>`, so the relations print in hash-table order.

**Go behavior.**
```go
outputs, err := rules.OutputPredicates()   // s.outputOrder: insertion order
for _, predicate := range outputs { ... }
```

**Impact.** A Datalog frontend file (`.datalog`/`-dl`) with more than one `printtuples`/`outputtuples` predicate prints its tuple blocks in a different order from z3. Any script or test that compares output text sees the difference.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. With `m.datalog`:
```
D 4

Seed(x:D)
Zed(x:D) printtuples
Alpha(x:D) printtuples
Mid(x:D) printtuples
Seed("a").
Seed("b").
Zed(X) :- Seed(X).
Alpha(X) :- Seed(X).
Mid(X) :- Seed(X).
```
g3 prints `Tuples in Zed`, then `Alpha`, then `Mid`. z3 prints `Alpha`, `Mid`, `Zed`. Other declaration orders give more cases. Declaring `Pa Pb Pc` gives g3 `Pa Pb Pc` and z3 `Pb Pc Pa`. Declaring `R1..R5` gives g3 `R1 R2 R3 R4 R5` and z3 `R2 R1 R3 R4 R5`.

**Fix.** Iterate the output predicates in `obj_hashtable` order.
- Preferred: keep `RuleSet`'s output set in an `ast.ObjMap` (`ast.NewObjMap(manager)`, which reproduces the core_hashtable layout), filled with `Insert` in `set_output_predicate` order. `OutputPredicates()` then returns `layout.Entries()` keys.
- Minimal: in `DisplayOutputTables`, build a local `ast.NewObjMap(m.manager)`, insert each `outputs[i]` in order, and loop over `Entries()`.

The same order is used by `pkg/muz/base/rule_set_display.go:40` and `rule_set.go:379,723`. Check each against its C++ counterpart: `rule_set::display` and `add_rules` both walk `m_output_preds`. Note that `OutputPredicate()`, which expects exactly one output, is unaffected.

**Regression test.**
- Extend `pkg/cmd/g3/datalog_frontend_test.go` with `TestDatalogOutputTuplesFollowDeclSetOrder`. Write the file above with `writeDatalogCommandFile`, run `runArguments([]string{path}, ...)`, and assert the tuple prefix `"Tuples in Alpha: \n\t(x=a(0))\n\t(x=b(1))\nTuples in Mid: \n...\nTuples in Zed: \n..."`. The existing `assertDatalogCommandOutput` helper checks the prefix.
- Add the `Pa Pb Pc` case, expecting `Pb, Pc, Pa`.

<a id="muz-rel-04-f2"></a>
#### muz_rel_04-F2: lazy_sparse nullary union target: z3 segfaults, g3 answers (z3-bug divergence not recorded)

- Severity: low
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/relation_manager_default_finite.go:66-89` (`NewDefaultFiniteTable`, Hash fallback for nullary) and `pkg/muz/rel/lazy_sparse_operations.go:186-307` (`evalFiniteNode`, nullary lazy nodes)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_instruction.cpp:657` (`instr_union::perform`: `r_src.get_plugin().mk_empty(r_src)`), which reaches `dl_lazy_table.cpp lazy_table_plugin::mk_empty` and then `sparse_table_plugin::mk_empty` on a 0-column signature

**C++ behavior.** When the union target register is empty, `instr_union` creates it with the *source's* plugin. For a nullary lazy_sparse source, that calls `lazy_table_plugin::mk_empty`, which wraps `sparse_table_plugin::mk_empty(empty signature)`. That plugin does not check `can_handle_signature` (`s.size()>0`), and it crashes in `sparse_table::column_layout::make_byte_aligned_end`. The gdb backtrace on `build_dbg/z3` confirms this.

**Go behavior.** Nullary lazy nodes are evaluated into a HashTable (`evalFiniteNode`), and `NewDefaultFiniteTable` falls back to Hash for nullary signatures. g3 prints the correct answer.

**Impact.** z3 4.7.1 crashes on a valid program and g3 answers it. That is a deliberate improvement, but the deviation is not documented next to the code and not listed in `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/z3_bug_exclusions.txt`. Without a documented entry, a reference comparison of such an input looks like a g3 bug.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. `l6.smt2`:
```
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(set-option :fixedpoint.datalog.default_table lazy_sparse)
(define-sort D () (_ BitVec 3))
(declare-rel q (D D D))
(declare-rel p (D D))
(declare-rel s (D))
(declare-rel z ())
(declare-var x D)
(declare-var y D)
(declare-var w D)
(rule (q #b010 #b001 #b100))
(rule (q #b011 #b001 #b101))
(rule (q #b011 #b011 #b101))
(rule (=> (and (q x #b001 y) (bvult x y)) (p x y)))
(rule (=> (and (q x w y) (q w x y)) (s x)))
(rule (=> (and (p x y) (s x)) z))
(query z :print-answer true)
```
g3 prints `sat` / `true`, which is correct: p(3,5) and s(3). z3 segfaults (exit 139). With `default_table sparse`, z3 prints `sat` / `true`.

**Fix.** No code change in g3 is needed. Follow the project's z3-bug workflow:
- Record it in `FORK_BUGFIXES.md` and `z3_bug_exclusions.txt` with this vector.
- Add a red C++ test in `src/` showing the crash.
- Add a comment at `NewDefaultFiniteTable`/`evalFiniteNode` naming the C++ crash site.

**Regression test.** Add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/z3_bug_lazy_sparse_nullary_union.smt2` (the input above), with expected output `"sat\ntrue\n"` in `scriptResults` (`pkg/cmd/g3/main_test.go`). Add its name to `z3_bug_exclusions.txt` so `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3` skips it.

<a id="muz-rel-04-f3"></a>
#### muz_rel_04-F3: Karr union/delta in the numeric explanation product does not follow `karr_relation::mk_union`

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/karr_relation.go:468-536` (`KarrRelation.Union`), `pkg/muz/rel/relation_explanation_product_numeric.go:686-691` (`relationExplanationNumeric.UnionFrom`, karr branch)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/karr_relation.cpp` `karr_relation::mk_union` (lines ~305-345)

**C++ behavior.**
```cpp
if (src.empty()) { if (delta) delta->m_empty = true; return; }
...
if (empty()) { m_basis = M; ...; if (delta) delta->copy(*this); return; }
... append missing rows ...
m_ineqs_valid = false;                       // always
if (N_size != N.size()) { if (delta) delta->copy(*this); }
```

**Go behavior.**
```go
// KarrRelation.Union
changed := oldSize != r.basis.Len()
if changed { r.inequalitiesValid = false }   // only when changed
// relationExplanationNumeric.UnionFrom
changed, err = b.karr.Union(source.karr)
if err == nil && changed && delta != nil { _, err = delta.karr.Union(source.karr) }
```
There are three differences:
1. Delta becomes `delta ∪ source` instead of a copy of the post-union target.
2. Delta is not emptied when the source is empty.
3. When nothing was added, the target keeps its old inequality rows instead of re-dualizing them from the basis. This changes later `to_formula` output and the row order seen by joins.

`KarrSourceUnion` (`karr_source_empty_basis.go:43-81`) already invalidates unconditionally. Only the general `Union` used by the explanation product deviates.

**Impact.** This affects relation-level explanation products with `karr_relation` numeric backing. In g3 that is reached only through the muz_fp_01-F4 path. In z3 Int columns are blocked by `check_infinite_sorts`. The effect is latent today, but the semantics are wrong.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: no CLI path reaches the C++ side (z3 rejects Int Datalog rules with "Rule contains infinite sorts").

**Fix.**
- In `KarrRelation.Union`, set `r.inequalitiesValid = false` unconditionally on the non-empty-target path.
- Change `UnionFrom` to a delta-aware Karr union that mirrors `mk_union`:
  - if the source is empty and `delta != nil`, set `delta.karr.empty = true` and keep its matrices;
  - if the target was empty, or rows were added, set `delta.karr` to a `Clone()` of `b.karr`, copying `empty`, `inequalities`/`basis` and both valid flags, as `copy()` does.
- Also apply the C++ `filter_equal` constant: the Go `FilterEqual` verifies against `x = 1`, see Needs verification.

**Regression test.**
- Add `TestKarrUnionDeltaCopiesTarget` to `pkg/muz/rel/karr_relation_test.go`. Use `NewKarrFull`/`AddFact` to build target {x=1} and source {x=2}, and delta {x=7}. After `relationExplanationNumeric.UnionFrom` with the karr kind, or a new `KarrRelation.UnionWithDelta`, expect delta's basis to equal the target's basis (2 rows).
- With an empty source, expect `delta.Empty()`.
- With an identical source, expect `inequalitiesValid == false` on the target.

**Go behavior.** No objective names and no verbose output at any level. The error is `muz/rel: operation was not verified`. The solver gets the user's `config`, and the union is built as `(or d0 s)`.

**Impact.**
- With `fixedpoint.datalog.check_relation=...` and `-v:3`, z3 prints `union verified`, `join verified` and similar lines that g3 does not print.
- On a real failure, z3 always prints "NOT verified" plus both formulas to stderr.
- User solver parameters such as a timeout can make g3's check return unknown, which passes, where z3's default solver decides.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: most check_relation targets are blocked by recorded fp issues (muz_fp_01-F6, muz_fp_02-F2).

**Fix.**
- Add an `objective string` parameter to `VerifyRelationFormulasEquivalent`, threaded with the C++ objective names (`"union"`, `"union_delta low"`, `"union delta0"`, `"union no overflow"`, and the join/project/filter names from check_relation.cpp).
- Print the level-3 and level-0 messages through the project's verbose stream.
- Build the union as `MkOrArgs({s, d0})`.
- Construct the checking solver from default parameters, not from `config`.

**Regression test.** Add `TestRelationFormulaCheckerVerboseObjectives` to `pkg/muz/rel/relation_formula_checker_test.go`. Capture the verbose stream at level 3, check two equivalent formulas, and expect `"union verified\n"`. A non-equivalent pair at level 0 should produce output starting with `"NOT verified true\n"`.

<a id="muz-rel-04-f6"></a>
#### muz_rel_04-F6: two Go-only relation layers have no production caller (LazyTable over HashTable, SieveRelation over HashTable)

- C++: `src/muz/rel/rel_context.cpp:110` registers only `lazy_table_plugin::mk_sparse` (lazy over sparse). The live C++ sieve use is the explanation product (`dl_mk_explanations.cpp`).

C++ `sieve_relation_plugin::mk_filter_by_negation_fn` (dl_sieve_relation.cpp:634-655) inverts its `r_col_inner`/`neg_col_inner` flags. As a result it skips equalities between two inner columns and maps two sieved-out columns through `get_inner_col(i)` with the loop index. The Go code is therefore not a port of the live C++ behavior either.

**Impact.** About 1,200 lines of unreached code, contrary to AGENTS.md ("Port only C++ code reached by retained source consumers"). It has tests, so it looks covered while no production path uses it.

<a id="muz-rel-05-f1"></a>
#### muz_rel_05-F1: `HashTable` iterates rows in insertion order; C++ `hashtable_table` iterates in hash-slot order

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/table.go:90-100` (`HashTable`, `rows *insdict.Dict`), and every reader of `t.rows.All()`: `Facts` (:229), `Clone` (:240), `Join` (:342), `Project` (:378), `Permute` (:432), `Union` (:494), `FilterByNegation` (:527), plus `table_display.go:12` (`HashTable.Display`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_table.h:76-79` (`typedef hashtable<table_fact, svector_hash_proc<table_element_hash>, vector_eq_proc<table_fact> > storage`), `src/muz/rel/dl_table.cpp:39-85` (`join_fn`), `:90-140` (`our_iterator_core`), `src/muz/rel/dl_base.cpp:465-486` (`table_base::to_formula`)

**C++ behavior.** The rows of a `hashtable_table` are stored in a `core_hashtable` and iterated in slot order. The slot depends on `svector_hash<uint64_hash>` of the fact, the table capacity, and the history of collisions and deletions:
```
typedef hashtable<table_fact, svector_hash_proc<table_element_hash>,
    vector_eq_proc<table_fact> > storage;
...
for(; it != iend; ++it) { ... conjs ...; brw.mk_and(...); disjs.push_back(fml); }
brw.mk_or(disjs.size(), disjs.c_ptr(), fml);
```

**Go behavior.** The rows sit in an insertion-ordered `insdict.Dict` keyed by the packed fact bytes. Every traversal (to_formula, display_tuples, join, project, union, negation) visits rows in first-insertion order:
```go
type HashTable struct {
	signature Signature
	rows      *insdict.Dict[string, Fact]
...
for _, fact := range t.rows.All() { result = append(result, cloneFact(fact)) }
```

**Impact.** This affects every predicate declared `tr_hashtable`, and every predicate when `fixedpoint.datalog.default_table=hashtable`. The disjunct order of `(query ... :print-answer true)` and of `datalog.print.tuples` output differs from z3. Joins and unions also insert rows in a different order, so intermediate tables differ as well. The answers are logically equivalent.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with `hf1.smt2`:
```
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(declare-rel e ((_ BitVec 4)) tr_hashtable)
(declare-rel p ((_ BitVec 4)) tr_hashtable)
(declare-var x (_ BitVec 4))
(rule (e #x3))
(rule (e #x1))
(rule (e #x2))
(rule (e #x5))
(rule (e #x4))
(rule (=> (e x) (p x)))
(query p :print-answer true)
```
g3:
```
sat
(or (= (:var 0) #x3)
    (= (:var 0) #x1)
    (= (:var 0) #x2)
    (= (:var 0) #x5)
    (= (:var 0) #x4))
```
z3:
```
sat
(or (= (:var 0) #x4)
    (= (:var 0) #x2)
    (= (:var 0) #x1)
    (= (:var 0) #x3)
    (= (:var 0) #x5))
```
The same divergence appears with two-column relations and transitive closure, and with `fixedpoint.datalog.default_table=hashtable`. The sparse default matches z3.

**Fix.** Replace the `insdict` storage of `HashTable` with a Go port of `core_hashtable<table_fact>` that has the C++ layout:
- the same initial capacity (8), load-factor growth, tombstone and deletion handling, and insert probing;
- the hash `svector_hash<uint64_hash>`, which is `get_composite_hash` over the facts with `uint64_hash(x) = (unsigned)x` (`src/util/vector.h:572`, `src/util/hash.h:142`).

The repository already ports `core_hashtable` slot order for the AST maps (`pkg/ast/ast_obj_map.go`). Reuse that probing and growth logic with a fact-vector hash. Keep `Add`, `Remove`, `Contains` and `Len` semantics. Make `All`/`Facts` walk slots in index order. `Clone` must rebuild the clone by re-inserting in slot order, the way `hashtable_table::clone` copies `m_data` (C++ copies the table, so the clone has the same slot layout). `FilterEqual`, `FilterIdentical` and `FilterByNegation`, which delete during iteration, must leave tombstones the way `core_hashtable::remove` does. Also check every other `HashTable` traversal (`lazy_table.go`, `sieve_*`, `finite_checked_pair.go`), because all of them inherit the order.

**Regression test.**
- Unit test: in `pkg/muz/rel/table_test.go`, add `TestHashTableFactsFollowCoreHashtableSlotOrder`. Build a one-column table with `NewHashTable(NewSignature([]uint64{16}))` (as `TestHashTableSetCloneAndValidation` does), add 3,1,2,5,4, and expect `Facts()` to return them in the slot order of a C++ `hashtable<svector<uint64>>` with the same inserts. Compute that order once with a tiny C++ positive control under `src/` (per AGENTS.md); for the program above it must agree with z3's 4,2,1,3,5.
- Vector: add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/datalog_hashtable_answer_order.smt2` with the input above. Its `scriptResults` entry is `"sat\n(or (= (:var 0) #x4)\n    (= (:var 0) #x2)\n    (= (:var 0) #x1)\n    (= (:var 0) #x3)\n    (= (:var 0) #x5))\n"`. Check it with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

<a id="muz-rel-05-f2"></a>
#### muz_rel_05-F2: `CanSelectSparseIntervalSieveProduct` refuses `tr_sparse interval_relation` on purely finite (and purely arithmetic) predicates, which z3 evaluates

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/sparse_interval_sieve_product.go:88-98` (`CanSelectSparseIntervalSieveProduct`), used by `pkg/muz/fp/sparse_interval_representation.go:12-27` (`selectSparseIntervalRepresentation`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/rel_context.cpp` `set_predicate_representation` (a multi-kind request builds a `product_relation` from the named plugins), `src/muz/rel/dl_product_relation.cpp`, `src/muz/rel/dl_sieve_relation.cpp` (a component plugin that cannot handle a column gets a sieve with that column ignored)

**C++ behavior.** Declaring `(declare-rel r (s s) tr_sparse interval_relation)` with bit-vector columns creates a product of a sparse table and an interval relation. The interval component is sieved down to zero inner columns, so it is the full relation. Evaluation is exact, and the answer is the sparse table's.

**Go behavior.**
```go
func CanSelectSparseIntervalSieveProduct(manager *RelationManager, sorts []ast.ASTHandle, kinds []string) (bool, error) {
	...
	return len(finiteColumns) != 0 && len(finiteColumns) != len(sorts), nil
}
```
A signature that is not mixed returns `false`. The fp caller turns that into `ErrSparseIntervalDatalogFragment` at the `declare-rel` command.

**Impact.** Any program that requests `tr_sparse interval_relation`, in either order, on a predicate whose columns are all finite gets a spurious `(error ...)` line, and the requested representation is silently dropped. The default representation is used instead, so here the answer is unchanged, but scripts that check for errors diverge. A mixed signature needs an Int/Real column, and the C++ Datalog engine rejects those with "Rule contains infinite sorts". So the only case z3 accepts at all is exactly the one g3 refuses.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed:
```
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(define-sort s () (_ BitVec 3))
(declare-rel r (s s) tr_sparse interval_relation)
(declare-rel e (s s))
(declare-var x s)
(declare-var y s)
(declare-var z s)
(rule (e #b001 #b010))
(rule (e #b010 #b011))
(rule (e #b011 #b001))
(rule (=> (e x y) (r x y)))
(rule (=> (and (r x y) (e y z)) (r x z)))
(query r :print-answer true)
```
g3 prints `(error "line 3 column 48: muz/fp: unsupported sparse/interval Datalog fragment")`. It then keeps the predicate's default representation and prints the same `sat` and 9-row closure as z3, so the only output difference is the extra error line. z3 prints no error. The same happens for `interval_relation tr_sparse`. Related cases outside this shard: `tr_hashtable interval_relation` and `tr_sparse bound_relation` fail in g3 with `relation plugin ... does not exist`, while z3 answers. Those are owned by the fp representation selection.

**Fix.** In `CanSelectSparseIntervalSieveProduct`, accept a purely finite signature. The product's interval component is then the full zero-inner-column sieve, as `newSparseIntervalSieveProduct` already builds when `pureFinite` is true. For pure finite, the simplest faithful mapping is to treat the predicate like `tr_sparse`; the answer is the same as z3's because the full interval component contributes `true` to `product_relation::to_formula`. Concretely:
- return `true` when `len(finiteColumns) == len(sorts) && len(sorts) != 0`;
- in `selectSparseIntervalRepresentation`, record the kinds so that `ensureSparseIntervalDatalog` classifies the predicate as `sparseIntervalFiniteOriginal`.

Pure-arithmetic and nullary signatures stay rejected only through the engine's infinite-sort check (muz_fp_01-F2), not here. Update `TestCanSelectSparseIntervalSieveProductRejectsNonMixedAndNames` in `pkg/muz/rel/sparse_interval_sieve_product_selection_test.go`; its "finite" case currently enshrines the refusal.

**Regression test.**
- Unit test: in `pkg/muz/rel/sparse_interval_sieve_product_selection_test.go`, add `TestCanSelectSparseIntervalSieveProductAcceptsPureFinite`. Use `intervalSieveFixture` and `NewRelationManager` as the neighbouring test does. With sorts `{f.boolean}` and kinds `{"tr_sparse","interval_relation"}` (and the reverse order), expect `(true, nil)`.
- Vector: add `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/datalog_sparse_interval_finite_only.smt2` with the program above. Its expected output is the z3 output, with no error line: `sat`, then `(or (and (= (:var 0) #b001) (= (:var 1) #b010))` and the remaining 8 disjuncts in z3's order. Check it with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

<a id="muz-rel-05-f3"></a>
#### muz_rel_05-F3: the full-table construction never emits `WARNING: creating large table of size N for relation P`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/table.go:262-293` (`HashTable.Complement`) and `pkg/muz/rel/sparse_functional_complement.go:3-41` (`SparseTable.ComplementFunctional`), which are the Go counterparts of `table_base::complement`. The confirmed path builds the full table through `fillTotalTable` (`pkg/muz/rel/instruction_construct.go:170`, outside this shard), which has no warning either.
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_base.cpp:367-404` (`table_base::complement`), reached from `table_plugin::mk_full`

**C++ behavior.**
```
uint64_t upper_bound = get_signature()[0];
bool empty_table = empty();
if (upper_bound > (1 << 18)) {
    std::ostringstream buffer;
    buffer << "creating large table of size " << upper_bound;
    if (p) buffer << " for relation " << p->get_name();
    warning_msg("%s", buffer.str().c_str());
}
```

**Go behavior.** Neither complement nor `fillTotalTable` checks the bound or calls the warning service.

**Impact.** When a full unary relation over a domain larger than 2^18 is materialised (for example, a negated tail whose variable is not bound positively), z3 writes the warning to stderr and g3 is silent.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed with `big2.smt2`:
```
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(declare-rel w ((_ BitVec 19)))
(declare-rel z ((_ BitVec 19)))
(declare-rel z2 ((_ BitVec 19)))
(declare-var y (_ BitVec 19))
(rule (w #b0000000000000000101))
(rule (=> (not (w y)) (z y)))
(rule (=> (and (z y) (bvult y #b0000000000000000011)) (z2 y)))
(query z2 :print-answer true)
```
z3 stderr: `WARNING: creating large table of size 524288 for relation z2`. g3 stderr is empty. Stdout is identical.

**Fix.** Add the source check to every Go counterpart of `table_base::complement`/`mk_full`:
- `HashTable.Complement`;
- the one-key branch of `SparseTable.ComplementFunctional`;
- `fillTotalTable` when it is called to build a full relation for a predicate (the `instruction_construct.go` and `lazy_sparse_complement.go` callers).

Thread the optional predicate declaration through, because C++ passes `func_decl* p` to `mk_full`; the compiler passes the head predicate of the rule being compiled. Emit the warning when `upper_bound > 1<<18`, before enumerating, through `diagnostic.BorrowProcessWarningService().Warningf("creating large table of size %d for relation %s", ...)`. Leave out the ` for relation <name>` suffix when no predicate is known. The C++ checks only column 0 of a one-key table; a wider total-table fill is not `table_base::complement` and should not warn.

**Regression test.** Add the vector `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/datalog_large_table_warning.smt2` (the input above). The stdout entry in `scriptResults` is `"sat\n(or (= (:var 0) #b0000000000000000000)\n    (= (:var 0) #b0000000000000000001)\n    (= (:var 0) #b0000000000000000010))\n"`. Add a focused test in `pkg/muz/rel/table_test.go`, `TestHashTableComplementWarnsOnLargeDomain`. It should install a buffer via `diagnostic.NewWarningService(&buf)` (or the process service's `SetWarningStream`), complement an empty one-column table with domain `1<<18 + 1`, and expect exactly `WARNING: creating large table of size 262145\n`. A second case with domain `1<<18` must produce no warning.

<a id="muz-rel-05-f4"></a>
#### muz_rel_05-F4: the HashTable-backed `SieveRelation` and `TableRelation.FilterByIntersection` have no production caller, and the sieve display text does not match C++

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/sieve_relation.go` (whole type), `sieve_relation_{estimates,formula,full_columns,interpreted,mixed_delta_union,table_conversion,table_join,table_negation,table_transfer,table_union}.go`; `pkg/muz/rel/table_relation_intersection.go:5-13`, `table_intersection*.go`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_sieve_relation.cpp:92-97` (`sieve_relation::display`), `:616-660` (`mk_filter_by_negation_fn`), `src/muz/rel/dl_relation_manager.cpp:1485-1493` (table `mk_filter_by_intersection_fn`)

**C++ behavior.** `sieve_relation::display` prints `Sieve relation (1,0,1)` (via `print_container`) and then the inner relation's own display. The live sieve logic in C++ is the generic plugin.

**Go behavior.** `grep` finds no non-test caller of `NewSieveRelation`, `AdoptSieveRelation`, `NewFullSieve`, `JoinTableRelation`, `UnionFromTableRelation*`, `TakeSieveRelationFromTable`, etc. outside the `sieve_relation*.go` files themselves. The live sieves are `interval_sieve*.go` and `udoc_sieve*.go`. `SieveRelation.String` prints `Sieve relation [1 0 1]` followed by `fmt.Fprintln(fact)` rows. `TableRelation.FilterByIntersection` is also uncalled.

The Go semantics also differ from the C++ they claim to port. C++ `mk_filter_by_negation_fn` names its flags inversely (`r_col_inner = r_sieved && !sr->is_inner_col(...)`). Because of that, with a sieved target and an ordinary negated table, C++ skips every equality and removes all inner rows when the negated table is nonempty. Go `FilterByTableNegation` instead keeps the target unchanged when a target column is not inner, and otherwise filters on the mapped columns. C++ table-level `mk_filter_by_intersection_fn` calls `mk_filter_by_negation_fn`, so on sparse tables "intersection" actually removes the matching rows; Go implements a real intersection.

**Impact.** No current output changes. The code is a maintenance hazard: anyone who wires it in later gets display text and negation/intersection semantics that do not match z3.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: there is no production caller.

**Fix.** Delete the HashTable `SieveRelation` layer and `TableRelation.FilterByIntersection`/`HashTable.FilterByIntersection` with their tests, following the policy of not porting dead code. If either is kept, make `String` print `Sieve relation (` + comma-separated `0/1` + `)\n` + the inner table display. Also mirror the C++ `mk_filter_by_negation_fn` flag logic exactly; see the Needs verification item about the live sieves.

**Regression test.** If the code is removed, none is needed. If it is kept, add `TestSieveRelationDisplayMatchesPrintContainer` in `pkg/muz/rel/sieve_relation_test.go`. It builds `NewSieveRelation(sig{2,2,2}, []bool{true,false,true})` and expects the text to start with `Sieve relation (1,0,1)\n`.

<a id="muz-rel-06-f1"></a>
#### muz_rel_06-F1: `applyBitVectorEquality` merges into a shared union-find, so equalities leak across the guard

- Severity: critical
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard_compile.go:641-667` (`UDocRelation.applyBitVectorEquality`), with the `classes` parameter threaded through `applyGuard` (419-562), `applyBooleanIff`, `applyConcatEquality` and `applyConcatPartsEquality`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/udoc_relation.cpp:788-795` (`udoc_relation::apply_bv_eq`) and `src/muz/rel/doc.h:300-310` (`union_bvec::merge(m, lo1, lo2, length, discard_cols)`)

**C++ behavior.** A var/var bit-vector equality is applied with a fresh union-find that holds only this equality's bit pairs. The `equalities` argument of `apply_guard` is passed along but never read by `apply_bv_eq`:
```cpp
if (is_var_range(e1, hi1, lo1, v1) && is_var_range(e2, hi2, lo2, v2)) {
    unsigned idx1 = lo1 + column_idx(v1); unsigned idx2 = lo2 + column_idx(v2);
    unsigned length = hi1-lo1+1;
    result.merge(dm, idx1, idx2, length, discard_cols);   // doc.h:
    return true;                                          //  union_find_default_ctx union_ctx;
}                                                         //  subset_ints equalities(union_ctx); ... fresh
```

**Go behavior.** Every var/var equality merges into the one `classes` union-find that `compileGuard` created for the whole guard. That includes equalities applied to temporary universes inside `not`, `or` and Boolean-iff subterms. A later `MergeRange` then also equates bits that an earlier, unrelated (even negated) equality touched:
```go
for i := uint32(0); i < length; i++ {
    classes.Merge(leftIndex+i, rightIndex+i)
}
for i := 0; i < len(r.elems.values); {
    valid, e := r.manager.MergeRange(r.elems.values[i], leftIndex, length, classes, discarded)
```

**Impact.** Any doc-engine rule whose interpreted tail has a var/var BV equality after another var/var equality applies the wrong filter. Under `not`/`or` the result can be the empty set, which is a wrong Datalog answer (unsat instead of sat). The result depends on conjunct order.

**Reproduction.** Confirmed. Input (`t1c.smt2`):
```smt2
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine datalog)
(set-option :fixedpoint.datalog.default_relation doc)
(define-sort B () (_ BitVec 2))
(declare-rel r (B B B))
(declare-rel q (B B B))
(declare-var x B)
(declare-var y B)
(declare-var z B)
(rule (r #b00 #b01 #b01))
(rule (r #b01 #b01 #b01))
(rule (=> (and (r x y z) (not (= x y)) (= y z)) (q x y z)))
(query q :print-answer true)
```
- `$S/bin/g3` prints `unsat`.
- `build/z3` prints `sat` and `(and (= (:var 0) #b00) (= (:var 1) #b01) (= (:var 2) #b01))`.
- With the two conjuncts swapped, both print the z3 answer.

A g3 built from HEAD with only the fix below (via `go build -overlay`, repository untouched) prints the z3 answer for both orders.

**Fix.** In `applyBitVectorEquality`'s var/var branch, build a fresh union-find for this equality only, as `union_bvec::merge(m, lo1, lo2, length, discard_cols)` does:
```go
fresh := backtrack.NewDefaultUnionFind()
for i := 0; i < len(discarded); i++ { fresh.MkVar() }
for i := uint32(0); i < length; i++ { fresh.Merge(leftIndex+i, rightIndex+i) }
... r.manager.MergeRange(r.elems.values[i], leftIndex, length, fresh, discarded)
```
The `classes` parameter of `applyGuard`, `applyBooleanIff`, `applyBitVectorEquality`, `applyConcatEquality` and `applyConcatPartsEquality` is then unused. Either remove it, or keep it only to mirror the C++ signature. `compileGuard` no longer needs to allocate it. `FilterGuardAndProject`'s own `extractRangeEqualities` classes are separate and correct; they mirror `m_equalities` and `m_roots` in `filter_proj_fn`.

**Regression test.** Add `TestUDocGuardEqualitiesDoNotLeakAcrossConjuncts` to `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard_compile_test.go`.
- Setup: use the helpers from `TestUDocCompileAndFilterGuardBitVectorAndBoolean`: `newTestDocManager(t, 6)`, `NewUDocRelation(docManager, []uint32{2,2,2})`, `closeUDoc`, `docASTManager` plus `RegisterBitVectorPlugin`, `m.BitVectorSort(2)`, `m.MkVar`, `m.MkEq`, `m.MkNot`, `m.MkAndArgs`.
- Facts: add `{0,1,1}` and `{1,1,1}`.
- Action: call `FilterGuard` with `(and (not (= v0 v1)) (= v1 v2))`.
- Expected: `requireFact(t, relation, []uint64{0,1,1}, true)` and `requireFact(..., []uint64{1,1,1}, false)`.
- Repeat with the conjuncts swapped; the result must be the same.

SMT-LIB vector: add the input above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/datalog_doc_guard_equality_scope.smt2`. The `scriptResults` entry is `"sat\n(and (= (:var 0) #b00) (= (:var 1) #b01) (= (:var 2) #b01))\n"`. Check it against the C++ with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

<a id="muz-rel-06-f2"></a>
#### muz_rel_06-F2: guard/rest splitting uses a DFS `and`-flattener and order, not `flatten_and` and `extract_equalities`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard.go:62-99` (`udocFlattenAnd`), used by `ExtractGuard` (18-51) and `extractRangeEqualities` (`udoc_guard_compile.go:218-293`)
- C++: `src/ast/ast_util.cpp:254-302` (`flatten_and`), `src/muz/rel/udoc_relation.cpp:646-716` (`extract_guard`, `extract_equalities`)

**C++ behavior.** `flatten_and` is a worklist that changes both the content and the order of the conjuncts:
- An `and` is replaced by its last argument (`result[i] = result.back(); pop_back`) and the other arguments go to the end of the list.
- `(not (not a))` becomes `a`.
- `(not (or ..))` and `(not (=> a b))` are pushed inward.
- `true` is dropped, and any `false` collapses the list to `[false]`.

`extract_equalities` also removes an extracted range equality with `conds[i] = conds.back(); conds.pop_back();` and then increments `i`. The conjunct moved into slot `i` is never examined, so it stays in the "rest". A non-range equality is re-pushed through `conds.push_back(m.mk_eq(e1, e2))`. Both effects change which conjuncts become guard and rest, and the order of `guard` and `m_reduced_condition`.

**Go behavior.** `udocFlattenAnd` collects `and` leaves in left-to-right DFS order. It does no negation pushing, no `true`/`false` folding, no swap-with-back reordering and no skip quirk. `extractRangeEqualities` additionally treats finite-domain vars as ranges (through `udocProjectEqualityRange`) but not Bool vars. In C++, `is_var_range` accepts any var, so a Bool var/var equality becomes a column merge there.

**Impact.** The guards are conjoined and compiled in a different order. Some conjuncts land on the other side of the guard/rest split, which changes discard-column merging in `filter_proj_fn`. The resulting DOC union has a different shape, so the order of the printed answer disjuncts can differ. `(not (or g r))` with a guard `g` and a non-guard `r` is split by C++ but not by Go.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted in isolation. Answer-order differences on doc programs were observed (for example `(rule (=> (and (r x y) (not (= x y))) (q x y)))`), but they could not be attributed to this function alone; see Needs verification.

**Fix.**
1. Replace `udocFlattenAnd` with the Go port of `flatten_and` (`ast_util`), including its in-place swap-with-back order and its rewrite cases. Check whether `pkg/ast` already exports one before writing a new one.
2. Make `extractRangeEqualities` iterate the `conds` slice with the same swap-pop-and-advance quirk, and re-append residual equalities through `MkEq`.
3. Use the C++ `is_var_range` acceptance: any var, with width `num_sort_bits` (Bool counts as 1 bit).

**Regression test.** Extend `TestUDocGuardSourceExpressionMatrix` in `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard_compile_test.go`:
- Feed `ExtractGuard` the condition `(and A (and B C))`, where A and C are guards and B is not. The expected guard is `(and A C)` in the order `flatten_and` produces it; derive the expected order from the C++ algorithm.
- Feed it `(not (or g r))` and expect guard `(not g)` and rest `(not r)`.

<a id="muz-rel-06-f3"></a>
#### muz_rel_06-F3: `applyGuard`'s `not`/`or`/iff branches skip `simplify` and use a raw `not`

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard_compile.go:492-527, 580-588` (`applyGuard` `ASTOpNot`/`ASTOpOr`, `applyBooleanIff`)
- C++: `src/muz/rel/udoc_relation.cpp:819-887` (`udoc_relation::apply_guard`)

**C++ behavior.** The general `not` branch does `result.subtract(dm, sub); result.simplify(dm);`. The `or` and Boolean `=`/iff branches negate through `ast_util::mk_not(m, e)`, which strips a leading `not` and folds `true`/`false`. The `not (= var ground)` case is a dedicated single-doc subtract.

**Go behavior.** There is no `Simplify()` after the `not` subtract. Negation uses `m.MkNot(arg)` (`ast_core_boolean_factories.go:19`, a raw node), so `(or (not a) ..)` produces `(not (not a))`. That term is evaluated through two nested temporary universes, where C++ applies `a` directly.

**Impact.** The set of tuples is the same, but the DOC representation differs, so later operations and the printed answer can show different disjunct shapes or order. The difference is observable only in answer formatting.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted in isolation. Adding `Simplify` alone did not change the observed ordering difference noted under Needs verification.

**Fix.**
- After `r.elems.Subtract(temporary.elems)` in the `ASTOpNot` case, call `r.elems.Simplify()`.
- In the `ASTOpOr` case and in `applyBooleanIff`, replace `m.MkNot` with `m.MkNotSimplified`, which is `ast_util` `mk_not`.

**Regression test.** Add a case to `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard_compile_test.go` that compiles `(or (not b) (= x #b01))` with `CompileGuard`. Compare `compiled.String()` against the doc shape the C++ produces; run the same input through `src` with a `doc` TRACE to capture the expected text.

<a id="muz-rel-06-f4"></a>
#### muz_rel_06-F4: projected UDoc results use push instead of `udoc::insert`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Go:
  - `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_guard_compile.go:119` (`FilterGuardAndProject` → `UDocRelation.Project`, `udoc_relation.go:255-287`, which appends)
  - `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_relation_filter.go:122-139` (`UDocRelation.FilterByNegation` slow path: `Join`, then `Project`, then `Subtract`)
- C++:
  - `src/muz/rel/udoc_relation.cpp:1238-1243` (`filter_proj_fn::operator()`)
  - `1013-1031` (`join_project_fn::join`)
  - `1170-1178` (`negation_filter_fn::slow_pass`)

**C++ behavior.** `filter_proj_fn` does `doc* d = dm.project(dm2, m_to_delete, m_udoc2[i]); r->get_udoc().insert(dm2, d);`. `insert` drops docs that are subsumed and removes docs that the new one subsumes. The negation slow pass calls `m_join_project(t, n)`, which also inserts each projected doc with `res.insert(dm_res, dm_prod.project(...))`, and then subtracts.

**Go behavior.** `FilterGuardAndProject` returns `filtered.Project(...)`, which appends every projected doc (the C++ `project_fn` behavior, not `filter_proj_fn`'s). The negation slow path inserts in the joined bit space (`Join` uses `InsertOwned`) and then appends after projection. Duplicate and subsumed projected docs are therefore kept, while C++ removes them.

**Impact.** The tuple set is the same, but the relation can hold redundant docs. Later operations (union delta, subtract, negation subtraction) then work on a different DOC union, which can change answer order and size estimates, and it costs extra work on projections that produce many duplicates.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: union into the head relation re-inserts, which hides the effect in most simple programs.

**Fix.**
- In `FilterGuardAndProject`, replace `filtered.Project(removed, destination)` with a loop that projects each doc and calls `result.elems.InsertOwned(projected)`.
- In `UDocRelation.FilterByNegation`'s slow path, call `r.JoinProject(negative, targetColumns, negativeColumns, removed, productManager, r.manager)`; `JoinProject` already inserts per projected doc like `join_project_fn::join`. Note that `negation_filter_fn` constructs `join_project_fn` directly, so the `join_project_and_fn` shortcut must not be taken here. Add a flag to `JoinProject`, or factor out its general loop.

**Regression test.** Add `TestUDocFilterGuardAndProjectInsertsSubsumed` to `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_relation_typed_filter_project_test.go`.
- Setup: build a 2-column relation of width 2 with facts `{0,1}` and `{0,2}`.
- Action: call `FilterGuardAndProject(m, true, []uint32{1}, dest)`.
- Expected: `NumRecords() == 1`; the current code gives 2.
- Add a matching test for `FilterByNegation` with a partial-column negative relation.

<a id="muz-rel-06-f5"></a>
#### muz_rel_06-F5: `UDocSieve.FilterByNegation` does not follow C++ `sieve_relation_plugin::mk_filter_by_negation_fn`

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high (that it diverges); medium (how often it is reached)
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_sieve_negation.go:8-31`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/dl_sieve_relation.cpp:620-648`

**C++ behavior.** The flags are misnamed in the C++: `r_col_inner` is true when the r column is *not* inner.
```cpp
bool r_col_inner = r_sieved && !sr->is_inner_col(r_cols[i]);
bool neg_col_inner = neg_sieved && !sneg->is_inner_col(neg_cols[i]);
if(r_col_inner && neg_col_inner) { ir_cols.push_back(r_sieved ? sr->get_inner_col(i) : i); ... }
else if(!r_col_inner && neg_col_inner) { return alloc(identity_relation_intersection_filter_fn); }
else { continue; }
```
As written, this means:
- both columns inner: the equality is skipped;
- r inner and neg full: identity;
- r full and neg inner: skipped;
- both full: a pair indexed by the loop counter `i` is pushed.

**Go behavior.** Go implements the intent described in the C++ comments instead:
- r full and neg inner: identity;
- both inner: join on the inner columns;
- otherwise: skipped.

Nothing documents this as a deliberate fork fix: it is not in `z3_bug_exclusions.txt` or `FORK_BUGFIXES.md`. The comment in the code describes it as "source" behavior.

**Impact.** This is reached from `RelationExplanationProduct.FilterByNegation` (`relation_explanation_product_negation.go:44`), that is, Datalog with `generate_explanations` over doc relations and negated tails. When both join columns are inner (the normal case), C++ filters on zero columns. `negation_filter_fn::slow_pass` then subtracts every target doc whenever the negative relation is nonempty, while Go removes only the matching rows. The answers differ.

**Reproduction.** Not confirmed. The SMT-LIB front end only accepts `(query <pred>)`, and on that path `generate_explanations` is not applied. The `(query q)` variant (`t4.smt2`) ends with a Go `unsupported doc Datalog fragment` error (already recorded under muz_fp).

**Fix.** Either port the C++ literally (same three branches with the same inverted flag meaning, including `get_inner_col(i)`), or record this as a z3-bug fork fix following the fork-fix workflow: an exclusion entry, a test vector, a red C++ test, the `src/` fix, and a `FORK_BUGFIXES.md` entry. Apply the same decision to `SieveRelation.FilterByTableNegation` and `FilterTableByNegation` (`sieve_relation_table_negation.go`), which implement yet another variant.

**Regression test.** Add `TestUDocSieveNegationColumnClassification` to a new file `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_sieve_negation_test.go`. Build the sieves with `NewEmptyUDocSieve` / `AdoptUDocSieve` (see the existing `udoc_sieve*_test.go` helpers) over sorts `(BV2, Bool)`, so the mask is `[true,false]`. Assert, for each column-classification case, the post-state the chosen semantics specifies:
- target `{00},{01}` against negative `{01}`, joined on column 0 (both inner);
- inner target column against full negative column;
- full target column against inner negative column.

<a id="muz-rel-06-f6"></a>
#### muz_rel_06-F6: `JoinProject` takes the intersection shortcut in fewer cases than C++ (documented, but changes behavior)

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Go: `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_relation_join_project.go:61-82`
- C++: `src/muz/rel/udoc_relation.cpp:1052-1068` (`udoc_plugin::mk_join_project_fn`)

**C++ behavior.** C++ uses `join_project_and_fn` (clone plus intersect) whenever `joined==removed`, both signature sizes equal `joined`, and for every `i` `removed_cols[i]==i && cols1[i]==cols2[i]`. Repeated join columns are not checked.

**Go behavior.** Go also requires distinct coverage of all `t1` columns, and that all three managers are the same. The comment says: "Require complete distinct coverage as well: its syntactic check accepts repeated join columns even though the intersection shortcut is then unsound."

**Impact.** With repeated join columns (for example `cols1=cols2=[0,0]` on binary relations), C++ returns the intersection and Go returns the real join-project. The answers differ from z3. This is a deliberate fix of a z3 bug that is not recorded as one.

**Reproduction.** Not attempted: the rule compiler seldom emits duplicate join-column pairs.

**Fix.** Either drop the extra `covered` check to match C++, or record it as a fork fix (exclusion entry, vector, `src/` fix, `FORK_BUGFIXES.md`).

**Regression test.** Add `TestUDocJoinProjectRepeatedColumns` to `pkg/muz/rel/udoc_relation_test.go`. Join `{(0,1)}` with `{(0,2)}` using `cols [0,0]/[0,0]` and `removed [0,1]`, and assert whichever result the chosen policy specifies.

### Area: Rule transforms (`pkg/muz/transforms`)

*muz_transforms_01.* This shard holds the muz rule transformers: array blast, array-eq rewrite, array instantiation, backwards, bit blast, the interp-tail simplifier with its Boolean normalizer, cone of influence, filter rules, Karr invariants with loop counter, magic sets, symbolic magic, quantifier abstraction, quantifier instantiation, and coalesce. Most files follow the C++ closely, statement by statement. Three divergences were confirmed against `build/z3`, all of them ordering problems: - The Boolean normalizer does not re-sort after it detects an equivalence (BR_REWRITE1). - Array instantiation walks equivalence classes in insertion order. - The cone-of-influence model converter is built in insertion order instead of `func_decl_set` order. Two more coalesce divergences were found by reading only: group order, and `bool_rewriter` and/or simplification. There are also three low-severity proof and estimate gaps. Counts: 0 critical, 0 high, 5 medium, 3 low.

*muz_transforms_02.* This shard holds the Datalog rule transformers: the rule inliner (eager, oriented-eager and linear), the rule unifier, slicing and its proof converter, unfold, scale, separate-negated-tails, simple joins, the subsumption checker and the unbound compressor. Unfold, scale and separate-negated-tails follow the C++ closely. The inliner, slice and subsumption code is mostly faithful but has a few concrete divergences. Simple joins and the unbound compressor are re-engineered rather than ported line by line, and the slice proof converter goes well beyond the C++ (this is recorded as a deviation). Findings by severity: 1 high (confirmed), 4 medium (1 confirmed), 2 low.

<a id="muz-transforms-01-f1"></a>
#### muz_transforms_01-F1: Boolean normalizer skips the BR_REWRITE1 re-reduction after an equivalence is detected

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/transforms/boolean_normalizer.go:386-465` (`booleanNormalizer.normalize`)
- C++: `src/muz/transforms/dl_mk_interp_tail_simplifier.cpp:334-361` (`normalizer_cfg::reduce_app`)

**C++ behavior.** After it sorts, removes duplicates and detects equivalences, `reduce_app` returns `BR_REWRITE1` whenever `detect_equivalences` replaced a pair:
```cpp
have_rewritten_args = detect_equivalences(m_app_args, m.is_or(f));
...
if (have_rewritten_args) {
    return BR_REWRITE1;
}
```
`rewriter_tpl` then visits the result at depth 1 (`rewriter_def.h:306-315`). That calls `reduce_app` again on the new `and`/`or`, so the argument list is sorted again (the new `(= a (not b))` term moves to its sorted position), duplicates are removed again, and equivalences are detected again. This repeats until it returns `BR_DONE`.

**Go behavior.** The Go code writes the equivalence into the slot of the earlier pair and stops there. The result is never reduced a second time:
```go
if found {
    resultArguments[priorIndex] = equivalence
    havePair = false
    continue
}
...
result, err = n.manager.MkAndArgs(arguments)   // no second sort/dedupe/detect pass
```

**Impact.** Any rule whose interpreted tail has a pair of complementary binary clauses (`(or a b)`, `(or (not a) (not b))`) next to other conjuncts gets its tail conjuncts in a different order from z3. Equivalences that only appear after the first replacement are also missed. The interp-tail simplifier runs in every Spacer/PDR/Datalog preprocessing pipeline (priorities 40000, 34980, 34950, and inside the inliner, bit-blast and array-blast plugins), so the different tail order reaches every later transform and the solver's search.

**Reproduction.** `work/muz_transforms_01/its1.smt2` (the array-instantiation dump prints the simplified rules):
```smt2
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine spacer)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.instantiate_arrays true)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.inline_linear false)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.inline_eager false)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.slice false)
(declare-rel p (Int Int Int Int))
(declare-rel q ())
(declare-var x Int)
(declare-var y Int)
(declare-var z Int)
(declare-var w Int)
(rule (p 0 0 0 0))
(rule (=> (and (p x y z w) (not (or (= (> y 0) (> z 0)) (> x 0) (and (> w 0) (> x 1))))) q))
(rule (=> (and (p x y z w) (or (> x 0) (> y 0)) (or (not (> x 0)) (not (> y 0))) (= (> w 0) (> z 0)) (> z 3)) q))
(query q)
```
`build/z3` prints the second `q` rule as:
```
q() :- 
 p(#3,#2,#0,#1),
 (= (<= (:var 2) 0) (not (<= (:var 3) 0))),
 (= (<= (:var 1) 0) (<= (:var 0) 0)),
 (not (<= (:var 0) 3)).
```
`bin/g3` prints the two equalities in the opposite order:
```
 (= (<= (:var 1) 0) (<= (:var 0) 0)),
 (= (<= (:var 2) 0) (not (<= (:var 3) 0))),
```
Both binaries then print `unsat`. The same swap shows up in the "Output rules" dump.

**Fix.**
1. Split the and/or branch of `normalize` (lines 386-465) into a helper, `reduceAndOr(op int32, args []ast.ASTHandle) (result ast.ASTHandle, rewritten bool, err error)`. It should do the sort, `remove_duplicates`, `detect_equivalences` and construction exactly as now. `rewritten` must be `len(resultArguments) != len(arguments)`, which is the C++ `read_idx != write_idx`.
2. In `normalize`, loop on that result: while `rewritten` is true and the result is still an `and`/`or` application of the basic family, call `reduceAndOr` again on the result's own arguments. Do not re-normalize the children; a depth-1 revisit does not rewrite them. If the result is not an and/or (for example a single surviving argument), a C++ `reduce_app` on it returns `BR_FAILED`, so stop.
3. Keep `n.keep` on every intermediate result, and memoize only the final result for `expression`.

**Regression test.** Add `TestInterpTailSimplifierResortsAfterEquivalence` to `pkg/muz/transforms/interp_tail_simplifier_test.go`. Use `newInterpTailFixture` and `f.predicate` as `TestInterpTailSimplifierRecognizesPairedClauseEquivalence` does. Build a rule with Int vars 0..3 and the tails `(or (> v3 0) (> v2 0))`, `(or (not (> v3 0)) (not (> v2 0)))`, `(= (> v1 0) (> v0 0))` and `(> v0 3)`. Apply the plugin through `base.NewRuleTransformer()`, then check the order of interpreted tails: the derived equality `(= (<= v2 0) (not (<= v3 0)))` must come before `(= (<= v1 0) (<= v0 0))`. Get the exact order from `build/z3`. Also add the SMT-LIB vector above as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/interp_tail_equiv_resort.smt2`. Its `scriptResults` entry must be the complete `build/z3` stdout (both rule dumps and `unsat`). Check it with `G3_CPP_REFERENCE=<repo>/build/z3 go test -run TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference ./cmd/g3`.

<a id="muz-transforms-01-f2"></a>
#### muz_transforms_01-F2: array instantiation `retrieve_all_selects` walks equivalence classes in insertion order, not the union-find `next` cycle from the array

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/transforms/array_instantiation.go:126-144, 222-277` (`representative`, `merge`, `linkedSelects`)
- C++: `src/muz/transforms/dl_mk_array_instantiation.cpp:243-268` (`retrieve_all_selects`), `src/ast/factor_equivs.h:69-119` (`obj_equiv_class`), `src/util/union_find.h:178-233` (`basic_union_find`)

**C++ behavior.** `eq_classes` is an `expr_equiv_class`, which wraps `basic_union_find`. `merge` links roots by size and swaps the `m_next` pointers. `retrieve_all_selects(array)` starts at `array`'s own id and follows `m_next` around the circular list:
```cpp
for(expr_equiv_class::iterator it = eq_classes.begin(array);
    it != eq_classes.end(array); ++it) {
  ... select_ops = selects[*it]; ... all_selects.push_back(rewrite_select(array, select_ops[i]));
```
The order therefore depends on which array is asked about and on the merge history.

**Go behavior.** The Go code uses its own parent map and walks `p.equivalenceOrder`, the order in which members were first seen, keeping those with the same root:
```go
root := p.representative(array)
for _, member := range p.equivalenceOrder {
    if p.representative(member) != root { continue }
    for _, source := range p.selects[member] { ... }
```
`createHead` also calls `p.representative(argument)`, which C++ never does (it only touches `selects`). That changes the Go membership order further.

**Impact.** With `xform.instantiate_arrays=true`, a predicate whose array argument is in a class with two or more members gets its `p!inst` instances, and the matching `(= var select)` equalities, in a different order. This changes the rule z3 prints to stdout and the rule handed to Spacer.

**Reproduction.** `work/muz_transforms_01/ai2.smt2`:
```smt2
(set-option :fixedpoint.engine spacer)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.instantiate_arrays true)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.inline_linear false)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.inline_eager false)
(set-option :fixedpoint.xform.slice false)
(declare-rel p ((Array Int Int)))
(declare-rel q ())
(declare-var a (Array Int Int))
(declare-var i Int)
(declare-var j Int)
(declare-var k Int)
(rule (=> (= (select a 0) 0) (p a)))
(rule (=> (and (p a) (p (store a i 1)) (> (select a j) 0) (> (select (store a i 1) k) 5)) q))
(query q)
```
In the output rules, z3 prints `p!inst(#5,#2,#3), p!inst(#6,#2,#0)` followed by `(= (:var 6) (select (:var 2) (:var 0))), (= (:var 5) (select (:var 2) (:var 3)))`. g3 prints `p!inst(#5,#2,#0), p!inst(#6,#2,#3)` followed by `(= (:var 5) (select (:var 2) (:var 0))), (= (:var 6) (select (:var 2) (:var 3)))`. Both answer `sat`. In the C++, the class built by `merge(store,a)` and then `merge(v4,store)` cycles `a -> v4 -> store`, so the select on `a` (index `#3`) comes before the select on `store` (index `#0`).

**Fix.**
1. Replace `equivalence` and `equivalenceOrder` with the existing `arrayEqClasses` type from `array_eq_rewrite.go`, a faithful `basic_union_find` with `obj_equiv_class`. Give it a method that iterates one class starting at a given object id along `next` (the C++ `begin(o)`/`end(o)`). It must call `addIfNotThere` first, as `begin(o)` does.
2. In `retrieveSelects`, use `classes.merge(expression, base)` for stores and `classes.merge(left, right)` for array equalities. Drop the `p.representative(array)` call on selects; C++ only does `selects.insert_if_not_there`.
3. In `createHead`, remove `p.representative(argument)`.
4. In `linkedSelects`, iterate the class of `array` from `array`'s id and concatenate `p.selects[member]` in that order.
5. Reset the classes per rule, as `eq_classes.reset()` does.

**Regression test.** Extend `pkg/muz/transforms/array_instantiation_test.go` with `TestArrayInstantiationFollowsEquivalenceCycleOrder`. Follow the fixture in `TestArrayInstantiationExpandsPredicateCellsAndIndices`, with `SetOutput(&bytes.Buffer{})` and `SetRuleMaker`. Build the `q` rule above in its normalized form, `q() :- p(#2), p(#4), (not (<= (select (store #2 #1 1) #0) 5)), (not (<= (select #2 #3) 0)), (= #4 (store #2 #1 1))`, then assert that the first two `p!inst` tails have third arguments `#3` and `#0`, in that order. Add `ai2.smt2` as `pkg/cmd/g3/test_vectors/array_inst_eqclass_order.smt2`. Its `scriptResults` entry is the full `build/z3` stdout, and `TestSMTLibRunnerCPPReference` checks it against the C++.

<a id="muz-transforms-01-f3"></a>
#### muz_transforms_01-F3: cone-of-influence model-converter entries are in rule order, not `func_decl_set`/`obj_map` hash order

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: confirmed
- Go: `pkg/muz/transforms/coi.go:148-199` (`topDownCone`, `prunedOrder`), `pkg/muz/transforms/coi.go:357-383` (`bottomUpCone`, `declarationOrder`)
- C++: `src/muz/transforms/dl_mk_coi_filter.cpp:120-158` (`mk_coi_filter::top_down`), `:102-114` (`bottom_up`)
